study.format: advice / tips explainer with a comedy gimmick: the whole script is in broken 'caveman' English, and every line is proven with a screenshot from the creator's own viral video
study.topic: A creator explains in caveman-speak that a viral video has three parts (hook, buildup, payoff), proves each with his 19.3M-view Bugatti video and its analytics, then tells you to double down and post more.
study.hook: The first words start at 0.00s: "You want viral video." (0.00–1.08, 4 words in ~1.1s, punchy and deliberately broken). In the first 2 seconds the frame is a medium-wide selfie shot from about chest up, with ceiling vent and crown molding visible above him. He holds an index finger up, a wireless mic sits in his other hand, and a backwards black cap reads as casual. A two-line white title, "How to go viral for caveman.", sits at the top (~10–16% of frame height) from frame one. By 0.56s, on the word "viral", an Instagram analytics card slams in under the title: 19,329,610 views, 7,236,931 accounts reached, 12s average watch time, 21,229 follows. It stops the scroll for three reasons: the caveman phrasing is odd and funny, it promises the thing every creator wants (viral), and proof (19M views) arrives within half a second, so the viewer trusts him before he has said anything of substance.

beats.what: "You want viral video. Viral video, good." Caveman title on screen plus a 19.3M-view analytics card at 0.56s.
"I have viral video. How do that?" A row of three of his videos (19.3M, 16.4M, 16M) pops in as credibility.
"Viral video, three part." He holds up three fingers on a wide shot; the title and overlays clear for a clean reset.
"Hook, buildup, payoff." Bugatti clips stack in one per word (1, then 2, then 3 thumbnails) so the three parts are shown visually.
"Hook, present question to viewer." The Bugatti hook clip ('Some idiot backed into my Bugatti') shows at the top.
"Viewer wants answers, so viewer watch buildup." A crop of the hook text with a 😱 emoji, then the buildup clip.
"Watch time, good." An 'Average watch time 19s' card appears.
"Buildup tells story. Story make viewer engaged." Buildup clip, then a '*WATCHES*' crying-headphones meme on 'story'.
"Story lead into payoff." The buildup still sits top-left and the payoff still ('trick' with the Bugatti door open) slides in beside it on 'payoff'.
"Payoff, answer viewer question." The payoff still appears with a 🤔 emoji.
"Viewer feel emotion." An 'ABSOLUTE CINEMA' meme.
Rapid list: "Viewer like. Viewer comment. Viewer share." A matching stat card per word: heart 1.3M, comment 9,040, share 155K.
"Video go viral. Viewer watch whole video. Video go viral." The 19,329,610 views card alternates with a retention graph (48% at 0:21).
"When video go viral, you double down. Post more. More chances." A clean frame on 'double down', then a grid of his posts on 'post more'.
"How I learn more. Follow me." His Instagram profile card (29.1K followers) appears.
"Why me? Best marketer in world." A cocky caveman punchline. It ends 0.44s after the last word, and 'world' flows back into 'You want viral video'.

study.jump_cuts: Extremely tight. Speech covers 99% of the runtime, the median gap between words is 0.00s, and there are no fillers. Only 3 gaps reach 0.3s or more: 0.38s after 'payoff' (6.92s), 0.36s after 'engaged' (15.68s) and 0.40s after 'More chances' (30.56s), the longest. Those small breaths are kept between ideas. There are 25 shots, 6.86 cuts per 10s, a median shot of 1.33s, a longest of 1.93s and a shortest of 0.87s. Almost every caveman sentence is its own shot. Cuts land at sentence boundaries, usually within 0.05–0.1s of the next sentence's first word: 1.23 before 'Viral' at 1.26, 7.33 on 'Hook' at 7.30, 9.2 on 'Viewer' at 9.16, 11.77 on 'Watch' at 11.72, 17.77 on 'Payoff' at 17.74, 33.27 on 'Best' at 33.18. A few fall mid-sentence: 4.27 just after 'Viral', 10.33 before 'so', 28.13 between 'you' and 'double down'. The two-to-four-word sentences make each cut feel like a new thought rather than a chop, and the pace feels relentless but readable.
study.zooms_punch_ins: There are no animated zooms; the framing changes come from cuts. Shots alternate between a wide framing, where head and cap sit lower with the ceiling vent and crown molding visible (0–1.2s, 4.27–5.57s, 28.13–29.17s, 30.87–31.73s), and tighter framings at roughly 1.1–1.25x, where the head fills more of the frame and the vent drops out (2.33–4.27s, 5.57–7.33s, most of 7–28s). The clearest punch-in-then-pull-out is 2.33 (tight, on 'I have viral video') then 4.27 (wide, on 'three part' with three fingers up). The reset to wide at 28.13 lands on 'double down'. Some of the scale change probably comes from him leaning toward and away from the phone, not a digital crop. Overall something visual changes every ~1–1.4s: a cut, a new overlay, or both, since nearly every cut also swaps the top overlay.
study.captions: Word-by-word captions, exactly one word on screen at a time and synced to each word's timing. Lowercase with punctuation removed ('viral', 'good', 'hook', 'payoff'). White, medium-bold rounded sans-serif (TikTok Classic style) with a soft dark shadow and no box. Small to medium size, about 7–8% of frame width per short word. Placed center-screen at ~67–68% of frame height, over his chest. No color highlighting, no emphasis words, no animation beyond a hard swap per word.
study.on_screen_text: Only one title: "How to go viral for caveman." White bold sans-serif with a thin black outline/shadow, two lines, centered at the top (~10–16% of frame height). It is visible from 0.00s until the cut at 4.27s (~4.3s), then removed so the overlays own the top of the frame. All other text lives inside screenshots: analytics labels and numbers, video titles like 'Some idiot backed into my Bugatti', and the 'ABSOLUTE CINEMA' and '*WATCHES*' meme text.
study.graphics_overlays:
Screenshot and meme overlays sit in the top third of the frame, above his head, and change on nearly every cut, each literally illustrating the word being said:
- 0.56–4.27: an IG insights card on dark rounded panels (views 19,329,610, reach, 12s avg watch, follows).
- 2.33–4.27: three portrait thumbnails of his videos with view counts (19.3M, 16.4M, 16M).
- 5.57–7.33: Bugatti video frames that build 1, then 2, then 3 across in sync with 'hook, buildup, payoff'.
- 7.33–9.2: the single hook clip.
- 9.2–10.33: a wide crop of the hook title plus a 😱 emoji to the right.
- 10.33–11.77: the buildup clip.
- 11.77–12.77: an 'Average watch time 19s' card.
- 12.77–14.07: the Bugatti clip.
- 14.07–15.93: the '*WATCHES*' crying-headphones meme.
- 15.93–17.77: a small top-left buildup still, joined by the payoff still ('trick') on 'payoff'.
- 17.77–19.47: the payoff still with a 🤔 emoji left.
- 19.47–20.8: 'ABSOLUTE CINEMA' meme.
- 20.8–23.4: a heart 1.3M tile, swapping in-shot to comment 9,040 at ~21.5 and then share 155K at 22.53.
- 23.4: views 19,329,610.
- 24.43: a retention curve (48% at 0:21).
- 25.97–28.13: views card again.
- 28.13–29.17: clean, no overlay.
- 29.17–30.87: a 3x3 grid of his posts.
- 30.87–31.73: clean.
- 31.73–35.0: his IG profile card (Robert McKeaveney, 19 posts, 29.1K followers).
Overlays hard-pop on and off with the cuts, with no visible slide or scale animation, and are sized about 40–65% of frame width.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only (jump cuts between takes). No whips, flashes or zoom transitions. The visual energy comes from overlay swaps that coincide with the cuts.
study.broll_and_interrupts: There is no full-screen b-roll; the speaker is always on screen. Pattern interrupts are the picture-in-picture screenshots and meme images, which change about every 1–1.9s (roughly 20 distinct overlay states in 35s). Emojis add extra beats at 9.2 (😱) and 17.77 (🤔). Meme cutaways at 14.07 and 19.47 add humor mid-explanation. Deliberate clean frames with no overlay at 4.27, 28.13 and 30.87 act as resets before new sections. Hand gestures act as props: one finger up for points, three fingers at 4.98 on 'three'. The handheld mic is visible throughout. No sound effects can be confirmed; the audio hits (e.g. 3.78, 5.47, 7.64, 9.74, 11.91, 12.81) line up with stressed words rather than cuts, so they are most likely voice emphasis, not SFX.
study.audio: Close, clean voice from the handheld wireless lav/mic, with a little room tone from the small room. Delivery is deadpan, clipped caveman cadence at 2.69 words/s: slow per word but with no dead air, so it feels fast. No clear music bed is evident and no identifiable sound effects. Silence is never used for effect; the longest pause is 0.40s.
study.length_and_ending: 35.0s, 93 words. The build is cumulative: hook, then buildup, then payoff, each defined and then 'proven' with a screenshot. It escalates into the like, comment, share, views stat run at 20.8–26.8s, where the framework payoff lands ('Video go viral' at 23.38s, ~67%, repeated at 25.96s, ~74%). A short bonus point follows: 'double down, post more, more chances' at 27–30.6s. The CTA 'How I learn more. Follow me.' runs 30.96–32.32s (~88–92%), backed by the profile card, then a comedic flex: 'Why me? Best marketer in world.' (33.18–34.56). It cuts 0.44s after the last word, and the ending loops cleanly into the opening line 'You want viral video'.
study.quality: 720x1280 at 30fps, HEVC at ~14.5 Mbps. Front-camera selfie at arm's length. Eye line is near the lens, with his eyes at roughly 35–40% of frame height and generous headroom; the top third is deliberately left empty for overlays. Warm, dim indoor lamp light, slightly underexposed, with a plain beige wall, crown molding, a ceiling vent and a framed picture behind. He holds the mic visibly in frame. Sharp enough, with a slightly soft phone look. It is casual on purpose (bedroom, cap, tee, handheld mic), while the edit is high-effort: a matched screenshot on nearly every sentence. That contrast reads as an authentic, proven creator.
study.why_viral: 1) The caveman gimmick makes a well-worn lesson (hook, buildup, payoff) funny, instantly understandable and quotable, and the broken grammar forces tiny, punchy sentences that suit 1.3s shots. 2) Proof stacked on every line: real analytics (19.3M views, 1.3M likes, 155K shares, retention graph) appear the moment each claim is made, so it is credible and screenshot-worthy for other creators. 3) Relentless visual change, with a cut or new overlay every ~1–1.4s and memes for comic relief, plus a 3-part promise that viewers wait out. 4) A cocky closing punchline that loops into the first line, which drives rewatches, comments and follows from aspiring creators.
lessons: Put a proof element on screen within the first 0.6s (a stats card, view count or result) on the exact word that makes the claim.
Script or cut talking footage into 2–5-word sentences and give each sentence its own shot; aim for a median shot of ~1.3s and nothing over ~2s for explainer content.
Cut 0.03–0.1s before the first word of each sentence, and keep only ~0.35–0.4s pauses between sections; everything else can sit at near-zero gaps.
Reserve the top third of the frame for overlays and swap the overlay on the same frame as the cut, so every cut brings a new visual idea.
Make each overlay literally illustrate the spoken word: say 'like', show the like count; say 'watch time', show the watch-time stat.
Build lists visually: when the speaker says 'three parts', add one thumbnail per part as each is named (1 → 2 → 3).
Drop in a meme or emoji every ~5s for comic relief (here at 9.2s, 14.1s, 17.8s and 19.5s) so dense information doesn't get heavy.
Use occasional clean frames with no overlays, and a wider framing, to signal a new section (here at 4.27s, 28.13s and 30.87s).
Alternate framing between wide and ~1.1–1.25x tighter across cuts to hide jump cuts and add rhythm.
Use single-word, lowercase, white captions at ~67% of frame height, kept off the face and away from the overlay zone.
End within ~0.5s of the last word, on a punchline that flows back into the opening line to encourage loops.
creator_advice: Viral video, three part: hook, buildup, payoff.
Hook, present question to viewer.
Viewer wants answers, so viewer watch buildup. Watch time, good.
Buildup tells story. Story make viewer engaged. Story lead into payoff.
Payoff, answer viewer question. Viewer feel emotion. Viewer like. Viewer comment. Viewer share. Video go viral.
Viewer watch whole video. Video go viral.
When video go viral, you double down. Post more. More chances.

study.format: explainer / how-to tutorial (talking head plus screen-recording demo)
study.topic: How to open Instagram's hidden 'Your algorithm' page, see what it thinks you like, and add or remove topics to steer your feed.
study.hook: "Did you know you can see your own Instagram algorithm?" starts at 0.00s with no lead-in. That is 10 words in 2.12s (~4.7 words/s). A second hook follows straight away: "And you can actually change it." (2.38–3.66). In the first 2s: a close handheld selfie at roughly chest-up, face in the center. The creator jabs a finger at the lens on 'Did you know' (0.15s frame), holding a small black device in his hand (probably a mic transmitter). A two-line hook title, 'HOW TO SEE YOUR INSTAGRAM ALGORITHM', sits in bold white uppercase with a dark shadow at about 17–28% of frame height, ending in a small Instagram glyph. It stays until about 2.4s and is gone by 2.80. Captions start with 'DID YOU KNOW', with 'YOU' in yellow. It stops the scroll because it promises a secret, personal thing everyone on the app is curious about ('your own algorithm'). The title restates it for silent viewers, and the 'you can change it' escalation plus 'literally nobody knows about' (3.80) raise the stakes before any instructions begin.

beats.what: "Did you know you can see your own Instagram algorithm?" Finger point to the lens, title card on screen.
Second hook escalates from 'see' to 'change': "And you can actually change it." The title card drops off here.
Exclusivity claim right after a jump cut at 3.87: "This is something literally nobody knows about."
Step 1, "All you need to do is navigate to your profile." Cuts to a screen recording at 6.6 mid-sentence, on 'navigate'.
Step 2, "click the three lines in the top right corner." The screen recording is punched in about 2x on the hamburger icon.
Step 3, "type in your algorithm, and it'll come right up." A Settings and activity screen; search typing 'your' surfaces 'Your algorithm'.

The reveal: "Then when you click on it, it'll show how your activity on Instagram has impacted your algorithm." The 'Your algorithm' page loads at about 13s with the AI summary 'Lately you've been into…' and topic chips.
Bonus feature: "You can also add topics to what you wanna see more…" Brief cut back to his face (17.13–17.8), then back to the dimmed 'Add a new interest' keyboard screen.
"…and remove topics from what you wanna see less." Screen shows the 'What you want to see less of…' input.
Back to his face for the closing instruction: "Use this to dictate your feed and see what you wanna see." Ends 0.2s after the last word.

study.jump_cuts: Extremely tight. Speech covers 99% of runtime, the median gap between words is 0.0s, and there are no fillers. Only one gap reaches 0.3s (after 'corner,' at 9.46), and it is covered by the cut to the settings screen at 9.7. Between-sentence pauses are 0.14–0.3s (2.12→2.38, 3.66→3.80, 5.64→5.88, 16.74→16.94, 21.68→21.96), so breaths were trimmed but not fully removed. 8 cuts in 24.9s is 3.21 cuts per 10s; median shot 2.0s, longest 7.43s (the continuous screen-recording demo, 9.7–17.13). The face jump cuts sit between thoughts: 3.87 right as 'This' begins, 5.87 between 'about.' and 'All'. The b-roll cuts land mid-sentence on action words: 6.6 on 'navigate', 7.83 on 'click', 9.7 on 'type', 17.8 on 'add', 22.07 on 'Use'. It feels breathless and brisk, with no room to swipe.
study.zooms_punch_ins: No real punch-ins on the face. Every talking-head shot (0–3.87, 3.87–5.87, 5.87–6.6, 17.13–17.8, 22.07–end) holds roughly the same chest-up selfie framing, with only handheld drift and small reframes between jump cuts. The one punch-in is on the screen recording at 7.83: it jumps from the full profile view to about 2x tight on the top-right corner (username, Threads icon, hamburger menu), landing exactly on 'click the three lines'. At 9.7 it widens back out to a full-height settings screen. The visual changes every ~0.7–2s during the setup (0–9.7). It then sits on the 7.43s screen-recording shot, which is kept alive by on-screen typing, the page loading and the animated AI text. After that it alternates face (0.67s) → screen (4.27s) → face (2.83s).
study.captions: Word-by-word karaoke style. 1–3 words on screen at once (e.g. 'DID YOU KNOW', 'YOUR OWN INSTAGRAM', 'TOP RIGHT CORNER,'), dropping to single words like 'INSTAGRAM' and 'ALGORITHM' on slower phrases. Heavy bold geometric sans (Montserrat-style), all caps, white with a soft black drop shadow/outline, no box. The word being spoken turns yellow (YOU, OWN, CAN, NOBODY, NEED, RIGHT, REMOVE, LESS…). The highlight walks through every word, including function words, rather than picking keywords. Large, roughly 85% of frame width for 3 words, centered horizontally at about 72–75% of frame height. They stay in the same spot over the screen recordings, sitting on top of the phone UI. Phrase pages swap instantly with no bounce.
study.on_screen_text: One hook title: 'HOW TO SEE YOUR INSTAGRAM ALGORITHM' on two lines, bold white uppercase sans with a dark shadow, centered at about 17–28% of frame height, with a small Instagram icon emoji at the end of line 2. It is on from 0.0s to about 2.4s (gone by 2.80, as the second hook sentence starts). It appears with no visible animation and is never shown again. No other headers, step numbers or labels.
study.graphics_overlays: Phone screen recordings used as a floating picture-in-picture over the talking-head shot, which stays visible around the edges and is not blurred. 6.6–7.83: roughly 90% width, about 26–73% of frame height, showing the feed then his profile. 7.83–9.7: the same box, zoomed about 2x on the top-right menu. 9.7–17.13 and 17.8–22.07: a tall phone screen at about 5–95% of frame height and roughly 80% width. These show Settings and activity, the search being typed, the 'Your algorithm' page with Instagram's own animated purple AI summary, and then a dimmed add-interest/see-less input with keyboard. No arrows, circles or highlight boxes; the zoom does the pointing. The only icon is the Instagram glyph in the title.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. Jump cuts between face takes, plus hard cuts in and out of the screen-recording overlay. No whips, flashes or zoom transitions.
study.broll_and_interrupts: The b-roll is the functional screen recording that shows each step as it's said. First cutaway at 6.6 (6.6s in), then visual changes at 7.83 (zoom), 9.7 (new screen), about 11–13 (typing and the page loading inside the shot), 17.13 (face), 17.8 (screen) and 22.07 (face). The motion graph spikes match these: 20.4 at 6.5s, 16.2/15.1 at 17–17.5s, 17.8 at 22s, 24.8 at the end. In total, screen recordings cover about 15.4s of 24.9 (~62%). The face returns briefly at 17.13 for 0.67s on 'You can also' to signal a new section, and again for the sign-off. No sound effects are evident; the audio peaks follow speech syllables. No props apart from the handheld mic and the hand gestures.
study.audio: A single clean, close voice, likely a wireless mic. He appears to hold the transmitter in his hand. There is a little room tone from a bare-walled room. Delivery is fast and upbeat at 4.05 words/s overall. No background music or sound effects are evident, and no silence is used for effect; every pause is under 0.3s.
study.length_and_ending: 24.9s and 100 words. Built as hook → second hook → exclusivity claim → 3 quick numbered-style steps (5.88–12.1) → reveal of the algorithm page at about 13.0s (~52%) → bonus 'add/remove topics' (16.94–21.68) → closing instruction. The main payoff lands at 13s (52%); the practical 'change it' payoff, which the second hook promised, lands at 17–21.7s (68–87%). It ends on a soft CTA/benefit line, "Use this to dictate your feed and see what you wanna see.", delivered to camera. The cut comes 0.2s after the last word. There is no follow/comment ask and no deliberate loop. The quick hard ending makes rewatching to catch the steps easy.
study.quality: Vertical 720x1280 at 30fps, HEVC at about 13 Mbps. Handheld selfie with the phone slightly below eye level. Eyes sit at about 40% of frame height, with generous headroom (a bare white ceiling fills the top ~30%). Soft natural window light from frame right; a plain grey wall, a dark TV corner and a window in the background. Sharp enough; screen recordings are crisp. It feels casual on purpose: a home setting, a plain maroon sweatshirt, a handheld camera, conversational gestures. The polish comes from the edit: tight cuts, karaoke captions, step-synced screen recordings and the punch-in on the menu.
study.why_viral: Curiosity plus self-interest. 'See your own Instagram algorithm' is personal and secret-feeling, and 'nobody knows about' adds exclusivity, so almost every Instagram user wants to know. It is instantly actionable and save-worthy: three steps shown on screen exactly as they're spoken, so viewers can follow along or save it for later, and saves and shares spike on how-tos. Payoff stacking keeps people watching past the reveal: 'see it' is paid off at about 52%, then 'change it' at about 70–87%. And it is short and dense: about 25s, 99% speech, a visual change every couple of seconds, with no fat to swipe on.
lessons: Open on the first word at 0.0s with a 'Did you know you can…' question about something personal to the viewer. Follow within 0.3s with a second line that ups the stakes ('and you can actually change it').
Put a 2–3s hook title at the top 15–30% of the frame that restates the promise as 'HOW TO …'. Remove it once the hook sentence is done so it doesn't fight the b-roll.
Cut every pause down to 0.15–0.3s and keep speech at 95%+ of runtime. Hide any gap that's left inside a cut to new b-roll.
For tutorials, cut to the screen recording on the action verb of each step ('navigate', 'click', 'type', 'add'), mid-sentence, so picture and instruction arrive together.
Punch the screen recording in about 2x on the exact button being named (e.g. the top-right menu) instead of drawing arrows, then widen back out on the next step.
Float screen recordings as a large picture-in-picture (80–90% width) over the face shot, and keep captions at about 72–75% of frame height so they read over both.
Return to the face for under 1s at section changes ('You can also…') and for the final line. It resets attention and makes the sign-off personal.
Use 1–3-word all-caps captions with the spoken word highlighted yellow; drop to single words when the speaker slows down.
Aim for under 25s with the main reveal around 50%, a bonus payoff after it, and the cut within 0.2–0.3s of the last word.

study.format: explainer (hook-template breakdown, with each spoken template followed by screen-recorded proof clips)
study.topic: Three fill-in-the-blank hook templates ('No, I don't want an (item)', 'No (thing) needed', 'Oh so (action) is your little hobby?'), each followed by a viral example and its view count and like rate.
study.hook: "No, I don't want an item" starts at 0.00s with no lead-in. That is 6 words in 1.36s, about 4.4 words/s, much faster than the video's 1.29 words/s average because most of the runtime is silent examples. The first 2 seconds: a static medium-wide shot of the speaker in a white tee and cap, sitting against an OSB wood wall and holding a small mic near his chin. His face sits at about 55–60% of frame height, with a lot of wall above him. A single-line white caption reads 'No, I don't want an (item)' at about 48% height, just above his head. The parentheses tell the viewer this is a template to steal. Why it stops the scroll: the opening 'No,' sounds like a reply mid-argument, which is odd and intriguing. Then at 1.63s it pays off with proof: a viral food video card showing 2,944,736 views. The viewer gets a reusable formula plus social proof in under 2 seconds.

beats.what: Template 1 spoken on camera: 'No, I don't want an item'. Caption shows 'No, I don't want an (item)'.

Floating card of an @overthefirecooking video with the caption 'No, I don't want a salad' and stats Views 2,944,736 / Like rate 10.38%. Five meat and fire clips cut at 1.63, 2.17, 3.1, 3.73 and 4.67 (0.53–1.2s each). The speaker is silent for 3.36s.
Back to the speaker for template 2, 'Nothing needed'. Caption reads 'No (thing) needed'.
@thepicklevision card: a pickleball net phone mount captioned '"No cameraman needed"', Views 2,944,194 / Like rate 1.09%. Four clips cut at 5.87, 7.3, 8.13 and 9.1. The speaker is silent for 3.85s.

Template 3. The speaker's 'Oh,' starts 0.31s before the picture cuts back to him at 9.8 (an audio-first J-cut). He says 'Oh, so action is your little hobby?' under the caption 'Oh so (action) is your little hobby?'.
Burger creator card captioned 'Oh so making Burgers is your little hobby?', Views 3,585,035 / Like rate 7.98%. It holds 3.6s on him deadpanning at a cutting board, the longest shot in the video.
Cut to a dripping bacon double cheeseburger close-up (@klburgers), the money shot. The video ends at 16.4s with no CTA.

study.jump_cuts: There are effectively no jump cuts inside the speech. Each talking segment is one uncut take: 1.63s, 1.2s and 2.07s long. The median gap between words is 0.0s and there are no fillers. Only two gaps exceed 0.3s, at 3.36s and 3.85s, and both are deliberate: the speaker goes quiet while the example clips play. The 7.32 cuts per 10s come almost entirely from the example montages, where clips last 0.53–1.43s each, plus a cut into and out of every example. Cuts land between thoughts. The speaker is cut out about 0.23–0.28s after his last word: 1.36→1.63, 5.64→5.87, 11.59→11.87. His return at 4.67 is followed by his first word just 0.05s later. The final return uses a J-cut, with his voice starting at 9.49 before the picture at 9.8. It feels tight and rhythmic: a short talking line, then a burst of b-roll.
study.zooms_punch_ins: None. All three speaker shots (0–1.63, 4.67–5.87, 9.8–11.87) use the identical static medium-wide framing, and the before/after frames show no scale change. Visual change instead comes from swapping between speaker and example card and from cuts inside the montages. The picture changes roughly every 0.5–1.4s in the montages, holds 1.2–2.1s on the speaker, and the longest hold is 3.6s on the burger creator.
study.captions: One phrase-level caption per template, shown in full for the whole speaker shot, with no word-by-word reveal. It is a single line of white bold rounded sans-serif in sentence case with a subtle dark drop shadow and no box. It is small-to-medium (about 75% of frame width for the longest line), centered, at about 48% of frame height, sitting just above the speaker's head on the plain wall. There are no colored highlights. The variable slot is marked with parentheses instead: (item), (thing), (action). The caption doesn't always match the speech: he says 'Nothing needed' but the caption reads 'No (thing) needed'. The caption carries the template; the voice is just a read. During the examples, the original creators' own burned-in captions show inside the card ('No, I don't want a salad', '"No cameraman needed"' with pin and tennis-ball emojis, 'Oh so making Burgers is your little hobby?').
study.on_screen_text: No separate title, headers or numbers. The only non-caption text is the stats strip under each example card: a dark translucent bar with small grey labels 'Views' and 'Like rate' over large white numbers (2,944,736 / 10.38%; 2,944,194 / 1.09%; 3,585,035 / 7.98%), plus the original creator handles (@overthefirecooking, @thepicklevision, @klburgers) inside the clips. The strip sits at about 75–82% height under the card. It appears with a hard cut and stays for the full example.
study.graphics_overlays: The main graphic is a picture-in-picture 'proof card'. The example video is shown as a rounded-corner vertical card about 60% of frame width (x≈20–80%) and from about 15% to 75% height, with the stats bar attached beneath it to about 82%. It is laid over the speaker's own shot, covering his face, so the wood wall frames it and his arms and torso show below. The card position never moves; only its contents cut. There are no emojis, arrows or stickers added by the editor beyond those already in the source clips.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only: talking head → proof card → talking head, plus hard cuts between clips inside each card. One J-cut at 9.49/9.8, where the speaker's voice leads the picture.
study.broll_and_interrupts: The example cards are the pattern interrupts and take up about 70% of the runtime: 1.63–4.67 (3.04s), 5.87–9.8 (3.93s) and 11.87–16.4 (4.53s). They alternate with roughly 1.2–2.1s speaker returns. Inside the cards, the food montage changes every 0.53–1.2s and the pickleball montage every 0.7–1.43s. The burger segment slows to a 3.6s hold before the final 0.93s hero shot. Motion stays around 1–2 on the speaker and jumps to about 7–14 during the montages, ending with a 28.1 spike on the burger close-up. No props besides the handheld mic, no angle changes and no added SFX are visible.
study.audio: The speaker's voice is clean and close, recorded on the small mic he holds near his mouth, with little room sound. While the examples play he is silent, and the strong audio hits cluster in those windows (0.46–1.59, 3.74–7.06, 9.83–11.72, 14.97–16.28). That points to the source clips' own audio or music playing through, giving each proof card its original energy. There is no obvious separate music bed. His silence during the examples is used on purpose so the proof speaks for itself.
study.length_and_ending: 16.4s total, 15 spoken words. It follows a 3× repeat structure (template → proof) in which each round is quicker to grasp because the pattern is learned. The highest view count (3.59M) is saved for last, and the visual payoff, the cheese-dripping burger, lands at 15.47s (94%). There is no CTA. It ends on the burger 4.81s after the last spoken word, which encourages rewatching and saving to note the templates down.
study.quality: 720×1280, 30fps, h264 at about 5.5 Mbps. The framing is a static locked-off medium-wide with generous headroom; the top half is OSB wall and a wooden cabinet, which leaves clean space for the caption and the card. The eye line is near lens and the light is soft natural daylight. The mic is visible in hand, so it reads as casual-pro. The source clips are screen-recorded inside cards, so they are slightly soft. Overall it is low effort to shoot but deliberately packaged: a reusable layout of speaker plate + proof card + stats bar.
study.why_viral: It hands viewers three copy-paste hook formulas, with (item)/(thing)/(action) blanks that make it feel instantly usable, so people save and share it. Each claim is backed with hard numbers (2.9M, 2.9M, 3.6M views) shown on screen, which builds trust without explanation. It is extremely short and fast: about 1.5s of talking, then 3–4.5s of satisfying food and gadget b-roll, repeated three times. It ends on a mouthwatering burger with no outro, so it loops cleanly.
lessons: For list or tip content, keep each spoken point to 1–2s (about 4 words/s) and let 3–4.5s of proof footage do the rest; this video is only 71% speech share with 1.29 words/s.
Show proof as a fixed-position card (about 60% width, 15–80% height) laid over the speaker's own shot, with a stats bar showing real numbers like views and like rate underneath.
Cut b-roll inside the proof card every 0.5–1.4s, but let the final example breathe (about 3.6s) before a hero close-up ending.
Cut away from the speaker about 0.25s after their last word, and come back right before their next word (about 0.05s); use an audio-first J-cut (about 0.3s) at least once to smooth a return.

Put the template on screen as one phrase-level caption with the variable in parentheses, e.g. '(item)', at about 48% height above the head. Let the caption carry the exact wording even if the read differs.
Keep the speaker framing identical across returns so the layout feels like a format; the contrast between a still speaker (motion about 1–2) and busy b-roll (motion 7–14) provides the energy.
Order examples by escalating proof and save the biggest number or most visual shot for the last 6–10% of the runtime.
Skip the CTA on very short template videos and end on the best visual 4–5s after the last word so it loops.
creator_advice: Hook template: 'No, I don't want an (item)', e.g. 'No, I don't want a salad' (shown with 2,944,736 views, 10.38% like rate).
Hook template: 'No (thing) needed', e.g. 'No cameraman needed' (shown with 2,944,194 views, 1.09% like rate).
Hook template: 'Oh so (action) is your little hobby?', e.g. 'Oh so making Burgers is your little hobby?' (shown with 3,585,035 views, 7.98% like rate).

study.format: listicle
study.topic: A self-described chronic procrastinator lists six productivity habits, ordered from common to increasingly niche: the five-minute lie, winning the first hour, a deliberately terrible first draft, body doubling, a fake deadline with real consequences, and time-lapsing your work.
study.hook: "Ten out of ten habits that actually help me get shit done as a chronic procrastinator, but they get increasingly more niche." She starts at 0.00s with no lead-in and delivers 21 words in 5.16s (about 4.1 words/s, slightly faster than the video's 3.93 average). From frame 1 the top third shows a 3x2 collage of six moody stills: spiral clock, Newton's cradle, a black-and-white draftsman, a vaporwave pair of heads, a pink moon and a Limitless-style man at a laptop. Under it, bold white text reads '10/10 habits to actually get sh*t done' with a smaller line '(from my 8 figure business)'. She sits chest-up in the lower two-thirds, holding a wired earphone mic. Why it stops the scroll: 1) mild profanity plus a relatable label ('chronic procrastinator'); 2) a credibility flex in the text ('8 figure business'); 3) the collage previews one image per habit, so viewers subconsciously count six items and want to see each one; 4) 'they get increasingly more niche' promises escalation, which makes people stay for the weirdest tip at the end.

beats.what: Title card, six-image collage and the spoken promise: 10/10 habits from a chronic procrastinator, getting more niche as they go.
Habit 1, 'The five minute lie' (spiral clock image): tell yourself you'll only do the daunting task for five minutes.
Mini-payoff: 'the hardest part was starting.'
Habit 2, 'Win the first hour' (Newton's cradle): make your first act of the morning productive, even making your bed. 'Momentum is your greatest friend.'
Habit 3, 'Make a deliberately terrible first draft' (black-and-white draftsman footage): do it badly. 'It's much easier to improve something that exists than to perfect something that doesn't.'
Habit 4, 'Borrow somebody else's concentration' (vaporwave heads): work next to productive people in a café or library. Named as 'body doubling'.
Habit 5, 'Fake deadline with real consequences' (Limitless clip): make plans for later and you can't go until the task is done.
Habit 6, the most niche: film yourself working on a time lapse (pink moon).
Double benefit: you can't use your phone, and watching hours of work become a 30-second clip gives 'the dopamine hit of being productive twice'. Video ends on this line.

study.jump_cuts: Almost no dead air. Median gap between words is 0.0s, speech fills 99% of the runtime, there are 0 fillers, and only 5 gaps reach 0.3s or more (longest 0.4s after 'stop.' at 10.22s; others 0.3s at 20.76, 0.38s at 31.44, 0.3s at 36.76, 0.3s at 39.54). Those longer gaps sit at sentence ends inside a habit, giving one short breath before the explanation or the 'why'. There are only 6 cuts in 55.8s (1.08 per 10s; shots 5.2 to 10.2s, median 7.97s). Every cut lands between thoughts, exactly at a habit change and within about 0.03 to 0.11s of the new habit's first word (5.23 to 'The' 5.34; 13.07 to 'Win' 13.08; 21.03 to 'Make' 21.06; 37.03 to 'Give' 37.06; 45.6 to 'Film' 45.62). The exception is 29.8, which falls just after 'Borrow' begins at 29.62. Each habit plays as one continuous take with no visible jump cuts inside it. The tightness comes from fast, scripted, fluent delivery, not chopping.
study.zooms_punch_ins: None. Frames before and after each of the 6 cuts show the same chest-up framing at the same scale, with only small posture shifts between takes. No digital zooms either: motion stays low (median 4.6, range 1.5 to 9.3). Visual change instead comes from the caption word swapping every ~0.25s and the top image changing at each habit (every 5 to 10s). The images are moving clips, so the top third is always animated, as with the spinning clock and swinging Newton's cradle.
study.captions: Starts at 5.34s; the hook has none because the title text does that job. One word at a time, synced word-by-word to speech. Bold rounded sans-serif, white, lowercase as spoken ('lie', 'only', 'task', 'momentum', '30second'), no box or heavy stroke, maybe a faint shadow. Medium size (about the width of a short word block), centered horizontally at roughly 33% of frame height, just under the image and above her head. No highlight colors, no emojis, and no animation beyond hard swaps per word.
study.on_screen_text: Only the hook title, 0 to 5.23s. Line 1, '10/10 habits to actually get sh*t done', is a large bold white sans in two lines centered at about 28 to 33% of frame height. Line 2, '(from my 8 figure business)', is smaller bold white at about 36%. No background box; it sits directly over the softly lit wall. Static, on from frame 1, and removed by the hard cut at 5.23s. There are no numbered headers for each habit; the spoken habit name plus the new image marks each section.
study.graphics_overlays: A media panel in the top third, about 10 to 29% of frame height and about 55 to 60% of frame width, centered. Hook (0 to 5.23s): a 3x2 collage of all six habit visuals. After that, one landscape clip per habit, swapped on each cut: a spinning spiral clock (5.23 to 13.07), Newton's cradle on paper (13.07 to 21.03), black-and-white footage of a draftsman sketching (21.03 to 29.8), two vaporwave heads facing each other on a checkerboard (29.8 to 37.03), a Limitless-style man at a glowing laptop (37.03 to 45.6), and a pink moon setting over hills (45.6 to end). Each is a moving clip, not a still. The cool, slightly surreal, film-grain aesthetic matches the pink-and-cream palette of her sweater. No emojis, arrows or progress bars.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only (6). Each cut swaps the speaker take and the top image at the same moment, at habit boundaries.
study.broll_and_interrupts: No full-screen cutaways; she is on screen the whole time. The top-third clip works as permanent picture-in-picture b-roll and changes every 5.2 to 10.2s (median about 8s), one per habit. The single-word caption below it changes about 4 times a second. No sound effects; the audio peaks (e.g. 5.24, 13.x, 21.35, 37.11, 45.24) are speech onsets at the cuts. No angle or location changes; the only movement is her own hand gestures (counting, open palms, a waved hand on 'dopamine' at 54s).
study.audio: Voice recorded close through a wired earphone mic she holds near her mouth: dry and intimate, with a little room tone and an ASMR-adjacent closeness. The data shows no clear music or sound effects; the strongest audio hits line up with word onsets. There are no pauses for effect; at 3.93 words/s and 99% speech coverage, the rhythm is relentless.
study.length_and_ending: 55.8s, 218 words, 6 habits. Each habit follows the same pattern: a bold named rule, one sentence of how-to, one sentence of why (a quotable line such as 'momentum is your greatest friend' or 'easier to improve something that exists'). The hook promised escalating nicheness, so the strangest tip, time-lapsing your work, is saved for last at 45.62s (82%). Its double-dopamine payoff runs from 48.22s to 55.48s (86 to 99%). No CTA and no outro: it cuts 0.32s after 'twice', ending on the payoff line. That abruptness invites a rewatch or save.
study.quality: 720x1280 vertical at 30fps, HEVC at a high ~15 Mbps, so it looks clean and sharp. Front/selfie camera at eye level, chest-up, centered. The head top sits at about 38% of frame height, leaving the top third deliberately empty for the image and caption; eyes are at about 50%. Warm, soft evening light from a practical lamp (frame left) plus a soft key on her face; the background is a styled living room with a shelf and white flowers, slightly soft. Polished makeup and a matching pink sweater and earring make it look premium, while the handheld wired earphone mic and casual sitting position keep it a friendly 'chatting with you' feel rather than a studio production.
study.why_viral: 1) The packaging promises a lot fast: profanity, a 'chronic procrastinator' label, an '8 figure business' credential, and 'increasingly more niche', which builds curiosity for the final tip. 2) The six-image collage acts as a visual table of contents, and each image reappears with its habit, so viewers track progress and stay to see all six. 3) The habits are dense and named, so they are easy to save and share. Each is under 10s with a quotable why-line, and they escalate from familiar (the 5-minute rule) to novel (body doubling, time-lapse dopamine). 4) Fast, filler-free delivery (3.93 words/s, max gap 0.4s) plus constantly moving top-third clips and word-by-word captions keep the eye busy despite only 6 cuts and no zooms.
lessons: Start talking at 0.00s and get the whole premise, plus a reason to stay to the end ('they get increasingly more niche'), into the first ~5s.
For list videos, show a collage of one thumbnail per item in the hook so viewers see how many items are coming; then reuse each thumbnail as that item's visual.
Put a static title over the hook for its first ~5s (main claim on the first line, credibility in a smaller parenthetical second line), then drop it and switch to captions.
Frame the speaker so their head top sits at ~35-40% of frame height, and use the empty top third for a moving b-roll panel (~55-60% of frame width) plus a single-word caption at ~33% height.
Swap the b-roll panel only at item boundaries (every ~5-10s), and make the cut land within ~0.1s of the next item's first word so the visual change marks a new section.

If delivery is fluent, you don't need jump cuts every 2s: target gaps of 0.3s or less between words and ~4 words/s; one continuous take per item with ~1 cut per 10s works when the overlays keep moving.
Script every item the same way: a bold named rule, then one sentence of how-to, then one quotable why-line. Keep each item to 7-10s.
Order items from most familiar to most novel and save the most surprising one for the last ~15% of the video; end within ~0.3s of the final payoff word, with no CTA.
Use one-word, lowercase, white bold captions synced word-by-word for calm, aesthetic creators; skip highlight colors when the style is minimal.
Pick b-roll for mood and palette, not literal meaning (surreal clocks, a moon, film clips), and match its colors to the speaker's outfit and room for a cohesive premium look.

study.format: listicle (advice / tips checklist about making content)
study.topic: A six-step checklist for small creators to get out of '1,000 view jail': lighting, audio, cutting dead space, auto captions, copying the format of proven videos, and following him (the CTA).
study.hook: "Six step checklist to get out of 1,000 view jail and never get under 1,000 views again" starts at 0.00s with no lead-in. That is about 17 words in 3.96s (~4.3 words/s), one breath. The first 2 seconds are a medium chest-up shot outdoors in front of green trees. He holds a small DJI mic at his chest and gestures with his other hand. A two-line hook title in bold white sans with a soft dark shadow sits at ~20–27% of frame height: "Escape 1000 VIEW JAIL / in Under 60 Seconds". White speech captions sit near the bottom. It stops the scroll because it names a pain every small creator feels and gives it a meme-able label ('1,000 view jail'). It promises a numbered, finite fix (6 steps) and a time box (under 60 seconds). The title and the voice say the same promise in different words, so it lands whether the sound is on or off.

beats.what: "Six step checklist to get out of 1,000 view jail and never get under 1,000 views again" with the 'Escape 1000 VIEW JAIL in Under 60 Seconds' title.

Credibility: "If you don't know who I am, I've created over 100 videos with at least 1 million views." From 5.53s a collage of view-count thumbnails (26M, 24.3M, 22.6M, 17.3M, 19.2M, 26.4M...) floods the frame.
"Step 1 is lighting." A yellow 'LIGHTING' keyword pops mid-frame.
"Find the best light source wherever you are and make sure it's in front of you." He points at camera.
Bad-lighting demo: the footage cuts to a dark, underexposed version of him. "Stop recording videos like this or everyone's going to scroll away every single time."
"Step 2, fix your audio." He holds up two fingers. A yellow 'AUDIO' keyword pops.
"Make sure you're being heard loud and clear and try to use a microphone." A 'DJI MIC 2' label with a curved yellow arrow points to the mic in his hand.
Bad-audio demo on a different, more saturated take: "Trust me, if your audio sounds like this, then nobody's going to watch that video."
"Step 3, cut out all of the dead space in your videos." A yellow 'DEAD SPACE' keyword pops.

"Especially at the beginning. People have very short attention spans. You have 1 to 3 seconds... and 7 seconds to keep them there." Text cards '1-3 SECONDS / FOR HOOK' and '7 SECONDS / BEFORE THEY SCROLL' appear.
"Don't waste any of that time with silence like this." It cuts to a 0.6s black-and-white shot of him standing silent, captioned '[dead space]'. This is the 0.76s gap, left in as the joke.
"Step 4 is auto captions." A yellow 'CAPTIONS' keyword pops. "Only use 1 to 2 lines max."
"Make sure all of your captions match this format." TikTok 'Captions' and CapCut 'Auto captions' button screenshots appear. Then "...fits into the viewable area right here."
"Not like this." A giant, frame-wide white caption demonstrates the wrong way.
"Step 5, find other videos with at least 100,000 views to use as a template." A yellow 'INSPIRATION' keyword shows, then a collage of viral video thumbnails (16M, 6.9M, 2.7M).
"Step 6, follow me and I'll show you more ways to increase those views." The CTA is disguised as the final checklist item.

study.jump_cuts: Very tight. Median gap between words is 0.00s. Only 7 gaps are 0.3s or more, and the longest is 0.76s at 38.5s, left in on purpose as the 'dead space' demo. The other gaps are 0.44s after the hook (3.96s), 0.40s at 8.22s, 0.46s at 9.66s, 0.32s at 17.28s, 0.30s at 31.58s and 0.38s at 52.64s. No fillers. The pace is 4.27 words/s with speech filling 100% of the runtime. There are 21 shots in 56.3s (3.55 cuts per 10s, median shot 2.43s). The longest shot is 7.83s (28.67–36.5), and text cards carry it. The shortest is 0.6s (the B&W dead-space gag). Cuts almost always land between sentences or clauses, right at each 'Step N' or the line after it, not mid-word. Several cuts come within ~0.1–0.2s of the next word (e.g. cut 26.13 → 'Step 3' at 26.10; cut 48.47 → 'Step 5' at 48.44). It feels breathless but clean.
study.zooms_punch_ins: No animated zooms. Framing changes are subtle reframes between takes, about 1.05–1.15x. The shots where the yellow keyword pops (LIGHTING ~9.4s, AUDIO ~18.2s, DEAD SPACE ~28.1s, CAPTIONS ~40.3s, INSPIRATION ~49s) read slightly tighter: his glasses span more of the frame than in the following explanation shot, roughly 1.1x. The next cut then goes back a touch wider. So the rhythm alternates tighter on the step headline and normal on the explanation. The 22.93–26.13 shot is a different take, with him slightly lower in frame and warmer, more saturated color. Counting cuts plus overlays that appear mid-shot (proof collage, keyword pops, mic label, 1-3/7 SECONDS cards, caption UI, 'Not like this', thumbnail collage), something visual changes every ~1.5–2.5s.
study.captions: Native TikTok-style captions. Medium-weight white sans, sentence case, with a light shadow and no box. Small size, about 4–5% of frame height. Centered at ~76% of frame height. Shown in phrase chunks of 3–6 words ('6 step checklist to get out', 'of 1000 view jail', 'and never get under'), each swapping as the phrase is spoken. One line most of the time, two lines only at the end ('and I'll show you more ways / to increase those views'). No word highlighting, colors or animation. Numbers are written as digits ('1-2 lines max', '100,000 views'). Exception: the 'Not like this' demo at 47.3–48.47 makes the caption huge and frame-wide at ~75% height on purpose, to show bad captions.
study.on_screen_text: 1) Hook title 'Escape 1000 VIEW JAIL / in Under 60 Seconds': bold white sans, mixed case with 'VIEW JAIL' in caps, dark drop shadow, two lines at ~20–27% height. On from 0s until the cut at 4.33s. 2) One-word step keywords: 'LIGHTING', 'AUDIO', 'DEAD SPACE', 'CAPTIONS', 'INSPIRATION'. Heavy black-weight all-caps yellow with a thick black outline, centered at ~44–46% height over his chest/chin. Each appears about 0.5–1s after 'Step N' is said and holds until the next cut (≈0.6–2s). 'INSPIRATION' holds ~1.8s. 3) Stat cards '1-3 SECONDS / FOR HOOK' (~32.5s) and '7 SECONDS / BEFORE THEY SCROLL' (~35.9s). Large bold white caps with a smaller second line and shadow, centered at ~42–52% height. Each shows for about 1s while the number is spoken. 4) '[dead space]' white text on the black-and-white shot at ~54% height, 38.67–39.27. 5) Labels 'TikTok:' and 'CapCut:' above the caption-button screenshots (42.73–44.87). 6) 'DJI MIC 2' bold white label (see graphics).
study.graphics_overlays: Proof collage, 5.53–8.6s: about 12 cropped TikTok/IG thumbnails with view counts (eye/play icon + 26M, 24.3M, 22.6M, 17.3M, 19.2M, 12.3M, 6.6M, 26.4M, 17.3M, 6.9M, 4.3M). Stacked like tiles over his face and torso, appearing on the cut and holding for the whole shot. Mic callout, ~20.4–22.93s: 'DJI MIC 2' label left of center at ~56% height, with a hand-drawn curved yellow arrow pointing to the mic in his hand. App UI screenshots, 42.73–44.87s: the TikTok 'Captions' button and CapCut 'Auto captions' button as dark square tiles, centered at ~50–58% height. Template collage, ~50.33–52.93s: three overlapping viral-video thumbnails (16M, 6.9M, 2.7M fried chicken) covering the center of frame. Color grading as graphics: a darkened, underexposed grade for the bad-lighting demo (13.13–16.8) and a black-and-white grade for the dead-space gag (38.67–39.27). No emojis, progress bars or borders.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. No whips, flashes or zoom transitions. The 'transitions' are grade changes on hard cuts: to dark at 13.13, back to normal at 16.8, to B&W at 38.67, back at 39.27.
study.broll_and_interrupts: No real b-roll; every interrupt is an overlay or a self-demo on the same setup. Proof collage at 5.53s. LIGHTING pop ~9.4s. Dark bad-lighting demo 13.13–16.8. Peace-sign gesture at 'Step 2' 17.0s. AUDIO pop ~18.2s. Mic label and arrow ~20.4s. Bad-audio demo take 22.93. DEAD SPACE pop ~28.1s. 1-3 SECONDS card ~32.5s. 7 SECONDS card ~35.9s. B&W silence gag 38.67. CAPTIONS pop ~40.3s. App screenshots 42.73. Giant 'Not like this' caption 47.3. INSPIRATION ~49s. Thumbnail collage ~50.3s. Interrupts land every ~2–4s, so no stretch over ~4s goes without a new visual idea. Hand gestures do counting work too: holding up fingers for step numbers, pointing at camera on 'in front of you', pointing at the caption area on 'right here'. No sound effects can be confirmed from the audio hits; they track speech emphasis rather than the overlay pops.
study.audio: Clean, close voice from the DJI Mic 2 he is holding, with little outdoor room sound. Delivery is fast and steady (~4.3 words/s). No clear music bed under it. The 22.93–26.13 'if your audio sounds like this' take is a different recording meant as the bad-audio example; a degraded sound there is implied by the script but can't be confirmed from the data. Silence is used for effect once: the 0.76s gap at 38.5s over the B&W '[dead space]' shot, so the viewer feels the problem he is describing.
study.length_and_ending: 56.3s, kept under the 60s the title promises. Built as a numbered countdown: 'Step N' is said at 8.62, 16.82, 26.10, 39.26, 48.44 and 53.02, so the viewer always knows how many are left. The densest value is in steps 3–4 (26–48s, with the 1-3/7-second rule and the caption demos). The last real tip lands at 48.44s (86%). The ending is a CTA disguised as step 6 at 53.02s (94%): 'Step 6, follow me and I'll show you more ways to increase those views.' It cuts 0.04s after the last word, with no outro, so it slides almost straight into a replay. The transcript shows a tiny garbled tail (a duplicate 'Step 6, follow me...' and 'Thank you' in 0.14s at 56.12–56.26), which is leftover audio from the last take; there are no visible extra frames.
study.quality: 720x1280 at 30fps, HEVC, high bitrate (~15.5 Mbps). Medium chest-up framing with his eyes at ~37–40% of frame height. He stands centered with modest headroom and the hook title sitting above his head. Natural outdoor daylight on his face and a bright, leafy green background that reads as fresh and backlit. Sharp. Plain dark tie-dye tee, glasses, mic visibly in hand as a prop that proves step 2. Casual and phone-shot by design, but the edit is high-effort: custom yellow keyword pops, a proof collage, labeled screenshots and grade-change demos. The look practices exactly what it preaches.
study.why_viral: 1) A specific, shareable pain label ('1,000 view jail') plus a numbered promise ('6 step checklist', 'Under 60 Seconds') gives a reason to stay until step 6 and to save the video. 2) Instant authority: the 26M/24.3M/22.6M view collage at 5.5s proves he can deliver before the first tip. 3) Show-don't-tell demos make each tip feel obvious and memorable, and they double as pattern interrupts every few seconds: dark footage for bad lighting, a bad-audio take, a B&W silence gag for dead space, a giant caption for bad captions. 4) The CTA is folded into the list as 'Step 6', so viewers stay to see the last step and follow without feeling sold to. The hard end with no outro pushes a rewatch.
lessons: Start speaking at 0.0s and put the full promise in the first sentence (under ~4s). Add a 2-line title at ~20–27% height that says the same promise with a number and a time box.
Put a proof beat in the first ~5–8s: if the speaker claims results, cover the frame with a collage of real screenshots for the whole ~3s claim.

For list videos, start every item with a spoken 'Step N' and cut exactly on it. Pop a 1–2 word, all-caps, yellow-with-black-outline keyword mid-frame (~45% height) about 0.5–1s later and hold it until the next cut.
Strip every gap over ~0.3s except gaps that make a point. Aim for a median word gap near 0s and ~4+ words/s, and keep one deliberate silence (~0.7s) only if the script calls for it.
Demonstrate the wrong way instead of describing it. Grade the clip dark, black-and-white, or give it a giant caption for 0.6–3.5s whenever the speaker says 'like this'.
Keep cuts at ~3–4 per 10s (median shot ~2.4s). When a shot must run long (~8s), carry it with on-screen stat cards timed to the spoken numbers, about one every 3–4s.
Name the gear or tool the speaker mentions with a small label and a curved arrow to the object. Show app button screenshots when they mention an app feature.
Use small native-style captions: white, sentence case, 3–6 word phrases, 1 line (2 max), at ~75–78% height, inside the safe viewable area.
Fold the follow CTA into the structure as the final numbered item, and cut within ~0.1s of the last word so the video loops.
creator_advice: Lighting: find the best light source wherever you are and make sure it's in front of you. Stop recording videos with bad lighting or everyone's going to scroll away every single time.

Fix your audio: make sure you're being heard loud and clear and try to use a microphone (he uses a DJI Mic 2) to cut out any excess sound. If your audio sounds bad, nobody's going to watch that video.
Cut out all of the dead space in your videos, especially at the beginning. People have very short attention spans.
You have 1 to 3 seconds to get people to watch your video and 7 seconds to keep them there. Don't waste any of that time with silence.
Use auto captions (TikTok 'Captions' or CapCut 'Auto captions'). Only use 1 to 2 lines max, match this format, and make sure it fits into the viewable area, not huge across the screen.
Find other videos with at least 100,000 views to use as a template.

study.format: business/day-in-the-life talk (timestamped vlog challenge, storytime told through selfie check-ins plus b-roll)
study.topic: A student creator tries to build and launch a personal-branding course ("ContentPreneur Academy") in one day, locking himself in a conference room and going live on TikTok to sell it, and ends the day with 4 sales and $390.
study.hook: "Is it possible to make an entire business in one day" starts at 0.00s with no lead-in: 11 words in 2.64s (~4.2 words/s), then "and make our first $1,000 or 20 sales offer?" by 5.84s. Frames 0-~1.0s: a tight handheld selfie outdoors on an overcast campus. The face fills ~60% of the frame, he wears a pink hoodie up under a brown jacket, and the eye line is about 40% down the frame. The only text is one-word white captions dead center ("Is", "possible", "to make"). Around 1.0s (an audio hit at 1.01, a motion spike) the picture switches to b-roll of hands typing on a MacBook in a glass conference room, with the screen showing "contentpreneur academy". The caption then lands "ONE DAY" in bold caps just before the 2.83s cut. It stops the scroll because it asks a yes/no challenge question with a concrete, measurable goal ($1,000 / 20 sales) and an extreme time limit. The first-second switch from face to 'proof it's happening' footage promises a watchable experiment, not a lecture.

beats.what: Challenge question: can you make an entire business in one day; selfie, then cut to laptop b-roll at ~1s.
Defines the win condition: first $1,000 or 20 sales. B-roll of a 'Let's create your new store' setup screen, then back to the selfie with a two-finger gesture on '20'.
Credibility: did this 3 months ago with his agency and got a $2,000 client day one. Tripod b-roll in a different room, then a Stripe/Square dashboard reading $2,000.00 as proof.
'9:08AM' timestamp, low-angle shot of him in class writing; cut to a handwritten notebook page: 'I crafted out my entire business plan.'
The plan: lock himself in a conference room for 9 hours, then go live on TikTok and sell the program. Walk-through of the empty room, wide tripod shot of him working, back to the outdoor selfie.
'2:19PM' check-in: two hours in, building course modules, 'hella energized, let's fucking go'. Split-screen stack of two, then three, panels of him filming modules plus a Google Doc screen recording.
'5:00PM': posts an IG story promising release in 4 hours and shows the phone to camera. Orange 'TIME LEFT: 4:00' countdown creates a ticking clock.
'7:31PM' rattled selfie: 'Fuck, okay', still has to film a module and polish the Discord (Discord screen b-roll), 'a little behind on schedule, a little bit stressed.'
'8:20PM' calm reflective check-in: spent all day making the product; believes it will reach the right customers. Screen-recording b-roll of a module being recorded.
'8:43PM' surprise: 'Holy shit, it's actually working… first client', with a Stripe stats screen and a laughing selfie captioned 'WE GOT OUR 1ST MEMBER'; he hasn't even put up the VSL yet.
'GOING LIVE 9:40PM': tripod shot of him on a TikTok live from his laptop, pitching ContentPreneur Academy to people who want to start a personal brand.
'1:28AM' red-lit night selfie: finished the live 2 hours ago, ends the day at 4 total sales, $390. Dashboard b-roll; misses the $1,000 goal.
Emotional resolution: always wanted to make this product, it's valuable, 'no matter what these sales numbers say today, I am proud of myself.'
'And that's what business is about, right? I'll see you guys tomorrow.' A series-style sign-off implying more episodes.

study.jump_cuts: Speech is wall to wall: speech share 1.0, median gap between words 0.0s, zero fillers, 327 words at 4.05 words/s. Only 3 gaps reach 0.3s or more: 0.86s at 52.2s (the scene change into the live-stream audio, so it reads as a location switch), 0.5s at 56.52s (between live-pitch phrases), and 0.54s after '$390' at 64.42s, left in so the disappointing number lands. All breaths and dead air in the selfie check-ins are gone. The picture cuts 25 times plus a few changes the detector missed (~1.0s, ~52s), about 2.97 cuts per 10s, median shot 3.07s, longest 4.67s. Because the voice runs continuously as a voiceover/sync blend, many picture cuts land mid-sentence over unbroken audio: 2.83 'and | make', 6.1 'Now I did this |', 14.05 'So my plan today | is to lock myself', 17.07, 22.64, 34.33 'we still have to film', 37.07, 48.8 'first client | we got'. Others land between thoughts (20.0, 29.0, 32.03, 40.13, 42.6, 46.13, 58.0, 65.0, 72.0). It feels tight and briskly paced, but loose and vlog-like in the frame itself.
study.zooms_punch_ins: No deliberate digital punch-ins or animated zooms. Framing changes come from switching between handheld selfie, tripod wide, low angle and screen close-ups. The only same-shot cut is at 34.33s, during 'we still have to film'. The before and after frames are the same selfie, re-framed by the phone moving (face goes from off-center bottom-left to centered, roughly ~1.1x tighter), a jump cut rather than a planned punch-in. Tightness instead alternates by shot type. Face-filling selfies (face ~50-60% of frame) at 0-1s, ~4.5-6.1, ~10, 17-20, 20-22.6, 32-40, 42.6-46, 46-~52 and 58-80. Wide tripod shots where he is ~25% of frame at 6.1, 14.05, 26.07, 29.0 and ~52-58. Extreme close-ups of screens at 2.83, ~9.4, 12.27, 36.8, 40.13, 48.35 and 62.8. Some visual change (cut, split-screen panel, timestamp or screen insert) happens every ~2.3-4.7s, median ~3s.
study.captions: Speech captions throughout, in two styles. Hook (0-~3s): one word or a two-word pair at a time, white, medium-bold sans, ~5% of frame height, dead center (~50% down), no box, light shadow; it lands 'ONE DAY' in bold caps as the emphasis word. After ~3s: short phrase chunks of 2-5 words, sometimes wrapping to two lines ('and actually sell this / program', 'I haven't even put up the / VSL yet'). These are white, regular-to-medium weight, sentence case, smaller (~3.5% of frame height), with a soft shadow and no stroke or box, centered at ~75% down the frame. They cut on with each phrase, without animation. Emphasis is done with ALL CAPS instead of color: 'let's FKIN GO' (censored swear), 'WE GOT OUR 1ST MEMBER' (in a slightly bolder style). Numbers become digits ('3 months', 'next 9 hours', '4 hours', '$390'). The captions are lightly cleaned paraphrases of the speech, not verbatim (e.g. 'first ever' becomes '1ST MEMBER', 'BSL' becomes 'VSL', 'in your academy' becomes 'ContentPreneur Academy', 'I really love what I've built').
study.on_screen_text: Time-of-day stamps carry the structure. Each is a large white sans (medium weight), ~7% of frame height, centered horizontally at ~25-28% down the frame (upper third, above the face), sometimes semi-transparent or fading in. In order: '9:08AM' at 10.33s; '2:19PM' at 20.0s; '5:00PM' at 26.07s; '7:31PM' at 32.03s; '8:20PM' mid-shot ~39s (faded/translucent); '8:43PM' at 46.13s; 'GOING LIVE / 9:40PM' (small caps label over a big time) at ~52s; '1:28AM' at 58.0s. Each stays for roughly the first 1-2s of its shot. A countdown appears at 29.0s: 'TIME LEFT:' in orange caps, then '4:00' in large orange digits beneath (~12% of frame height) at ~29.5s, upper-middle of frame, held until 32.03s. This is the only colored text in the video.
study.graphics_overlays: Split-screen stack at ~22.4-25s. First two panels stacked vertically (top: him filming in a different room; bottom: him at the desk). At the 22.64 cut it becomes three stacked strips. Around 23.8s the middle strip becomes a screen recording of a Google Doc ('HOW YOUR CONTENT STRATEGY WILL WORK') with his webcam bubble, showing that course modules are being made in parallel. There are no emojis, stickers, arrows or progress bars. Proof is shown as real screen footage filmed off the laptop or phone: the store setup page (2.83), a $2,000.00 sales dashboard (~9.4), a handwritten business plan (12.27), the IG story announcement on his phone (28.15), the Discord course channels (36.8), a module recording (40.13), Stripe stats with $146.00 and 1 payment (48.35), and the final dashboard with $389.00 gross and 4 payments (62.8).
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. There are no whips, flashes or zoom transitions. The split screen at ~22.4s is a hard layout change, and the timestamp text simply appears with each new shot.
study.broll_and_interrupts: More than half the runtime is cutaways. Screen inserts (store setup, dashboards, notebook, IG story, Discord, recordings) last ~0.5-2.5s each and recur every ~5-10s. Tripod or third-person shots (working in conference rooms, class, the TikTok live) provide location and angle changes. Locations change constantly: overcast campus outdoors, lecture hall, two different conference rooms, a desk by windows, a red-lit stairwell at night, a dark street. The lighting shift to saturated red at 58s marks 'late night'. A new timestamp lands roughly every 6-10s (10.3, 20.0, 26.1, 32.0, ~39, 46.1, ~52, 58.0) and acts as a chapter marker and pattern interrupt. The 'TIME LEFT' countdown at 29s and the split screen at 22.4s are one-off interrupts. A cluster of strong audio hits at 26.06-28.69 coincides with the 5:00PM story/phone section; no distinct sound effects are identifiable from the data. Props: laptop, phone held to camera, notebook.
study.audio: Phone-mic voice, close in the selfies and roomier in the conference-room tripod shots. Outdoor clips have some wind and air, and the live-stream section (53-57s) is room-sound sync audio from the laptop pitch. The voice is mostly continuous: daytime-outdoor narration (hook, plan) is laid over b-roll, and the in-the-moment check-ins are kept as sync sound, so the energy shifts with the day (hyped at 2:19PM, stressed at 7:31PM, giddy at 8:43PM, tired and sincere at 1:28AM). The audio hits suggest a light music bed or beat under the voice, but genre and level can't be confirmed from the data; the voice clearly dominates. Silence is used once for effect: the 0.54s pause after '$390' at 64.42s.
study.length_and_ending: 80.8s. It builds as a ticking-clock timeline: goal (0-6s), proof he's done it before (6-10s), plan (10-20s), progress check-ins with escalating stakes (20-38s: public 4-hour deadline, behind schedule), a mini-payoff with the first client at 46-52s (~57-64%), the live sell (53-57s), then the real payoff, '4 total sales, $390' at 61.0-64.42s (~76-80%). That outcome undercuts the $1,000 goal and turns into a sincere 'I am proud of myself' at 74.06s (~92%). It ends on 'And that's what business is about, right? I'll see you guys tomorrow,' a soft series CTA promising day 2. It cuts 0.17s after the last word, with no lingering and no explicit loop.
study.quality: 720x1280 at 29.39 fps, h264, ~6.1 Mbps; shot on a phone. Selfies are tight with little headroom (hair often touches or crosses the top third, eyes ~35-40% down) and slightly low or handheld angles. Tripod shots are wide and low on the conference table. Lighting is whatever exists: flat overcast daylight, fluorescent office light, harsh red stairwell light, dim streetlight at the end with visible noise and softness. Background clutter and screens filmed off the laptop (moiré, glare) are left in. It feels casual on purpose: raw vlog footage that sells authenticity. The effort is in the structure (time stamps, receipts and screen proof, split screens, captions), not in polish.
study.why_viral: A clear, measurable challenge with a hard deadline ($1,000 in one day) plus timestamps and a 'TIME LEFT' countdown gives viewers a reason to stay until they learn the result. Real receipts (dashboards showing $2,000, $146, $389, 4 payments) make it believable and screenshot-worthy for aspiring entrepreneurs. The honest emotional arc of hype, stress, surprise first sale, missing the goal and pride is relatable and more shareable than a fake win, and 'that's what business is about' gives a takeaway to comment on. Constant visual change (a new shot every ~3s, 8+ locations and lighting looks) keeps a vlog with no polish moving fast.
lessons: Open on the question itself at 0.0s: state the challenge plus a concrete number in the first ~5s (here: one day, $1,000 or 20 sales), then cut away from the face within ~1s to footage proving it's happening.

For day-in-the-life or challenge edits, put a big time-of-day stamp in the upper third (~25% down) at the start of each chapter, every ~6-10s, and hold it 1-2s. It works as structure and as a pattern interrupt.
Add one ticking-clock graphic (e.g. orange 'TIME LEFT: 4:00') at the midpoint (~35% in) to re-raise the stakes when attention dips.
Show receipts as real screen footage (dashboards, notebooks, DMs, Discord) for 0.5-2.5s right on the words that claim them ('$2,000 client', 'first client', '$390').
Cut picture every ~3s (median 3.07s, never over ~4.7s) and let the voiceover run continuously across cuts. Picture cuts can land mid-sentence as long as the audio never breaks.
Strip all dead air (target median word gap ~0.0s, ~4 words/s) but leave one 0.5-0.9s pause after the key result number so it lands.
Use ALL CAPS in captions instead of color for the 1-2 peak emotional lines ('WE GOT OUR 1ST MEMBER'), and keep regular captions as 2-5-word phrases at ~75% frame height.
Keep the in-the-moment mood shifts (hyped, stressed, giddy, tired) and let lighting changes (e.g. red night light) signal time passing. Don't color-match them away.
Put the outcome at ~75-80% of runtime, follow it with a 10-15s honest reflection, and end on a series hook ('see you guys tomorrow') within 0.2s of the last word.
Use a 2-3 panel vertical split screen for 2-3s to show parallel work or a montage without adding runtime.

study.format: listicle
study.topic: A numbered-style list of increasingly niche habits for building 'disgustingly good taste': borrow from unrelated worlds, keep your own archive, study why art was made, notice everyday design, find the thread in what you love, and let yourself get bored instead of filling silence with the algorithm.
study.hook: "10 out of 10 habits to build disgustingly good taste, but they become increasingly more niche." The first word lands at 0.00s with no lead-in. That is 16 words in 3.76s (~4.3 words/s), delivered conversationally with a smile while he holds the earbud mic wire near his chin. In the first 2 seconds the frame is a static medium close-up. His head sits in the middle third, and the top ~35% of the frame is beige ceiling, used as a graphics zone. That zone holds a 2x3 collage of six moody, aesthetic stills: an office wall covered in notes, B&W photos on a table, a man lying under cassette tapes, a hand sketching, a handwritten legal-pad list, and a man lying upside down on a bed. Under the collage is a white title, '10/10 habits to build disgustingly good taste', with a smaller '(niche edition)' line beneath. It stops the scroll for three reasons. 'Taste' is an identity-flex topic people want. 'Disgustingly good' is an unusual intensifier. 'Increasingly more niche' is an escalation promise that rewards watching to the end. The six-image grid previews every upcoming section, so viewers subconsciously wait to see each image explained.

beats.what: Title promise plus escalation: '10 out of 10 habits… increasingly more niche', over a six-image collage preview.
Habit 1: 'Steal from a world you got no business in.' The collage is replaced by one image (an office wall of notes).
'A sport you hate, a genre you never touch.'
Reason: 'the ideas no one's seen come from connecting two worlds no one thought to combine.' Cut lands here but the image stays.
Habit 2: 'Stop building a mood board of everyone else's life. Keep an archive of your own.' New image: B&W photos spread on a table.
'The screenshots, the voice notes, the things only you notice', then the mini-payoff 'that becomes your fingerprint.'
Habit 3: 'Take a song or painting you love and dig into why the artist made it. Not just what they made.' New image: man lying under cassette tapes.
Reframe: 'taste was never copying what was good, it's understanding the why beneath it.'
Habit 4: 'Study the design of the things you touch every day. The cup, the app, the chair.' New image: hand sketching a cup.
'Someone chose all of it… once you start seeing the choices, you… start seeing it appear everywhere.'
Habit 5: 'List everything you love… and find the thread running through all of it.' New image: handwritten legal-pad list.
Habit 6, the most niche: 'Force yourself to get bored.' New image: man lying upside down on a bed.
'We fill every second, the shower, the walk, the commute, with someone else's voice.'
Closing sting: 'that's not your taste forming, it's the algorithms.' Ends right on the word.

study.jump_cuts: There is almost no dead air. Speech covers 99% of the runtime, the median gap between words is 0.0s, and only one gap reaches 0.3s or more: 0.34s after 'choices,' at 31.54s, a natural comma beat left in. There are zero fillers, false starts or repeats, and the first word lands at 0.00s. Between sentences, gaps run ~0.08–0.18s (e.g. 3.76→3.88, 7.40→7.56, 11.06→11.24), so breaths are trimmed to a sliver. There are only 7 cuts in 44.4s (1.58 per 10s; median shot 5.4s, longest 7.73s). This reads as a tightly scripted read with breaths trimmed rather than a heavily chopped ramble. Every cut lands between thoughts, at the start of a sentence: 3.9 'Steal', 7.53 'Because', 11.27 'Stop', 18.27 'Take', 25.87 'Study', 33.6 'List', 37.5 'Force'. Six of the seven mark a new habit, and the 7.53 cut sits between a habit and its 'because' explanation. It feels brisk and dense (4.45 words/s) but not frantic.
study.zooms_punch_ins: None. Comparing the frames before and after every cut, the framing is identical: same medium close-up, same head size, same headroom, roughly 1.0x throughout. The cuts are plain jump cuts in the same framing. The main regular visual change is the top-of-frame image swapping on 6 of the 7 cuts (3.9, 11.27, 18.27, 25.87, 33.6, 37.5). That gives an image change every ~3.9–7.7s, plus the one-word caption changing every ~0.15–0.6s. Motion stays low (median 4.4/100), with a 25.1 spike only in the final half-second.
study.captions: One word on screen at a time, synced to each word's timing, so the word changes every ~0.1–0.6s. All lowercase ('steal', 'business', 'algorithms'), white, medium-bold clean sans-serif. There is no box and no heavy stroke, maybe a faint soft shadow. Size is modest, about the same as the title's main line. The caption sits centered directly under the top image, at ~33% of frame height (above the speaker's head, not over the chest). No colored or highlighted words and no visible pop animation; each word simply replaces the last. Because the caption sits in the same block as the image, the eye stays in one top-center reading zone.
study.on_screen_text: Hook title only, from 0.0s to the first cut at 3.9s. Line 1–2 reads '10/10 habits to build disgustingly good taste' in white sentence-case sans-serif, medium-bold, centered at ~33–38% of frame height. Below it is '(niche edition)' in a smaller, lighter weight. There is no background box. It sits directly under the six-image collage and disappears with the collage at the hard cut to habit 1. After that, there are no numbered headers, labels or point counters; the speech captions carry everything.
study.graphics_overlays:
Hook (0–3.9s): a 2x3 grid collage of six film-still-style images, about 67% of frame width, at ~13–31% of frame height. The images are an office wall of pinned notes, B&W photos on a table, a man lying under a wall of cassette tapes, a hand sketching, a handwritten legal-pad list, and a man lying upside down on a bed. After that, one image per habit, sized to ~57% width and placed in the same top zone. Each appears on a hard cut and stays for the whole habit:
- 3.9–11.27: the notes wall, with a tiny 'abc' bug, so it is likely a TV/film still.
- 11.27–18.27: B&W photo prints.
- 18.27–25.87: cassette-tape listener.
- 25.87–33.6: sketching a cup, which matches 'the cup'.
- 33.6–37.5: handwritten list, which matches 'List everything'.
- 37.5–end: bored man on bed.
The images are mostly static stills or near-static clips, with no borders, frames or emojis. The six grid tiles are exactly the six sections, so the hook visually 'table-of-contents' the video.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. Each cut also swaps the top image, so the cut and the graphic change land on the same frame. The final half-second shows a motion spike (25.1), consistent with a quick end or loop jump rather than a styled transition.
study.broll_and_interrupts: There is no full-screen b-roll and no angle or location change; the speaker is on screen 100% of the time. The pattern interrupts are the top-zone image swaps at 3.9, 11.27, 18.27, 25.87, 33.6 and 37.5s (gaps of 7.4, 7.0, 7.6, 7.7, 3.9s), plus the cut-without-image-change at 7.53. The images act as picture-in-picture b-roll that illustrates each habit while the face stays visible. The constant one-word caption changes are the micro-interrupt. No sound effects are identifiable. The strongest audio hits (0.37, 3.88-ish 5.03, 18.25, 25.99, 37.45…) line up with word onsets, especially the first word after each cut ('Take' 18.26, 'Study' 25.92, 'Force' 37.46). That suggests vocal emphasis rather than added SFX. Props: the white wired earbuds, whose mic wire he fiddles with, a casual self-filmed signal.
study.audio: Voice-forward and clear, likely recorded through the wired earbud mic close to the mouth. A slightly roomy indoor tone, no echo problems. Delivery is fast (4.45 words/s), warm and confident, with a slight smile, and punches the first word of each habit ('Steal', 'Stop', 'Take', 'Study', 'List', 'Force'). The given data doesn't confirm any music bed; any music would be low enough not to compete. No identifiable sound effects. Silence is never used for effect; the only pause over 0.3s is a 0.34s comma beat at 31.54s.
study.length_and_ending: 44.4s total, 196 words. The structure is six habits that get progressively more abstract and personal: borrowing from other fields, then a personal archive, then the why behind art, then everyday design, then the thread in your loves, then boredom. That delivers on 'increasingly more niche'. Small payoffs land inside each habit ('becomes your fingerprint' 17.74s, 'understanding the why beneath it' 25.2s, 'appear everywhere' 32.94s). The big payoff comes at 42.16–44.0s (95–99%): 'that's not your taste forming, it's the algorithms'.
