study.format: advice / tips (explainer with visual demonstration overlays)
study.topic: A 14-second cheat sheet for framing a vertical talking-head video: where the eyes, captions and title hook go, the safe, danger and avoid zones, keeping the eyeline matched on punch-ins, and stroking text over busy backgrounds.
study.hook: "This is where your eyes go" starts at 0.00s with no lead-in, at roughly 5 words/s. On screen: a medium waist-up shot of him at a desk, pointing at his own eyes. By 0.35s a translucent yellow pill wipes across his eyes at about 38% of frame height, and the single-word caption "this" sits at about 71% height. There is no title card. It stops the scroll because the first sentence is a promise the viewer sees answered instantly: he points, the graphic marks his eyes, and creators recognize it as a framing template they want to screenshot or save.

beats.what: "This is where your eyes go". A yellow pill highlights his eyes at about 38% frame height while he points at them.
"This is where your caption goes". A yellow rounded box appears behind the caption at about 71% height (around 1.77s).

"That's where you tie[title] the hook". A large yellow pill at the top (about 14% height) types out "Title hook" letter by letter (2.48s 'Ti', 2.80s 'Title ho', 3.19s 'Title hook'). He points up at it.
"This is your safe zone". Cut at 3.6s to a green translucent rounded rectangle covering the center (about 14–86% height, inset from the edges).
"This is your danger zone". Cut at 4.8s: the green flips to a red tint over everything outside the safe rectangle.
"This is where you should avoid at all costs". Cut at 5.87s: red now covers only the bottom strip and the lower-right side, where the platform UI sits.

"If you're going to punch in, keep the eyeline the same". A punch-in cut lands at 8.27s, mid-phrase on 'to [punch in]'. A white dashed horizontal line across his eyes (about 39% height) appears around 9.3–10.3s to show the eyeline matching the wide shot.
"If you have a busy background, add a stroke to your text". Still in the tight shot; the caption appears to gain a dark outline around 'stroke' / 'text'.
"So just remember next time." Cut back to the wide shot at 12.6s on 'So'. He holds up a finger and ends with a smile/nod. The video ends at 14.2s.

study.jump_cuts: Extremely tight. 0 gaps of 0.3s or more and 0 fillers. Median gap between words is 0.0s and the longest is 0.22s (3.22→3.44, between the first and second sentence). Sentence-boundary pauses of about 0.2s are left in (3.22–3.44, 7.72–7.92, 12.40–12.52). Speech fills 97% of the runtime at 4.96 words/s. 6 shots, 3.52 cuts per 10s, median shot 2.0s, longest 4.33s. Every cut lands mid-sentence rather than between thoughts: 3.6 between 'This' and 'is', 4.8 between 'is' and 'your', 5.87 between 'and' and 'this' / 'is', 8.27 between 'going' and 'to', 12.6 between 'So' and 'just'. Because the framing barely changes on most of these, they read as graphic-state changes, not jumps. It feels breathless and dense, but smooth.
study.zooms_punch_ins: One punch-in and one punch-out. At 8.27s it cuts from the wide (head top around 25% height, desk visible) to roughly 1.2x tighter (head and shoulders fill more, desk mostly gone), landing on 'going | to punch in'. The edit literally punches in on the words 'punch in'. The eyeline stays at about the same height in both, which is the point he's making. At 12.6s it cuts back to the original wide on 'So', starting the wrap-up. The other cuts (3.6, 4.8, 5.87) keep the same wide framing; only the overlay changes. Overall the visual changes about every 0.5–1.2s in the first 8s (eye pill, caption box, title pill typing, green, red, avoid zones). From 8.27–12.6 it relies on the dashed line and the caption alone, roughly every 1–2s.
study.captions: One word at a time, synced to each spoken word (word-by-word pop). White, bold rounded sans-serif, lowercase as spoken. Small-to-medium size, about 25% of frame width for longer words. Centered horizontally at about 71% of frame height. No box by default. From about 1.77–2.8s a yellow pill box sits behind the caption to demonstrate 'caption goes here'. Near the end ('stroke', 'text') the words appear to carry a thin dark outline to demonstrate the stroke tip. There are no color-highlighted keywords. One typo is left in: 'remmeber' at about 13.1s. The word 'tie' is captioned as 'title', matching the intended meaning.
study.on_screen_text: One text element besides captions: "Title hook" in white bold sans, centered inside a large translucent yellow / mustard pill at the top of frame (about 8–22% height). It types on letter by letter in a typewriter style from about 2.4s ('Ti' → 'Title ho' → 'Title hook' by about 3.2s). It disappears at the 3.6s cut, staying on screen about 1.2s.
study.graphics_overlays: All overlays are diagrams of the frame itself. (1) A translucent yellow horizontal pill over his eyes at about 38% height, wiping in by 0.35s and fading as the title appears (about 0.3–2.9s). (2) A yellow rounded box behind the caption at about 71% height, about 1.7–2.8s. (3) The yellow 'Title hook' pill at the top, about 2.4–3.6s. (4) A green translucent rounded rectangle 'safe zone' covering about 13–87% of the width and 14–86% of the height, 3.6–4.8s. (5) An inverted red tint over everything outside that rectangle as the 'danger zone', 4.8–5.87s. (6) Red tint only over the bottom strip (about the bottom 12%) and a right-side band from mid-frame down, the 'avoid at all costs' areas where the UI buttons and caption sit, 5.87–about 8.3s; it carries briefly into the tight shot. (7) A white dashed horizontal line through his eyes at about 39% height, about 9.3–10.3s, showing the eyeline. Each overlay switches on a cut or a spoken word with no flashy animation, just a quick wipe or fade.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. Five cuts: three disguised as overlay-color changes on the same framing (3.6, 4.8, 5.87), one punch-in (8.27) and one punch-out (12.6). There is a big motion spike (51.2) at about 14.0s right at the end, likely the final cut or loop frame.
study.broll_and_interrupts: No b-roll, no angle or location change, no props beyond the handheld wireless mic he holds the whole time. The pattern interrupts are entirely the diagram overlays, landing about every 1.1–1.2s for the first 8s (0.3, 1.2/1.7, 2.4, 3.6, 4.8, 5.87). After that come the punch-in at 8.27, the eyeline line at about 9.3 and the punch-out at 12.6. His hand gestures (pointing at eyes, at the caption area, upward at the title, open palm for 'safe') act as built-in interrupts synced to each overlay. The strongest audio hits track syllables roughly every 0.3–0.5s. None clearly stands out as a separate sound effect, so any whoosh or pop is unconfirmed.
study.audio: Clean, close voice from a handheld wireless mic, with minimal room sound. Delivery is fast (about 5 words/s) and upbeat, with list-like rhythm and parallel phrasing ('this is where… this is where… that's where…'). The data does not confirm any background music; speech covers 97% of the time. No silence is used for effect. The only breathing room is about 0.2s between sentences.
study.length_and_ending: 14.2s, 68 words. It builds as a rapid list of six framing rules, each shown visually: three placements in 0–3.2s, three zones in 3.4–7.7s, then two technique tips in 7.9–12.4s. The last and most practical tip (stroke on text) lands at 11.5–12.4s (about 81–87%). It ends on a soft CTA, "So just remember next time" (12.52–13.72s), and cuts 0.48s after the last word. The vague 'next time' plus a 14s runtime packed with diagrams encourages rewatching and saving rather than a hard follow ask.
study.quality: Native 720x1280, 30fps, HEVC at about 12.7 Mbps, sharp. Medium waist-up framing centered, with the top of the head at about 25% height and eyes at about 38%, so he practices what he preaches (eyes in the upper third). Soft, even daylight-style key from the front-left. A warm, tidy background: arched wooden bookshelf with soft amber accent light, a YouTube play button plaque, framed line art, and a desk with laptop and tablet in the foreground. A visible handheld mic signals 'creator who knows gear'. It feels high-effort and polished but personal: a real office, natural gestures, a smile, and one caption typo left in.
study.why_viral: It is pure utility in 14 seconds: every rule is shown on top of his own frame, so viewers screenshot it, save it as a reference and rewatch to catch each zone. The narration and the graphics are perfectly synced, with a new visual about every 1.2s for the first half and gestures pointing at each overlay, so there is nothing to skim past. It is meta: the video demonstrates its own advice (punching in on the words 'punch in', eyes on the line he describes), which is satisfying for creators and makes it shareable to other creators and editors. Its short length plus a soft 'remember next time' ending drives loops and completion.
lessons: Start talking at 0.0s with a sentence the visual answers in the same second: point and overlay together within 0.3–0.5s.
For explainer tips, make every claim visible: change an overlay or graphic about every 1–1.2s while listing points, and switch it exactly on the spoken keyword.
Hide cuts behind graphic changes: cut mid-sentence on the word where the overlay changes (e.g., 'this is | your'), keeping the framing identical, so the jump is invisible.
Trim to zero dead air: remove every gap of 0.3s or more and all fillers, and leave only about 0.2s breaths between sentences, targeting at least 95% speech share for short tips.

Use a punch-in of about 1.15–1.2x for the second half of a list or a new section, keep the eyes at the same height (about 38–40% from the top) in both framings, and punch back out to the wide for the wrap-up line.
Place single-word captions at about 70% frame height, centered, in white bold sans; keep the face in the upper 40% and the title or hook text in the top 10–20%.
Keep all text and faces inside a central safe zone (about 13–87% width, 14–86% height) and never place key text in the bottom ~12% or the lower-right band, where platform UI sits.
Over busy backgrounds, add a dark stroke or shadow to white caption text so it stays legible.
Type the hook title on letter by letter (about 0.8s) inside a semi-transparent rounded pill so it reads as an element being built, not a static card.
Keep tip videos under 15s and end within about 0.5s of the last word with a soft 'remember this' line to encourage saves and loops.
creator_advice: This is where your eyes go: put your eyes in the upper part of the frame (shown at about 38% height).
This is where your caption goes: in the lower-middle of the frame (shown at about 71% height).
That's where you put the title hook: at the top of the frame.
This is your safe zone: the central area of the frame.
This is your danger zone: the area outside the safe zone, around the edges.
This is where you should avoid at all costs: the bottom and lower-right of the frame, where the platform UI sits.
If you're going to punch in, keep the eyeline the same.
If you have a busy background, add a stroke to your text.

study.format: storytime / hot take hybrid: personal confession that turns into advice (selfie-style talking head)
study.topic: A founder at $400k/month admits he fell back into a 'productive' addiction (binge-watching YouTube business and self-improvement advice), explains why that content makes you feel worse by design, and tells ambitious people to focus on doing more of what already works.
study.hook: The first words start at 0.00s: "After my business hit 400k a month, I fell back into the same addiction that I had before I had even hit my first 10k a month." That is 26 words in 6.18s (~4.2 words/s, faster than his 3.43 average). In the first 2 seconds: a handheld selfie framing at night, his face centered with the eye line at roughly 40% of frame height, a blue-lit apartment and city windows behind. Two stacked overlays sit in the top third. The first is a screenshot of a YouTube video card (a 'Just Start.' thumbnail with a bearded creator's face, 9:59 duration, title 'You can have everything you want in 90 days', '505K · 1y ago'). Below it is the title text 'the dangerously “productive” addiction for ambitious men'. Captions read 'After my business hit $400k a month,'. It stops the scroll for three reasons: a big money flex ($400k/month) paired with a vulnerable confession ('addiction'), the paradox in the title ('dangerously productive'), and a recognizable YouTube-guru thumbnail that tells the viewer this is about the content they are consuming right now.

beats.what: $400k/month flex plus 'fell back into the same addiction' from before $10k/month. Title overlay and YouTube screenshot are on screen.
He used to think watching creators' self-improvement advice and 'secret hacks' was the path to $10k/month.
Contrast: when he actually hit $10k he 'oddly enough' watched the least YouTube.
Plateau. A hand-on-forehead frustration pose follows a 0.56s pause, then '400k, then 405k, then 420k' counted on his hand.
He cuts to hands on his head: he thought the fix was more 'how to scale to a million a month' videos.
Relatable scene: after a productive day, he eats a Yasso ice cream bar and watches YouTube to 'end my day on a fun note'. This is the longest shot, 24s.
He ended up feeling worse and questioning his own strategies despite a productive day.
'What hit me like a truck': every YouTube video is someone shilling their propaganda, likely because they sell a product.
It's a marketer's job to make you feel worse about your current state, so you feel deprivation and pay for a solution.
That explains his constant anxiety and shiny object syndrome.
Only ~10% of the info is practical. The other 90% is entertaining million-dollar funnels he'd never execute.
It's wasted energy he could have spent making another video or just working more.

'Subtle reminder to myself and anybody chasing the next ambitious goal: focus deeply on your goal. Do not let your energy get pulled away by 10 different people on YouTube.' Cut rhythm speeds up here.
'Ironically' he quotes Alex Hormozi: 'do more, then better, and then new.'
YouTube tempts you to do new instead of more. You should post more or better videos, but instead you're thinking 'new content, personal branding, niche strategy'.
Ends abruptly on 'niche strategy' with no CTA.

study.jump_cuts:
Dead air is almost fully removed: median word gap is 0.0s, 0 fillers, speech share 1.0, and only 8 gaps of 0.3s or more in 169s. The longest gap is 0.56s at 26.46s, after 'last three months,', left in as a dramatic beat before 'I hit 400k'. Others are kept for rhythm: 0.44s after 'month,' at 20.04 before 'oddly enough', 0.40s at 139.26 before 'focus deeply on your goal', and 0.42s at 165.94 between the list items. A verbal stumble was left in ('these YouTube video guides, these more of these YouTube video guides' at 36.7-38.6), so it isn't scrubbed perfectly clean. Cut rate averages 1.42 cuts/10s (25 shots, median 6.27s), but it's back-loaded:
- 0-141s: shots of 5-24s, about 0.9 cuts/10s.
- 141.9-148.8s: cuts every 1.1-2.1s (141.9, 143.0, 144.73, 146.83, 148.77).
- End: 163.53, 164.8, 167.07.
Most early cuts land between sentences (6.27, 25.47, 33.67, 65.17, 84.27, 94.13, 101.5, 134.93). Several land mid-sentence to hide pauses or swap takes (13.43 'hacks|trying', 41.17 'was|sitting', 70.5 'years|ago', 113.73, 123.17, 123.97, 136.97). Long takes are carried by fast, animated delivery rather than cutting, so it feels tight in audio and relaxed in picture.
study.zooms_punch_ins:
There are no digital zooms; framing changes come from re-takes and him moving the handheld phone.
- 13.43: the frame goes noticeably wider (more window and desk, head smaller, ~0.85x), coinciding with the title overlay disappearing.
- 25.47 and 33.67: same wide-ish frame, but a new acted pose (hand on forehead, then both hands on head).
- 70.5-84.27: drifts tighter; by ~83s his face fills more of the frame, ~1.25x vs the 60s shots.
- 84.27: back to medium.
- 141.9-148.77: rapid jump cuts alternate small framing shifts, ~1.05-1.1x.
- 164.8: medium with a wide-eyed 'oh' face on 'you're thinking, oh'.
- 167.07: the tightest frame of the video, ~1.4x, face filling the upper half, on 'new content, personal branding, niche strategy'.
Visual change interval is ~6-7s for most of the video (24s max, 41.17-65.17). It drops to ~1-2s in the CTA/takeaway stretch (141-149s) and the last 6s. Constant hand gestures keep motion in frame: median motion 6.0, with spikes of 13-21 between ~143-152s.
study.captions:
Phrase-chunk captions, not word-by-word. Each chunk runs 4-12 words over 1-3 lines and stays up for a clause or sentence (e.g. 'I thought the solution / would come from / watching more of these / YouTube video guys,'). Styling and position:
- Font: clean sans (TikTok/Inter-style), regular-medium weight, sentence case, white.
- Effects: a soft drop shadow only, no box, no highlight colors, no emphasis words.
- Size: modest, about 4% of frame height per line.
- Position: centered horizontally, sitting around 58-68% of frame height (chest level, just below the chin).
- Animation: none; chunks swap on cut or at phrase boundaries.
Numbers are formatted ('$400k', '10K', '10%', '$1 million'). Auto-caption errors were left in: 'guys' for 'guides', 'photos' for 'funnels', and a lowercase 'hormozi'. That casual, unpolished caption look is native-TikTok on purpose.
study.on_screen_text: One hook title: 'the dangerously “productive” addiction for ambitious men'. It's all lowercase, white, medium-weight sans with a soft shadow, two lines, centered at about 29-34% of frame height, directly under the YouTube screenshot. It is on from 0.0s with no animation in and disappears at the 13.43s cut (on screen ~13.4s, first two shots). No numbered points, headers or keyword pop-ups after that.
study.graphics_overlays: A screenshot of a YouTube video listing (thumbnail 'Just Start.' with a bearded creator's face, '9:59' duration badge, title 'You can have everything you want in 90 days', '505K · 1y ago'). It's placed in the top ~17-27% of frame, centered and about 60% of frame width. It is static, from 0.0s to 13.43s, removed together with the title. It works as visual proof of the 'addiction' (guru YouTube content). No emojis, arrows, progress bars or other overlays.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. They are jump cuts within the same location and setup, often paired with a pose or framing change; no whips, flashes or zoom transitions.
study.broll_and_interrupts:
No b-roll or cutaways at all; it's 100% face to camera. The pattern interrupts are performed by the speaker:
- 25.47: hand on forehead (frustration) on 'But for the last three months'.
- 28-32s: counting revenue on hand gestures.
- 33.67: both hands on head.
- 43-53s: crossed arms and a smug look for the ice cream 'fun note' moment.
- 113.73: eyes rolled up, dreamy, on 'entertaining these new ideas'.
- 164.8: exaggerated 'oh' face.
The only graphic change is the overlay removal at 13.43. No sound effects are evident; the listed audio hits (e.g. 5.87, 29.64, 117.42) line up with stressed words, not SFX. Interrupts land roughly every 5-15s early, then thin out in the 65-135s explanation section, where hand gestures carry it.
study.audio: A single voice, recorded close on a phone or lav. It's clean with a little room tone from the apartment and sounds intimate, like late-night talking. No music is evident from the data; the audio hits all coincide with spoken stresses. No sound effects. Delivery is fast and conversational: 3.43 words/s overall, faster in the hook. Silence is used sparingly for emphasis: 0.56s before 'I hit 400k', 0.40s before 'focus deeply on your goal'.
study.length_and_ending:
169.0s long, 579 words. The build:
- Confession hook (0-6s).
- Backstory of $10k vs $400k (6-40s).
- Relatable ice-cream scene and the 'felt worse' turn (40-65s).
- First payoff, the principle that videos are marketing propaganda, at 65.16s (~39%).
- Mechanism: a marketer makes you feel deprived (84-94s, ~50-56%).
- The 10%/90% stat at 107s (~63%).
- Main actionable takeaway, 'focus deeply on your goal', at 139.66s (~83%).
- Hormozi quote at 151.5s (~90%).
No CTA. It ends abruptly 0.28s after the last word ('niche strategy.' ends at 168.72), mid-list on the tightest frame. That leaves an unresolved, almost-cut-off feeling that encourages rewatching or commenting rather than a formal sign-off.
study.quality: Selfie handheld at arm's length (his arm is sometimes visible), eye line around 38-45% of frame height with small headroom. Framing drifts between medium and close because it's handheld. Lighting is moody: cool blue/purple ambient room light plus a soft key on his face. The background is a high-rise window with night city lights, a desk and a camera on a tripod, which subtly signals success and creator status. Picture is sharp; 720x1280 at 30fps, h264, ~6.3 Mbps. Mic sound is clean. The overall effect is casual on purpose: plain auto-captions with typos, no music, no b-roll, plain black tee. It reads as an honest late-night confession, not a produced ad, which fits a video criticizing over-produced guru content. The effort shows in the aesthetic setting and tight audio editing.
study.why_viral:
1) A paradox hook with credibility: a $400k/month founder confessing an 'addiction' that looks productive, which the target audience (ambitious young men watching business content) is literally doing while watching.
2) It flips the platform on itself, calling the creator economy 'propaganda' designed to make you feel deprived. That's validating, a little contrarian and highly shareable ('this is me').
3) Specific, relatable details (400k→405k→420k plateau, a Yasso ice cream bar, 10% practical/90% fantasy) make it feel true rather than preachy.
4) A clear, simple takeaway borrowed from a famous name (Hormozi's 'more, better, new') gives viewers something to quote and send to friends.
lessons: Open with the credibility number and the confession in the same first sentence. Start speaking at 0.0s and keep the hook under ~6s at a slightly faster pace (~4 words/s) than the rest.
Stack a lowercase paradox title (e.g. 'the dangerously “productive” addiction') above the face in the top 25-35% of frame. Remove it after the setup (~13s) so it doesn't compete with the story.
Use a screenshot of the thing you're talking about (a YouTube card, a DM, a stat) as the hook visual. It gives instant context without b-roll.
Cut every pause over ~0.3s except 1-3 deliberate beats of 0.4-0.6s placed right before the key number or the main takeaway.

Long shots (up to 24s) are fine if the speaker is animated. Let gestures and acted poses (hand on forehead, hands on head, eye-roll) do the pattern-interrupting, and place cuts where the pose changes.
Back-load the cut rhythm: ~1 cut per 7s through the story, then 1-2s cuts in the takeaway section (here 141-149s) to signal 'this is the important part'.
Put the tightest frame (~1.4x) on the final line, and end within 0.3s of the last word for an abrupt, rewatchable finish instead of a slow outro.

Plain white sentence-case captions with a shadow, in 1-3 line phrase chunks at ~60-65% height, fit confession/storytime videos better than flashy word-pop captions. Format numbers ($400k, 10%) for skimmability.
Mid-sentence cuts are acceptable to splice takes or hide breaths if the audio flows; most should still land between thoughts.
Structure long yaps as: hook → old belief → contrast → relatable scene → 'what hit me' principle (~40%) → mechanism → stat → takeaway (~80%) → borrowed quote.
creator_advice: It is sort of a marketer's job when they make a video to make you feel worse about your current state, so then you feel in this state of deprivation, like you need to pay for a solution.
Roughly 10% of that information [YouTube business/self-improvement content] is actually practical; 90% of the time you're entertaining new ideas and new funnels you'd never actually execute.
Instead of watching, I could have spent that extra energy making another video, or just working more.
Focus deeply on your goal. Do not let your energy get pulled away by 10 different people on YouTube every single time you open up social media.
Quoting Alex Hormozi: do more, then better, and then new.

When you watch YouTube you're always tempted to do new rather than simply do more of what you're already doing. Post more videos or better videos, instead of thinking 'new content, personal branding, niche strategy'.

study.format: advice / tips (episode 1 of a 'how I edit' tutorial series), talking head plus phone screen-recording demo
study.topic: A stay-at-home mom and new creator shows the first steps of how she edits her talking-head 'yap' reels in the free Edits app: trim out silences and fumbles, then add text before anything else.
study.hook: She starts talking at 0.00s with no lead-in: "here's exactly how I edit my talking head reels aka my yaps". That is 12 words in about 3.3s, then "part one of I don't know, we're gonna see how this goes" by 5.4s. The frame is a medium chest-up shot in a softly lit bedroom, and she holds a fuzzy lav mic near her chin. A large white serif title sits in the upper third from the first frame: "How I edit my yapping reels". Under it, a handwritten typewriter-style subtitle types itself out: "as a no…" at 0.15s, "as a non-techy SAHM" at 0.6s, "…to 3 boys" at 1.0s. A tilted handwritten tag "(highly requested series)" pops in at about 2.0s, and a script "Episode 1" appears at about 5.2s. Why it stops the scroll: it promises an exact, practical process ('exactly how'). It names the niche format ('yaps') and qualifies the viewer with a relatable underdog identity ('non-techy SAHM'), which says 'even you can do this'. The live-typing subtitle adds motion in the first second.

beats.what: "here's exactly how I edit my talking head reels aka my yaps". Title card, typing subtitle and 'highly requested series' tag.

study.why_viral:
1) Hyper-specific, saveable value for a huge aspiring-creator audience. 'Exactly how I edit my yaps', with a fonts/animations card she literally tells you to screenshot, drives saves and shares.
2) The relatable underdog frame ('non-techy SAHM to 3 boys', 'only been editing a few weeks', 'if I can do this so can you') makes viewers feel capable and lowers the barrier.
3) The video demonstrates the style it teaches. Zero pauses, word-by-word aesthetic captions, memes and text pops prove the method works while she explains it.
4) Series framing ('Episode 1', 'highly requested', agenda list, keyframes cliffhanger) creates open loops that push follows and return viewing.
lessons: Remove every pause: target zero word gaps over 0.3s and no fillers. This video runs 4.41 words/s with a 0.0s longest gap. Hide trims inside continuous speech so cuts feel invisible.

Put a big title card on screen from frame 0 that restates the promise (here 'How I edit my yapping reels'). Animate a qualifier subtitle typing in during the first second to add motion and niche identity.

Alternate wide and about 1.1–1.15x tight framings on cuts. Make punch-ins subtle and put them on sentence starts. Front-load cut density (about 3.4 cuts per 10s in the first 30s) and allow longer holds once the content carries itself.

Every 2–5s in the first minute add a new visual event: a text tag, a disclaimer line, an emoji note, or a 0.7–2s reaction meme that literally matches the words ('I didn't see that coming', 'mom' → MOM DAWG).
When the speaker lists what's coming, build the agenda on screen line by line in sync with each spoken item, then clear it on the next cut.
Switch format around the halfway point (here a screen-recording demo at 52%) to reset attention. Annotate it with arrows, cursor icons and highlight boxes on the exact button being named.
Make one 'screenshot this' asset (a clean card of tools/fonts/settings) near 80–90% of the runtime to drive saves.
Use word-by-word captions in a single consistent aesthetic font placed beside the face (about 50–55% of height). Tint topic nouns and action verbs a second color.
End within 0.2s of the last word, with a specific next-episode tease plus 'follow along' rather than a generic CTA.
creator_advice: Trim down your video: edit out any fumbles and remove silences.
Remember people's attention spans are shot, so keep the pauses out and keep quick transitions between thoughts.
On the main track you can use the split button to remove chunks of footage, or the slider to shorten or lengthen the clip.

After trimming, go through the whole video and add your text. Do not, and I repeat, do not do anything else at this point. Learn from my mistakes: do not add sound effects yet. You're going to move things around and change the text later, and it's much easier when you don't also have to move around sound effects and everything else.
Save your favorite text styles (click the little flag button) so it's super easy to go in and use what you know you like.
Your content will become more recognizable if you stay consistent with what you use (fonts, animations).
I do everything in the Edits app on my iPhone; it's pretty user-friendly and everything is free.
Make it your goal to improve ONE thing with each video. Just try to get a little bit better every day with each video.
Take what works for you, and if I can do this, so can you.

study.format: listicle
study.topic: Part 2 of a Portuguese-language 'ganchos visuais' (visual hooks) series: the creator acts out four physical opening moves you can use to start a video, set to Bee Gees' 'Stayin' Alive' with no spoken voiceover.
study.hook: There are no spoken first words. The 'words' in the transcript ('You can't tell by the way I used my', starting at 0.18s and running about 3.6 words/s) are the song lyric of 'Stayin' Alive', which kicks in right away. At 0.15s the frame is an empty dark window-and-brick wall, with the creator just entering from the right edge. At 0.33s a hard cut on a beat (audio hit at 0.29) shows her already in frame, smiling. The title 'GANCHOS' appears in huge neon-green condensed caps with 'visuais' in white bold lowercase underneath, at about 12–22% of frame height. By 0.91s she is centered with arms crossed. At about 1.2s she tilts her head up to look skyward. At about 1.5s 'parte 2' is added above the title. It stops the scroll because the opening is itself a visual hook: movement into an empty frame, then a confident pose. A recognizable song lands on the downbeat, and 'parte 2' signals a series worth catching up on.

beats.what: Empty frame of a dark window and brick wall. She walks in from the right as 'Stayin' Alive' starts.
Hard cut on the beat. Title 'GANCHOS visuais' appears. She settles center with arms crossed, then looks up at about 1.2s.
'parte 2' is added above the title, framing this as a series installment.

study.on_screen_text: 1) Series title from 0.33s to about 2.7s. 'GANCHOS' is in a tall condensed bold all-caps sans (Bebas/Anton style), neon light green (#B6F58A-ish) with a soft outer glow. study.broll_and_interrupts: The whole video is a string of pattern interrupts. Each roughly 2s segment brings a new location, angle, outfit or prop: the overhead bench shot at 2.1s, the book slammed toward the lens at about 4.2s, the empty chair and walk-in at 6.4s, and the bottle toss at about 8.5s. Two segments (0s and 6.4s) start on an empty frame and have her enter, which builds anticipation. study.audio: No voiceover. The audio is entirely Bee Gees 'Stayin' Alive' at full level from frame one, so the lyric 'You can't tell by the way I use my…' is what the transcript picked up. study.length_and_ending: 12.2s. It builds as a quick list of four demonstrated hooks, each about 2s, so the value is delivered continuously rather than at one payoff moment. The last hook ends at 10.53s (86%), then the CTA 'comente PARTE 3 para o próximo vídeo' holds for 1.67s over a smiling shot until the end. The ending is a comment-bait CTA that also teases the next installment. The music keeps running, so the short length makes it easy to rewatch on loop.
study.quality: 720x1280, 30fps, HEVC at about 12 Mbps (high bitrate for the size). It looks like a dedicated camera: cinematic grade with teal/dark shadows against warm brick and wood, soft overcast natural light, and a sharp subject with a softer background. Framing is mostly medium with generous headroom, which leaves room for the top-third titles; the eye line is at camera, and the bench shot is overhead. There is no mic sound because the track is music only. It feels high-effort: multiple outfits, locations and props, a polished grade and consistent branded typography.
study.why_viral: The video practices what it teaches: each segment is itself a visual hook, so viewers get four live demos of scroll-stopping openings in 8 seconds. It's an ultra-short, save-worthy listicle with clear 2–3 word labels, and it's easy to rewatch to copy the moves. A famous, upbeat song with beat-synced cuts makes it pleasant to watch and loop. The 'parte 2' framing and the 'comente PARTE 3' CTA drive comments and follows for the series.
lessons: Start on movement: open on an empty or near-empty frame and have the subject enter within 0.3s, then cut on the first beat.
Put the topic title in the top 10–22% of the frame within the first 0.4s, in one high-contrast style such as condensed caps with a neon glow, and keep it for about 2s.
For listicles, give each item its own setup (angle, location, outfit or prop) and hold it about 2s; change something visual every 1.7–2.3s.
Label each item with a 2–3 word all-caps header at the same position and in the same style so viewers can scan and screenshot it.
Snap cuts to the music's beat grid (here hits about every 0.3s); land major changes on a hit.
Use a light-leak/film-dust overlay sparingly to hide scene changes and add texture, roughly every other transition, with hard cuts at the open and the CTA.
Let physical actions play uncut (closing a book toward the lens, a toss, sitting or leaning); props moving toward the camera are free pattern interrupts.
End with a 1.5–2s on-screen comment CTA that names the next part (e.g. 'comment PART 3'), placed mid-frame over the subject, while the music keeps going.
creator_advice: Visual hook ideas shown on screen (no speech): 'Deitar e falar': lie down and talk to the camera (shot from above).
'Fechar o livro': close a book toward the camera to open the video.
'Entrar e apoiar': walk into an empty frame and lean on something (e.g. a chair) as you start talking.
'Arremessar': toss or throw an object toward or past the camera as the opening move.

study.format: listicle
study.topic: A creator rattles off 10 fill-in-the-blank opening lines ('hooks') that work for short-form videos, as templates viewers can save and reuse.
study.hook: "10 hooks that actually work." The first word lands at 0.00s with no lead-in, and the line runs 0.00–1.54s (5 words, about 3.2 words/s). On screen from frame one: a waist-up medium shot of the speaker centered behind a glossy dark table, against a blurred red-lit brick wall. He holds both hands up with all ten fingers spread on "10". A persistent two-line title sits at the top (~13–22% of frame height): '10 Hooks' in large bold white and 'That Actually Work' in smaller bold white. It stops the scroll for three reasons. It promises a concrete number of copy-ready templates. 'Actually' implies the other advice viewers have seen doesn't work. And the ten-finger gesture makes the number visual before the title is even read.

beats.what: "10 hooks that actually work." Ten fingers raised, top title already on screen.
#1 "No one told you about this." The '#1' label and caption fade in.
#2 "You are doing this wrong."
#3 "This changed everything for me." Follows the only noticeable pause, 0.38s after 4.10s.
#4 "X won't fix your Y." Caption shows '[X] WON'T FIX YOUR [Y]' as a template.
#5 "Here's what no one told you."
#6 "I almost didn't post this."
#7 "Watch this before you X."
#8 "This is your sign to X."
#9 "I wish someone told me this sooner."
#10 "You need to hear this." Video ends 0.12s after the last word. The line is itself a hook, so it rolls straight back into "10 hooks that actually work" on replay.

study.jump_cuts: No cuts at all: one 15.8s take (0 cuts per 10s). The tightness comes from delivery, not editing. Speech fills 99% of the runtime and the median word gap is 0.00s. Only one gap exceeds 0.3s: 0.38s after 'wrong' at 4.10s. Pauses between hooks are only ~0.10–0.20s (e.g. 1.54→1.74, 2.88→3.04, 7.40→7.52, 13.18→13.28). There are 0 fillers, 0 false starts and 0 repeats, at 3.83 words/s. It feels as tight as a heavily jump-cut video because the script is pre-written as 11 short lines (4–7 words each) delivered back to back. If the speaker breathed between lines, those breaths are tiny or already removed without visible cuts.
study.zooms_punch_ins: None. The framing stays constant at the same medium waist-up shot for the full 15.8s, with no punch-ins or digital zooms. Motion stays low (median 2.8/100), and the only spike, 10.2, is at the very end (~15.5s) from a hand gesture. Visual change instead comes from the text: a new number label and caption every ~1.2–1.6s (11 text changes in 15.8s), plus constant hand gestures.
study.captions: Phrase captions, not word-by-word: each whole hook appears as one block when the speaker starts it and stays until the next hook replaces it. They run 4–7 words over 2 lines, in bold white ALL CAPS sans-serif, small (roughly 4% of frame height per line). There is no box, a light shadow at most, and no highlighted or colored words. Placement is centered at ~52–56% of frame height, over the speaker's chest just above the shirt graphic. Each block fades in over a few tenths of a second: '#1' and 'NO ONE TOLD YOU ABOUT THIS' are semi-transparent at 1.98s and fully opaque by 2.77s. Placeholder brackets are kept in the text ('[X] WON'T FIX YOUR [Y]', 'WATCH THIS BEFORE YOU[X]', 'THIS IS YOUR SIGN TO [X]') so the captions read as fill-in templates. Caption timing matches speech start: #1 at 1.74, #2 at 3.04, #3 at 4.48, #4 at 6.12, #5 at 7.52, #6 at 8.70, #7 at 10.06, #8 at 11.60, #9 at 13.28, #10 at 14.74.
study.on_screen_text: 1) A persistent title, '10 Hooks' (large, heavy bold white sans) over 'That Actually Work' (smaller bold white, title case). It is centered at ~13–22% of frame height, above the speaker's head, on screen from 0.00s to the end with no animation. 2) Numbered counters '#1' through '#10' in large bold white sans, left of the head at ~43–46% of frame height. Each swaps in with a short fade at its hook's first word and stays until the next. '#10' is wider and sits slightly further left. study.graphics_overlays: none
study.transitions: hard cuts only (in fact zero cuts: a single continuous take; the only 'transitions' are text blocks fading in/out at each new hook)
study.broll_and_interrupts: No b-roll, cutaways, angle changes or sound effects. The pattern interrupts are all typographic: a new '#N' counter plus a new caption block about every 1.2–1.6s. The speaker's hands also move constantly: ten fingers on '10', open palms, pointing, and a shrug-like spread on #6 and #10. These keep the picture alive without edits. The audio hits (0.83, 1.11, 1.36 … 14.73s, about every 0.25–0.5s) follow his stressed syllables, not effects.
study.audio: Clean, close voice with a dry, controlled-room feel and no echo, delivered fast and evenly at 3.83 words/s. Nothing in the data indicates a music bed or sound effects; the strongest audio hits line up with spoken syllables. No silence is used for effect. The longest pause is 0.38s.
study.length_and_ending: 15.8s total. There is no build or argument: it is a flat, rapid list where each item is equally weighted. The 'payoff' is completing the list. #10 lands at 14.74s (93%), and the last word ends at ~15.68s, with the video cutting 0.12s later. There is no CTA spoken or written. The final line 'You need to hear this.' is itself a hook-style opener, so the end flows straight into '10 hooks that actually work' on autoplay. That creates a seamless loop and encourages rewatching to catch all ten.
study.quality: 720x1280 at 30fps, HEVC at ~11.9 Mbps, so cleanly encoded and sharp on the subject. It is a medium waist-up shot with the speaker centered, eyes at ~30% of frame height, and deliberate extra headroom left for the title. He leans on a glossy dark table that reflects him in the lower third. The background is a red-lit brick wall with shelves, heavily defocused (shallow depth of field), so it looks like a cinema camera or fast lens in a moody bar or studio set. The face is softly key-lit against the red ambience. Mic sound is clean and close. It feels high-effort and polished visually, yet the edit itself is minimal: one take plus text. That makes the format cheap to reproduce.
study.why_viral: 1) Pure save-bait utility: ten copy-paste templates with [X]/[Y] placeholders, delivered in 16 seconds, so people save and share it to use later. 2) Extreme density: the first word at 0.00s, 3.83 words/s, 99% speech share, and a new item every ~1.4s leave no room to scroll. 3) The visible '#1–#10' counter creates a completion urge: viewers stay to reach #10. 4) The last line is itself a hook, so it loops seamlessly into the opening and drives rewatches.
lessons: Start speaking at frame 0. The first word should land within 0.0–0.2s, and the title should already be on screen in the first frame.
For listicles, write each item as one short line (4–7 words) and space items ~1.2–1.6s apart; trim inter-item pauses to ≤0.2s and any single gap to under 0.4s.
Put a persistent title at the top (~13–22% of frame height) that states the number and the promise; leave it up for the whole video so late joiners know what they're watching.
Add a large '#N' counter that swaps at the exact first word of each item; it acts as a progress bar and makes viewers stay to the last number.
When there are no cuts, refresh the screen with text: aim for some visual change (new caption or counter) at least every ~1.5s.
Show the item as a full phrase caption (2 lines, bold white ALL CAPS, centered ~52–56% height) fading in over ~0.2–0.5s rather than word-by-word when the line itself is the takeaway.
Keep template placeholders like [X] and [Y] in the on-screen text so the viewer reads it as something to copy, which drives saves.
End on a line that could also be an opener and cut within ~0.1–0.2s of the last word so the video loops cleanly into the first line.
Encourage the speaker to gesture on key words (e.g. ten fingers on '10') so a single locked-off shot still has motion.
A polished one-take shot (shallow depth of field, colored practical light, clean close mic) can replace heavy cutting when the script is dense enough.
creator_advice: Hooks that actually work, use as templates:
"No one told you about this."
"You are doing this wrong."
"This changed everything for me."
"X won't fix your Y."
"Here's what no one told you."
"I almost didn't post this."
"Watch this before you X."
"This is your sign to X."
"I wish someone told me this sooner."
"You need to hear this."

study.format: listicle
study.topic: A creator starts rattling off a numbered list of 50 meme sound effects (Vine Boom, Bruh, Emotional Damage...) to use in short-form content, with a 1-50 checklist on screen that fills in as she names each one.
study.hook: "50 sound effects for your short form content" starts at 0.00s with no lead-in and is delivered fast: 8 words in about 2.0s (whole clip 3.37 words/s, no gaps over 0.2s). In the first 2 seconds we see a medium-wide shot of her sitting low in frame in a gray armchair, holding a fuzzy lav mic up to her mouth like a handheld mic, with a calico cat in the lower right. The top ~45% of the frame already shows a bold yellow-green title, '50 SOUND EFFECTS', above an empty numbered list from 1 to 50 in three columns. It stops the scroll because the number 50 plus a visibly empty 50-slot list promises a big, saveable resource. The blank slots create a 'fill-in' itch, so viewers want to watch the list complete.

beats.what: "50 sound effects for your short form content": the promise, said over the title and an empty 1-50 list. Phrase captions 'for your' / 'short form content' appear under her face.
"Vine boom": she names #1, captions disappear and 'Vine Boom' types into slot 1 at about 2.28s.
"Bruh": #2, 'Bruh' appears in slot 2 at about 3.00s.
"Emotion(al damage)": #3, 'Emotional Damage' appears in slot 3 at about 3.37s. The clip ends at 3.64s mid-list, 47 slots still empty.

study.jump_cuts: No visible cuts: one continuous 3.64s shot (0 cuts per 10s). Speech is nearly wall-to-wall: 98% speech share, median word gap 0.0s, longest gap 0.2s, no gaps of 0.3s or more and 0 fillers. The 0.14s gap before 'Vine boom', the 0.2s before 'Bruh' and the 0.04s before 'Emotion' are the only breaths. Either it was delivered in one rapid take or any trims are invisible. It feels very tight, like a rapid-fire countdown.
study.zooms_punch_ins: None. Framing is locked for the full 3.64s with no punch-ins or digital zooms. Motion stays between 0.7 and 1.7 out of 100 (median 0.9), so the only movement is her head and hand. Visual change comes entirely from text: captions at 1.00s, 1.37s and off at about 2.28s, then list entries at about 2.28s, 3.00s and 3.37s. That is a new visual element roughly every 0.4-0.8s.
study.captions: Phrase-based speech captions used only during the hook: 'for your' at about 1.00s, replaced by 'short form content' at about 1.37s and held until about 2.2s. They are 2-3 words at once, white bold sans-serif in lowercase with a soft shadow and no box, medium size, centered at about 69% of frame height (over her chest, just below the mic). No highlighted words. The first words ('50 sound effects') have no caption because the title already says it. Captions are dropped entirely once the list starts, and the list entries do the captioning job.
study.on_screen_text: 1) Title '50 SOUND EFFECTS': heavy, extra-bold rounded sans-serif in all caps, yellow-green/lime fill with a slight shadow, spanning nearly the full width at about 12% of frame height. On screen from frame 0 to the end, static. 2) A numbered list '1.' to '50.' in small white regular-weight text, in three columns (1-18 left, 19-34 middle, 35-50 right), filling about 15-47% of frame height over the ceiling area. On from frame 0. Entries appear instantly (no visible animation) about 0.04-0.12s after each word starts: 'Vine Boom' in slot 1 at about 2.28s, 'Bruh' in slot 2 at about 3.00s, 'Emotional Damage' in slot 3 at about 3.37s. The text shows the full meme name even though she clips the word ('Emotion.'). Entries stay once added, so the list accumulates.
study.graphics_overlays: none besides the text list; no emojis, stickers, arrows or progress bars. The empty numbered list itself works as a progress bar.
study.transitions: hard cuts only (actually none — single continuous shot)
study.broll_and_interrupts: No b-roll, cutaways or angle changes. The pattern interrupts are text events: caption swaps at 1.00s and 1.37s, captions clearing and the first list entry at about 2.2s, then entries at about 3.0s and 3.4s. The interval shrinks from about 0.9s to about 0.4s as the list speeds up. The cat in frame is a passive prop/curiosity element, and the lav mic held like a handheld mic is a visual gag. The audio hit at 3.51s may be the start of a demo sound, but the clip doesn't make clear whether each effect is actually played, so no SFX are confirmed.
study.audio: Close, clean lav voice (she holds the lav right at her mouth) with a little room tone. No audible music bed in the data. Delivery is quick and punchy, with each list item said as a short standalone word. No silence is used for effect; the longest pause is 0.2s.
study.length_and_ending: 3.64s total. The promise takes 0-2.02s (55%) and the list payoff starts at 2.16s (59%), then accelerates to 3 items in 1.4s. It ends 0.08s after the last word, mid-list with 47 slots unfilled, an abrupt cliffhanger. Viewers either loop it, open the full video or save it, and the hard stop makes the loop nearly seamless back to the '50 sound effects' promise. No verbal CTA.
study.quality: 1284x2778 HEVC at 44.66fps, 9578 kbps: a high-resolution phone capture. She sits low in frame (eyes at about 56% of frame height), with the large space above deliberately left for the title and list over a neutral arched ceiling. Soft warm indoor daylight, slightly flat and pinkish on the face. A casual home background: gray wingback chair, wood-beam ceiling, cat. Sharp enough. The casual sweatshirt-and-cat setup makes it feel low-effort and authentic. The effort is in the pre-built 50-slot text template, which is what makes it look organized and valuable.
study.why_viral: 1) A big concrete number plus a visible empty 50-slot checklist creates a completion urge and a 'save this for later' reflex: utility content that gets saved (3.5K saves vs 3K likes in the visible counts). 2) The meme names (Vine Boom, Bruh, Emotional Damage) are instantly recognizable, so each item gets a small hit of recognition and humor. 3) A rapid-fire pace (3.37 words/s, 0.2s max gap) with a new text element every 0.4-0.9s leaves no room to scroll. 4) Ending abruptly mid-list drives loops and clicks into the full video or series.
lessons: Start speaking at 0.00s with the number and the promise in one sentence; keep the hook under about 2s.
For list content, put the full empty numbered template on screen from frame 0 so the scale of the payoff is visible before any item is said.
Reveal each list item on screen within about 0.1s of the speaker starting the word, and leave earlier items visible so the list accumulates.
Write the full, searchable name of each item even if the speaker clips it (spoken 'Emotion', text 'Emotional Damage').
Drop speech captions once the list text takes over, so two text systems never compete. Use 2-3-word phrase captions at about 65-70% of frame height only during the intro.
Keep word gaps at or under 0.2s in rapid-fire lists, and let the items speed up (about 0.9s down to 0.4s apart) to build momentum.
With a locked, static shot (motion under 2/100), a new text event every 0.4-0.9s is enough to replace punch-ins.
Frame the speaker low (eyes around 55% of frame height) when the top half needs to hold a title and list, and keep the background above plain enough for small white text to read.
Cut within about 0.1s of the last word, and consider ending mid-list to force a loop or a click to part 2.
creator_advice: Use sound effects in your short-form content; her list starts with: 1. Vine Boom, 2. Bruh, 3. Emotional Damage (of 50).

study.format: advice / tips (filming hack tutorial with a live demo at the end)
study.topic: A filming hack for talking-head Reels: switch the phone to the other hand for every sentence, so the background changes with each clip and you get a natural break to check your notes.
study.hook: "I want to show you one of my favorite hacks for talking head reels that makes them so much easier to film and so much more engaging" starts at 0.00s with no lead-in. The first sentence runs about 20 words in 3.82s (~5.2 words/s, faster than the video's 4.22 average). The first 2 seconds are a handheld selfie shot from a low angle. At 0.15s he is mid-word with his mouth wide open and the camera still swinging into place (motion 33.1 in the first half-second, the highest in the opening). At 0.56s he pushes an open palm toward the lens. The captions read '🔍 I want to / SHOW YOU', then '🤩 one of my / FAVORITE HACKS', then 'FOR TALKING HEAD REELS' in big yellow caps. It stops the scroll because of the energetic face filling the frame, the hand reaching into the lens, a clear promise ('favorite hack') aimed at a specific audience (talking-head creators), and a double benefit ('easier to film' + 'more engaging').

beats.what: Handheld selfie: 'I want to show you one of my favorite hacks for talking head reels…' Hand pushes toward the lens, the camera moves constantly.
Double benefit: 'so much easier to film and so much more engaging in the process.'
Cut to a static, phone-propped medium shot with the phone held as a prop: 'All you're going to do is switch hands with each sentence.' He physically switches the phone between hands while saying it.
Step one: he mimes recording a selfie: 'record yourself saying the hook or beginning the video.'
Quick 0.6s wide shot on 'Then', then a cut to 'switch hands, check your notes, remind yourself of what you wanted to say for the second sentence.'
New take with the phone up in his other hand: 'and record yourself saying that. Switch back for the third, back for the fourth and continue switching back and forth…'
Punch-in on 'remainder of your video' marks the end of the method steps.
Why it works: 'With each clip, the background will change and it will make editing and remembering what you wanted to say so much easier.' Punch-in on 'so much easier' at 29.33.
'Here's what it looks like.' A 0.58s pause, then the hand covers the lens (black/blurred frames around 31.7s) as a transition into the demo.
Demo clip 1, right-hand selfie with the curtain/window background: 'This is my video's hook, the first sentence of my reel.'
Demo clip 2, left-hand selfie with the kitchen background: 'I've now switched to my left hand… filming the second clip.'
Demo clip 3, back to the right hand and the curtain background: 'Now my phone is back in my right hand.'
'It's easy to remember what I wanted to say and I can keep going.' It ends mid-flow with a smile and a thumbs-up emoji, implying the method continues forever.

study.jump_cuts: Extremely tight. Speech fills 99% of the runtime, the median gap between words is 0.00s, there are 0 fillers, and only 2 gaps reach 0.3s or more. The first is 0.3s after 'sentence' (9.0s), a natural breath before 'So step number one'. The second is 0.58s after 'like.' (31.2s), left in on purpose as the beat before the demo while the hand covers the lens. 13 cuts in 43.5s = 2.99 cuts per 10s. The median shot is 3.15s, the longest 6.43s (6.83–13.27), and the shortest 0.6s (13.27–13.87). About half the cuts land between thoughts: 5.8 before 'All', 13.27 before 'Then', 24.2 before 'With', 31.7 before 'This', 34.93 before 'I've', and 39.47 before 'Now'. The other half land mid-sentence: 6.83 'is | switch', 13.87 'Then | switch', 18.1 'sentence | and record', 23.13 'for the | remainder', 25.13 'each clip, | the background', 29.33 'say so | much easier', 36.4 'hand, | reminded'. The mid-sentence cuts work because each is a fresh take or angle, so they read as momentum rather than errors. The method itself is a jump-cut system: each sentence is its own take, so breaths and note-checking fall outside the clips by design.
study.zooms_punch_ins: Few true punch-ins; most visual change comes from take or angle changes. 23.13s: punch-in to ~1.2x (face and shoulders fill the frame, the couch is cropped out) on 'remainder of your video', held 1.07s. 24.2s: back out to the medium framing on 'With each clip'. 25.13s: slightly wider/re-framed medium showing the full torso and both shirt pockets, on 'the background will change'. 29.33s: punch-in to ~1.2–1.25x on 'SO MUCH EASIER', the benefit line, held 2.37s until the demo. 13.27s: a brief re-framed, slightly wider take (more couch and window visible), 0.6s, on 'Then'. 18.1s: a new framing with him shifted left, phone raised in his other hand. Selfie sections (0–5.8 and 31.7–43.5) have constant handheld drift and a natural push/pull from the arm instead of digital zooms. The pattern goes medium → tight on the summary/benefit phrases → back out. Overall the shot changes every ~3.1s median (range 0.6–6.4s), while captions and emojis change every ~0.5–1s, so something on screen moves at least once a second.
study.captions: Phrase-by-phrase captions, 2–4 words on screen at a time, changing every ~0.5–1.2s in sync with speech. Two-line layout: a small top line in white mixed-case condensed sans with one word set in italic for emphasis ('That *makes* them', 'so much *easier*', 'and so *much*', 'is to *record*', '*saying* the', 'or *beginning*', '*Check* your', 'and it will *make*', 'the *first*', 'I can *keep*'), and a much larger bottom line in ALL-CAPS heavy condensed sans for the keyword. The keyword is colored lime green (SHOW YOU, FAVORITE HACKS, TO FILM, MORE ENGAGING, SWITCH HANDS, HOOK, THE VIDEO, NOTES, WANTED TO SAY, SO MUCH EASIER, SWITCHED, FILMING) or yellow (FOR TALKING HEAD REELS, SENTENCE, YOURSELF, SECOND SENTENCE, BACK & FORTH, LEFT HAND), alternating so the color itself changes often. The highlighted words are the action verbs and nouns of the method (switch, record, hook, notes, sentence, editing, background). Occasionally the order flips (big 'THE BACKGROUND' on top, small 'will change' below), and a few short phrases are a single small line in yellow or white ('All you're / going to do', 'Here's what it / looks like', 'is back in / my right hand' with a green second line). Soft dark drop shadow, no box. Centered horizontally, sitting at ~60–70% of frame height (chest level), below the face. They appear with a quick pop; no word-by-word karaoke.
study.on_screen_text: none (no title card, headers or numbered labels; all text is speech captions)
study.graphics_overlays: Small animated emojis/icons attached to the caption block, roughly one every 1–3s: 🔍 (I want to show you), 🤩 (favorite hacks), 🎥 (to film), 👀 (more engaging), a 🔁 swap icon with curved arrows under 'SWITCH HANDS' (7.2s and 13.9s) and 'BACK & FORTH', 🎥 (record yourself), a speech-bubble icon (hook / second sentence), 🤔 (remind yourself), a clip/film icon (each clip), 👨‍💻 (editing), ✨ (so much easier), 🎥 (my video's), 💡😀 (reminded myself), 🗣️ (wanted to say), a phone icon (filming / my phone), 👍🏼 (keep going). They sit beside or just under the keyword line and pop in with the caption. No arrows, progress bars, screenshots or split screens.
study.transitions: Mostly hard cuts between takes and angles. Two moments carry motion-blur energy: at 6.83s and 13.87s the frame before the cut is blurred from him moving the phone in his hands, so the cut feels like a whip on action. At ~31.5–31.8s the lens is covered by his hand (blurred skin tone, then a near-black frame; motion spikes to 45.7, the highest in the video) and opens into a blurred whip into the selfie demo, a hand-over-lens / whip transition marking the switch from explanation to demo. Inside the demo, each hand switch (34.93, 39.47) is a hard cut that also flips the background (curtains → kitchen → curtains), which is the whole point.
study.broll_and_interrupts: No b-roll. The pattern interrupts are built into the filming: (1) the format change from selfie (0–5.8) to propped medium shot (5.8–31.7) back to selfie (31.7–end), (2) a physical prop, the phone being passed between hands on the words 'switch hands' at ~7s, ~14s and ~20–23s, plus him miming recording at 9.5–13s and 18–19.5s, (3) a background change on every cut in the demo (31.7, 34.93, 39.47), and (4) color-alternating captions and emojis every ~0.5–1s. Visual changes come every ~3s from cuts, with gestures and emoji pops filling in between. No sound effects are evident; the strongest audio hits (0.37 through 30.93) line up with stressed syllables in his speech.
study.audio: Clean, close voice with light room tone from a bright home interior, likely a phone or lav mic. The delivery is fast (4.22 words/s average, ~5.2 in the hook) and energetic, with big stresses on 'show', 'favorite', 'switch' and 'easier'. No music bed is evident from the audio peaks, which follow the speech. No sound effects are detectable. The only intentional silence is the 0.58s beat at 31.2s, used to set up the demo.
study.length_and_ending: 43.5s, 182 words. It builds as promise (0–5.6) → one-line method (6.06–8.9) → step-by-step (9.3–24) → benefit (24.2–29.9, 'so much easier' at 29.5–29.9, ~68%) → 'Here's what it looks like' (30.4) → proof demo (31.7–43.1, 73–99%). The real payoff is the demo, where the viewer sees the background flip on each hand switch. It ends on 'It's easy to remember what I wanted to say and I can keep going.' with a thumbs-up emoji; there is no CTA. The open 'keep going' ending and the jump back to the same right-hand framing create a soft loop into the selfie opening. It cuts 0.35s after the last word.
study.quality: 720x1280, 30fps, h264 at ~1360 kbps (compressed upload, fine for phone viewing). Bright natural daylight from large windows, a clean airy home background (white walls, exposed wood beams, walnut kitchen cabinets, linen curtains) and a distinctive cream-and-green bowling shirt that keeps him recognizable. The propped shots are medium (waist up), eyes at ~30–35% from the top, with a modest amount of headroom. The selfie shots are close, chest up, at arm's length, slightly low angle. Sharp enough, with some motion blur during the hand switches. It deliberately mixes 'casual' phone selfie footage with a more produced propped shot plus polished two-tone captions and emojis, so it feels approachable but edited with care.
study.why_viral: 1) It solves a real, specific pain for a huge creator audience (forgetting lines, boring single-angle talking heads) with a zero-cost trick anyone can try today, which makes it highly saveable and shareable. 2) Show-don't-tell: the last 12s prove the hack live, with the background visibly flipping on each hand switch, so the payoff is visual and instant. 3) Relentless pacing: the first word lands at 0.00s, there is no dead air (median gap 0s), cuts come ~every 3s, and the two-color captions with emojis refresh every second. 4) The video is an example of its own advice: sentence-per-clip cutting is the edit, so viewers absorb the technique just by watching.
lessons: Start the first word at 0.0s and make the first sentence both the promise and the audience callout ('favorite hack for talking head reels'), delivered faster than the rest (~5 words/s versus ~4.2 average).
Open on movement: a handheld frame still settling, or a hand pushing toward the lens in the first 0.5s, gives a motion spike that stops the thumb.
Cut every breath and note-check: aim for a median word gap of 0s, fewer than 1 gap of 0.3s+ per 20s, and leave one deliberate 0.5–0.6s pause only before the big reveal or demo.
Treat each sentence as its own clip and change something visual on every cut (angle, hand, background, crop). Target a shot every ~3s (≈3 cuts per 10s), with nothing held longer than ~6.5s.
Save punch-ins (~1.2x) for summary and benefit phrases ('for the remainder of your video', 'so much easier'), hold them 1–2.5s, then return to the base framing.

Use two-tier captions: a small white mixed-case setup line with one italic emphasis word, and a big all-caps keyword line alternating lime green and yellow. Place them at ~60–70% of frame height so the face stays clear.
Attach a relevant emoji to roughly every second caption to add a micro visual change every 1–3s without adding b-roll.
After explaining a process, prove it: say 'Here's what it looks like', use a hand-over-lens or whip transition, and give the demo the final ~25% of the runtime.
Have the speaker act out verbs with a prop (passing the phone on 'switch hands', miming recording on 'record yourself') so the edit can cut on the action.
End within ~0.35s of the last word on an open, forward-moving line ('I can keep going') rather than a long outro, so it loops cleanly.
creator_advice: One of my favorite hacks for talking head reels makes them so much easier to film and so much more engaging: all you're going to do is switch hands with each sentence.
Step number one is to record yourself saying the hook or beginning of the video.
Then switch hands, check your notes, remind yourself of what you wanted to say for the second sentence, and record yourself saying that.
Switch back for the third, back for the fourth, and continue switching back and forth for the remainder of your video.
With each clip the background will change, and it will make editing and remembering what you wanted to say so much easier.

study.format: hot take / advice with a sales CTA (contrarian talking head, heavily edited with b-roll, text cards and screenshots)
study.topic: A personal-branding coach argues that posting more won't grow you; you need a posting strategy built on content only you can make and honesty that builds trust, then he pitches a free call.
study.hook: "Stop posting more, I mean it" starts at 0.00s, the first frame, with no lead-in. The first 6 words land in 1.66s, then he settles into the overall ~3.9 words/s. The frame is a wide, eye-level desk shot in a bright white apartment with windows behind and hands gesturing. Big white bold uppercase sans text builds word by word at center, around 60-70% of frame height: 'STOP' (0.0s), 'STOP POSTING' (~0.3s), 'STOP POSTING MORE.' (~0.64s). At ~1.2s a green bar flicks on screen before it switches to single-word captions. It stops the scroll because it is a direct command that contradicts the advice every creator has been given ('post consistently'), so viewers who post a lot feel called out. The next line, 'you've been told for two years… and your views haven't changed at all', names their pain inside 9s.

beats.what: 'Stop posting more, I mean it.' Contrarian command, with the title stacking word by word.

'You've been told for two years to post consistently, every day, twice a day, three times a day, with carousels and stories.' A cream bullet-list card at 4.2s, then an Instagram carousel screenshot pops in on 'carousels'.
Pain: 'and your views haven't changed at all.' 'ALL' in caps.
Einstein insanity quote on a black quote card. The serif text types on in sync with the words (9.33-14.73s).
'You can't just post more bad content and expect to grow. What you really need is clarity, and you just don't have that yet.'
New camera angle plus a 'THE DAILY NEWS' headline graphic: 'the rules for building a personal brand on Instagram has completely changed.'
'The old rule was simpler': 'Post more / Be consistent / Follow the trends' pills stack at the top, then 'EVENTUALLY, the algorithm rewards you.'
'Here's why that doesn't work now' (punch-in). Billions of people, millions posting daily, shown over stock b-roll of phone scrolling and eyes with floating images.
'If you're posting the content everyone else is posting, how could you expect to stand out?' Black icon card, then a circle-cropped talking head among floating post icons.
'You don't. And that's the problem no one is naming for you.'
Reframe: 'You don't have a posting frequency problem (clock icon), you have a posting strategy problem (chess king icon).'
'You can't fix that by doing more of the wrong thing. The fix is posting content only you can post.' Cream kinetic text card, then his old day-in-the-life vlog clips.
'That's what standing out means in 2026. You don't have to be an influencer to win' (influencer and Lamborghini screenshots) '…post the thing no one can take from you.'
'We're all online looking for the same thing: a solution to something we're stuck on from someone we trust.' Black, then cream kinetic text cards.
Trust isn't built with a 'perfectly staged video' (behind-the-scenes studio b-roll) or a 'pretty background'. It's earned with 'honesty' about what you're figuring out (raw vlog clip).
'People buy from people they resonate with, and selling to those people isn't being salesy.' Black text card.

Proof/credentials: 'my name is Jun' (on-stage waving clip), 5M followers (profile screenshot with the count circled), 'my family's first millionaire' (surprising-dad clip), 'biggest launch of my career all in public' (Instagram story screenshot).
'Yeah, so this definitely works and I'm proof of it.'

New close-up setup: 'If you're serious about building your presence online, book a call, completely free, with my team… tap the link below… I'd really love for you to finally have someone on your side.'

study.jump_cuts: Extremely tight. The speech share is 1.0, there are zero gaps of 0.3s or more between words, the median gap is 0.0s, and there are 0 fillers. Every breath, pause and restart is removed, so it reads as one continuous run of words at 3.93 words/s. No pause is left in for effect. Hard cuts run 2.25 per 10s (median shot 4.2s, longest 6.53s). Most cuts land mid-sentence or right on a word boundary inside a thought: 4.2 'every|day', 9.33 'albert|einstein', 32.4 'now|there are', 47.07 'you can't|fix', 58.87 'from you|we're'. This keeps momentum and hides the trims. A few land between thoughts (14.73 'result|you can't', 39.87 'out?|you don't', 91.7 into the CTA). It feels breathless but controlled.
study.zooms_punch_ins: Two camera setups alternate in the main body: Angle A, frontal, wide, used 0-21s; Angle B, slightly angled with windows and couch on the right, used 21-91s. Each has wide and tighter versions. Punch-ins (tighter versions of the same shot): ~1.15x at 17.67s on 'What you really need is clarity'; ~1.3x by ~31s on 'here's why that doesn't work now' (face fills the upper frame); ~1.15x around 40.7-43s on 'that's the problem no one is naming for you', which cuts back wide at 43.03 for the reframe line; ~1.15x around 57-58.9s on 'the thing no one can take from you'; ~1.2x at 63.97s on 'and trust isn't built'; ~1.15x around 69.5s on 'the one thing money can't fake'; ~1.15x at 73.33s on 'that's why people buy from people'; ~1.15x around 88.6s on 'exactly how it works', back wide at ~90.4 on 'definitely works'. Counting overlays, cards, b-roll and caption style switches, the visual changes roughly every 1.5-3s and never sits unchanged longer than ~4s.
study.captions: Mostly one word on screen at a time, popping exactly on each spoken word. Short 2-4-word phrases appear sometimes ('The old rule was', 'expect to grow.', 'take from you.', 'book a call', 'We'll look at', 'you want to go', 'and grab', 'and I'd really'). Base style is a bold rounded sans in white, sentence case (capitalized at sentence starts), with a soft drop shadow and no box. It is medium size, centered at ~60-63% of frame height, roughly chest level and just under the face. Emphasis words switch style: ALL-CAPS large sans for intensity ('STOP POSTING MORE.', 'ALL', 'COMPLETELY', 'EVENTUALLY,'); elegant italic serif for emotional or key words ('consistently', 'expect to grow.', 'now.', 'take from you.', 'background.', 'biggest', 'exactly', 'definitely'); black or cream rounded pill boxes for punchy nouns and judgments ('bad', 'you.', 'posting', 'perfectly staged video', 'honesty', 'public'). Larger words call out numbers ('2026.'). Captions also sit over b-roll and black or cream cards in the same position, so the reading spot stays fixed.

Cream full-screen card at 4.2s with black bold sans bullet text ('• every day', listing frequencies).
