In order: cream list card 4.2s; IG screenshot ~6.2s; Einstein card 9.3-14.7s; newspaper banner 21.4s; rule pills ~26-29s; stock b-roll of phone scrolling, eye with glasses reflection and floating-images eye, 32.4-36.1s; black icon card 36.1s; circle-PiP 39s; clock and chess icons 44-47s; cream text card 47.1s; his own old vlog b-roll (whiteboard 6am, lab 1:10pm) ~50-52.3s; influencer screenshots ~55.6s; black and cream cards 58.9-64s; behind-the-scenes studio clip on 'perfectly staged video' ~65.4-66.7s; raw coffee vlog on 'honesty' ~70.8-73.3s; black card ~75.7s; on-stage clip 77.8s; profile screenshot ~80s; family millionaire clip ~82-83.7s; story screenshot 86.4s; new CTA setup 91.7s. B-roll is literal to the words ('staged video' shows a staged set, 'honesty' shows messy real footage, 'proof' shows receipts). Strong audio hits cluster on these moments (4.78, 15.01, 16.57, 36.37, 47.06-49.92, 55.27-62.73, 75.56-78.88, 83.08-86.81, 96.47), which suggests pop or whoosh sound effects on text cards and overlays. The hits are densest under the kinetic text cards (47-50s, 58.9-62.7s).
study.audio: Clean, close voice: bright and dry, with no room echo, recorded on a lav (a DJI mic is visible in the CTA shot). Delivery is fast and continuous at 3.93 words/s with no silence anywhere (no gaps of 0.3s or more). Whether a music bed runs under it can't be confirmed from the data. The clustered audio hits line up with text cards, icon pops and overlays, which points to UI-style pops and whooshes as sound design. Silence is never used for effect.
study.length_and_ending: 106.7s and 418 words. It builds as: myth, quote, 'rules changed', old rule, why it fails, the reframe 'frequency vs strategy problem' (44.6-46.6s, ~43%), the fix 'post content only you can post' (49.4-51.9s, ~48%), the trust/honesty principle (~64-73s), then credentials as proof (77.8-91.5s), then the CTA. The CTA runs 91.62-106.46s, ~14% of the runtime: 'book a call completely free with my team… tap the link below and grab a time that works for you and I'd really love for you to finally have someone on your side.' It ends on a warm line, not a loop, and cuts 0.23s after the last word.
study.quality: 720x1280, 30fps, h264 at ~914 kbps (platform-compressed). Main footage is a phone- or camera-on-desk wide: eye level, generous headroom in the wide (head at ~35-45% of frame height), bright soft window daylight, airy white apartment background with depth (windows, couch, ceiling fan). The CTA setup is more premium: tight close-up, warmer practical lighting, bookshelf arch background, visible lav. Sharp enough. It feels high-effort through the editing (custom typography system, kinetic cards, licensed-style stock, receipts) while the talking itself is relaxed and casual. That contrast fits his message that the honesty matters, not the set.
study.why_viral: The contrarian command hook ('Stop posting more') attacks the most common creator advice and names a pain (views flat for two years) that a huge audience shares. The reframe 'you don't have a posting frequency problem, you have a posting strategy problem' is a quotable, shareable line that relieves guilt and gives a new mental model. The relentless visual variety (a new card, overlay, b-roll or caption style every ~1.5-3s) and zero dead air make 107s feel short. Receipts (5.1M followers circled, first millionaire, public launch) turn advice into proof right before the ask, so the CTA feels earned.
lessons: Open on the first frame with a 3-5-word contrarian command and stack it as a big uppercase title word by word, synced to the speech (each word on screen by its spoken time, done by ~1s), then drop to normal captions.
Cut every gap: target 0 pauses of 0.3s or more and 0 fillers, which gives ~3.5-4 words/s; place cuts mid-sentence on word boundaries so the trims vanish into momentum.
Change something on screen every 1.5-3s even when there are only ~2 cuts per 10s: use punch-ins (~1.15-1.3x), overlays, caption style switches and full-screen text cards.
Use punch-ins of ~1.15-1.3x on thesis lines ('here's why…', 'no one is naming…', 'trust isn't built…') and return to the wide on gesture-heavy or listing lines.
Build a 3-tier caption system: plain white one-word sans at ~60% height; italic serif for emotional or key words; caps or pills for intensity and judgment words (about 1 emphasized word every 2-4s).
Turn the core reframe into a full-screen typographic moment with icons for each side (clock = frequency, chess = strategy), and land it before 50% of the runtime.
Make b-roll literal to the word: show a staged studio on 'staged', raw phone footage on 'honesty', a circled follower count on 'followers'. 2-5s cutaways, each with a pop or whoosh sound effect.
Cut to black or cream kinetic text cards (1.5-4s) for the abstract lines that have no visual; type the text on in sync with the voice.
Stack credentials as rapid receipts (3-4 clips/screenshots in ~10s) right before the CTA, then switch to a new, tighter camera setup for the ask so it reads as a direct personal invitation.
End within ~0.25s of the last word, on a warm closing line rather than a sign-off.
creator_advice: Stop posting more. You've been told to post consistently, every day, twice a day, three times a day, with carousels and stories, and your views haven't changed at all.
You can't just post more bad content and expect to grow. What you really need is clarity.
The old rule was simpler: post more, be consistent, follow the trends, and eventually the algorithm rewards you. That doesn't work now.
If you're posting the content that everyone else is posting, how could you expect to stand out? You don't.
You don't have a posting frequency problem, you have a posting strategy problem. You can't fix that by doing more of the wrong thing.
The fix is posting content only you can post. You don't have to be an influencer to win; you just have to post the thing no one can take from you.
We're all online looking for a solution to something we're stuck on, from someone we trust.
Trust isn't built with the perfectly staged video or the pretty background. It's earned with honesty about what you're actually trying to figure out.
People buy from people they resonate with, and selling to those people isn't being salesy.

study.format: hot take or opinion (advice-flavored explainer about growing on social media)
study.topic: Growing on Instagram/TikTok is easier than ever because audiences now reward ordinary, relatable people over polished experts and gurus.
study.hook: "We're in the gold rush of short-form content right now." The first word lands at 0.00s with no lead-in, and the 11 words take 2.12s (~5.2 words/s, faster than the 3.65 w/s average). The first 2 seconds are a close handheld selfie: the face fills the upper two-thirds, he holds a wired earbud mic to his mouth, and a city skyline window is behind him. A two-line hook title, "ironically, growing on instagram just got easier," sits at ~19-22% of frame height in white sans with a soft shadow. A small phrase caption ("We're in the") sits at ~55%. It stops the scroll because the title promises good news with an 'ironically' twist, the spoken line adds urgency ('gold rush... right now'), and by 2.5s it is backed by proof: a real 24.5K-follower profile screenshot.

beats.what: "We're in the gold rush of short-form content right now" over the title 'ironically, growing on instagram just got easier'.
Proof #1: a 15-year-old in his community grew 20,000 followers talking about making varsity basketball. A profile screenshot (24.5K circled) appears, then his video thumbnails (3.7M, 413K views).
"Think about how insane that is." A reaction beat; cuts back to full-frame face.
Contrarian thesis: being an expert/guru actually gets you fewer views.
Winners have authentic, down-to-earth, relatable personal brands, just showing up on camera with an ordinary life. Ordinary-life thumbnails are shown.
Proof #2: Brad grew a million followers this year DoorDashing to afford a diamond ring. Shows IG 589K and TikTok 586.6K screenshots, then Day 1 / Day 89 / Proposal thumbnails (15.4M, 21.3M, 5M).
The 'subtle reason': we're starved for true human connection. Location/setup changes to a wider couch shot with a drink can.
Platforms meant to connect us haven't; AI and the internet isolate us. A movie-still PiP appears above his head.
Working content replicates the feeling of connection to a friend. A Friends-cast PiP appears.
Top creators model a 'close to home' feeling: 'holy shit, this person is living the same exact life as me.'
Speaks directly to the viewer's objection: 'I would post... but I don't feel qualified to be an influencer.'
Reframe as a rhetorical question: 'isn't that the exact point' for people starved of seeing normal people. Ordinary-creator thumbnails return.
'Why can't you be the person' who serves an underserved, under-connected audience?
Contrast: most influencers don't live relatable lives; the ones blowing up model a regular life.
Whatever your regular life is, the content that gets you your first 100,000 followers will be simpler and easier than you think 'right now.' This echoes the opening 'right now.'

study.jump_cuts: Extremely tight. Speech covers 100% of the runtime, the median gap between words is 0.00s, and there are 0 fillers. Only 1 gap is ≥0.3s: 0.52s after 'camera' at 27.22s, left in as a breath right before the green-screen thumbnails for 'showcasing a very ordinary life.' Cut rate is 2.05 per 10s (25 shots, median 4.43s, longest 8.93s). Most cuts land mid-sentence, even mid-phrase, with the same caption on both sides (13.63 'we're in the age', 17.6 'I think the people', 21.77 'with authentic', 24.63 'where it's', 40.47, 43.7 'And these', 48.63 'haven't really', 53.07, 58.83, 64.23, 75.33 'an influencer'). That means the cuts join takes or trim breaths without waiting for sentence ends. Some cuts land between thoughts (10.47 'Think about...', 29.73 'There's another creator', 97.3 'Because most'). It feels continuous and breathless: it reads as one rant, not a sequence of clips.
study.zooms_punch_ins: No digital zooms or smooth push-ins. All framing changes come from switching handheld takes and two filming setups. Setup A is a tight arm's-length selfie with the face filling ~60-70% of width (0-36.9s, 68.67-75.33s, 97.3-117.35s). Setup B is a wider leaning shot on the couch with torso and drink can visible, roughly 0.6x as tight as A (36.98-68.67s, 75.33-84.27s, 88.3-97.3s). Within setup A, some cuts act as mild reframes/punch-ins: ~1.1x tighter at 17.6 on 'I think the people', and 109.87 is noticeably tighter (~1.2x) on 'the content that'll help you get to your first 100,000 followers.' The tight-wide-tight alternation happens at 36.98 (wide), 68.67 (tight), 75.33 (wide), 97.3 (tight for the ending). Something visual changes about every 2-5s: a cut, an overlay swap or a PiP appearing. The longest static stretch is 8.93s (75.33-84.27), and even that contains handheld motion.
study.captions: Phrase captions of 1-3 words at a time (e.g. 'gold rush', 'of short-form', 'content right now'), swapped roughly every 0.4-0.8s in sync with speech. Small white sans-serif (TikTok Classic/Proxima-style), medium-bold weight, sentence case with original punctuation removed. Thin dark drop shadow, no box, no colored or highlighted words, no emojis. Small size, about 1/3 frame width at most. Positioned centered at ~54-56% of frame height, over the mouth/chin area. In green-screen sections they stay at ~55%, between the screenshots above and the cut-out face below. Hard swaps, no pop animation.
study.on_screen_text: One hook title: 'ironically, growing on instagram just got easier'. All lowercase, two centered lines, white regular-weight sans with a soft shadow, no box, at ~19-22% of frame height. Visible from 0.0s, it persists through the first green-screen section and the cut at 10.47, and is gone by ~11.5s, so it stays ~11s. No animation in or out. No other titles, numbers or headers. Any text inside screenshots ('Day 1', 'Day 89', 'The Proposal Episode 1', 'DoorDash for a Diamond Ring') belongs to the source thumbnails.
study.graphics_overlays:
Green-screen-style layout used 4 times. The speaker is cut out with a soft feathered vignette edge, placed in the bottom ~35% on a near-black background, with proof screenshots in the top half.
(1) ~2.5-7.8s: Instagram profile header of rayedqureshi19 (103 posts, 24.5K followers) plus 4 reel thumbnails. A hand-drawn tan/orange ellipse circles '24.5K followers' by ~7.3s, as he says 'followers.'

A Friends-cast living-room still appears ~57-58.8s on 'a feeling of true connection... to a friend.' These are literal visual metaphors. All overlays pop on and off with hard cuts, no animation.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. These include jump cuts within a take, cuts between two filming setups (selfie vs couch), and hard switches into and out of the green-screen screenshot layout. No whips, flashes or zoom transitions.
study.broll_and_interrupts: Instead of b-roll, the interrupts are proof screenshots in a green-screen layout: ~2.5-10.47, ~28-29.7, ~31.5-36.9, 84.27-88.3. They cluster in the first 37s, where each claim needs evidence, then return once at 84s. Two meme-like PiP stills appear at ~51s and ~57s. The hand-drawn circle on follower counts appears at ~7.3s and ~32s. The location/setup changes at 36.98 (to the couch with a Yerba Mate can as a casual prop), 68.67, 75.33, 88.3 and 97.3 act as the main mid-video interrupts, every ~6-30s. Some interrupt lands roughly every 3-5s overall. No identifiable sound effects. The 34.24s audio hit sits on the 34.27 overlay swap, but the other audio peaks track speech emphasis.
study.audio: Voice only, recorded on wired Apple earbuds held near the mouth: close, dry, slightly compressed phone-mic sound with little room echo. No music bed is evident. The audio peaks (e.g. the 73-78s cluster on 'qualified... influencer... flashy') follow speech energy, not hits. Silence is barely used; the single 0.52s pause at 27.22s is the only breath left in. Delivery is fast and continuous at 3.65 words/s, with one casual curse ('holy shit') for authenticity.
study.length_and_ending: 117.35s total, 428 words. It builds from claim (0-2s) to two proof examples (2-37s, ~31% of runtime), then the psychological 'why' (37-69s), the viewer objection and reframe (69-107s), and finally the payoff. The payoff sentence 'the content that'll help you get to your first 100,000 followers will probably be a lot simpler and a lot easier to create than you probably think right now' runs 109.68-117.14s (~93-100%). No explicit CTA. The ending's 'right now' echoes the hook's 'right now,' giving a soft loop into the replay. Cuts 0.21s after the last word.
study.quality: 720x1280, 30fps, h264 at ~1.8 Mbps: mid-quality phone upload. Handheld front-camera selfie at arm's length with a slightly low angle; the eye line looks into or just past the lens and often drifts up while thinking. Headroom is minimal or cropped in the tight setup and generous in the couch setup. Natural window light gives warm sun and hard shadows on his face. The background is a lived-in apartment: white walls, figurines on a shelf, a red couch with laundry. He wears a tank top and holds wired earbuds as a mic. Deliberately casual and 'ordinary'; the low-effort look is the message. The effort is in the edit: zero dead air, two interleaved setups, sourced proof screenshots with hand-drawn circles, and meme PiPs.
study.why_viral: 1) The hook title 'ironically, growing on instagram just got easier' plus 'gold rush... right now' promises hopeful, actionable news to the huge audience of aspiring creators. 2) Concrete proof arrives inside 3s: real profiles with circled follower counts and multi-million-view thumbnails, so the claim feels verified, not guru talk. 3) It names and dissolves the viewer's exact objection ('I don't feel qualified... nothing flashy about my life'), which is very shareable to friends thinking about posting. 4) The form matches the message: a normal guy in a tank top with earbuds, talking nonstop with zero dead air, so the video itself proves that relatable beats polished.
lessons: Start speaking at 0.00s and put a lowercase 'ironically/surprisingly X just got easier' style title at ~20% height for the first ~10s. It frames the payoff before the viewer can decide.
Back the first claim with visual proof within 3 seconds: a screenshot of a real profile or result, laid out green-screen style with the speaker cut out in the bottom ~35% under the evidence.
Draw a hand-drawn circle on the single number that matters (follower count, views) about 0.5s before or as the speaker says it.
Cut every breath and pause: target a median word gap of 0s, no fillers, and at most one deliberate ~0.5s pause, placed right before a visual reveal.
Cut mid-sentence whenever needed to join takes. Keep the caption phrase identical across the cut so it reads as continuous speech.
If the speaker filmed the same script in two setups (tight selfie vs wider seated), alternate them every 6-30s as the main pattern interrupt, and return to the tightest setup for the final payoff.
Keep something visually changing every 3-5s on talking footage (~2 cuts per 10s), and never let a single static frame run past ~9s.
Use small 1-3 word white phrase captions at ~55% height with a thin shadow. Plain captions suit a 'casual, authentic' message better than flashy highlighted ones.
Drop small literal meme or pop-culture PiP stills (~1/3 width, above the head) on abstract lines like 'isolation' or 'friendship' to make the idea visual for 2-4s.
End on the payoff sentence and cut within ~0.2s of the last word. Echo a phrase from the hook ('right now') so the replay loops naturally.
creator_advice: We're in the gold rush of short-form content right now.
Being an expert and being a guru, I think, actually gets you less views.

The people who are truly succeeding on social media right now are people with authentic, down-to-earth, relatable personal brands, where it's very clear that they're just showing up on camera showcasing a very ordinary life.

The content that's really working almost replicates this feeling of true connection that you would have to a friend. The best creators model this feeling of close to home, where it feels like 'this person is living the same exact life as me.'

If you ever told yourself 'I would post on social media, but I don't feel qualified to be an influencer': it might not feel like there's anything flashy about your life, but isn't that the exact point, for people who are starved of watching normal people on their For You page who live similar lives to them?
Be the person who makes content speaking to a large demographic of viewers who've felt underserved and under-connected with through creators on their screens.
Whatever that regular life looks like to you, the content that'll help you get to your first 100,000 followers will probably be a lot simpler and a lot easier to create than you probably think.

study.format: listicle
study.topic: A rapid-fire list of ways to film more natural talking-head ("yap") content, with each tip shot in the very situation it describes.
study.hook: "Record while walking" starts at 0.00s with no lead-in, said quickly (the full 45-word video averages 3.68 words/s). In the first 2 seconds there is a handheld selfie shot of the creator walking outside past a white wall and hedges, framed chest-up with the phone at arm's length. A persistent white bold title, 'How to "yap" better:', sits at about 20% of frame height, and the caption 'record while walking' sits at about 70%. At 1.13s it hard-cuts to a mirror selfie in a floral-wallpaper bathroom. It stops the scroll for three reasons: the title promises a practical skill in 4 words, the first tip is being acted out as he says it, and a whole new location arrives within 1.1s, which tells the viewer this will be a fast montage.

beats.what: Title 'How to "yap" better:' plus tip 1, 'Record while walking', filmed walking outdoors.
'record it in the mirror': cut to a mirror selfie in a floral bathroom, different outfit (red sweatshirt).
'record it in your car': selfie from the driver's seat.
'record it while getting ready': at a bathroom sink rubbing his face, in a black tee.
'leave the bloopers in': kitchen shot where he stumbles ('boop-- bloopers'). The stumble is kept, and the caption spells it out, so the tip proves itself.
'record it outside': in front of pine trees.
'record it with just your phone': he holds up a phone showing its camera app.
'record while eating': kitchen shot holding a cereal bowl. He takes a bite during the 0.56s pause after 'eating'.
Final tip, 'hold your phone in your hand instead of on a tripod': handheld in front of a hedge, back in the same sage polo as the opening shot. He gestures at the camera.
Ends 0.41s after 'tripod'. There is no CTA, and the matching outfit and outdoor greenery flow back into the opening shot.

study.jump_cuts: Speech covers 97% of the runtime. The median gap between words is 0.0s, and only 3 gaps are 0.3s or longer: 0.34s after 'outside' (7.54s), 0.30s after 'phone' (8.94s), and 0.56s after 'eating' (10.0s). The 0.56s gap is left in on purpose so he can take a bite on camera. There are 0 filler words. The one verbal stumble ('boop-- bloopers', 5.24–6.08s) is deliberately kept because it illustrates the tip. There are 8 cuts in 12.65s (6.32 per 10s). The median shot is 1.33s, shots run 1.13–2.05s, and the first three are exactly 1.13s each. Each cut falls between list items, landing right at or just before the next 'record' (1.12, 2.30, 3.54, 4.94, 6.60, 7.88, 9.24, 10.56). No cut lands mid-sentence, because every item is a separate clip. It feels extremely tight, like one continuous run-on sentence stitched across 9 days and places.
study.zooms_punch_ins: None. There are no punch-ins or digital zooms; every cut goes to a completely different location, outfit and lighting. The visual changes every 1.13–2.05s (median 1.33s) through the location swaps alone. Handheld movement adds constant micro-motion: median motion is 15.4, peaking at 33.5 around 10.5–12.5s in the gesturing final shot.
study.captions: Captions are phrase-level, one tip per caption: 'record while walking', 'record it in the mirror', 'record it in your car', 'record it while getting ready', 'leave the boop-- bloopers in', 'record it outside', 'record it with just your phone', 'record while eating', and a 2-line final caption, 'hold your phone in your hand / instead of on a tripod'. That is about 3–7 words on screen at once. The style is white, bold rounded sans-serif (Poppins-like), all lowercase, with a soft drop shadow and no box or stroke. They are small (roughly 5% of frame width per word) and centered at about 70% of frame height. There are no highlighted words and no word-by-word animation. study.why_viral: The form proves the content. Each tip is shown in the exact situation it describes, including a real blooper on 'leave the bloopers in', which is satisfying and shareable. Density and speed also help: 9 tips in 12.6s with a new location every 1.3s gives no moment to swipe, and the short length plus the seamless loop drives rewatches. The advice also lowers the barrier for aspiring creators ('just your phone', 'leave the bloopers in'), so people save it and send it to friends who want to post. Finally, the persistent 'How to "yap" better:' title names a trending format, so it reads instantly as a useful reference.
lessons: For list content, give each item its own clip and cut exactly at the start of the next item (within about 0.05s of the first word), so the list plays as one unbroken sentence across locations.
When the footage allows, illustrate each point visually by filming it where it applies. A location change every 1.1–2s replaces the need for zooms or b-roll.
Keep shots between 1.1s and 2s for rapid lists. Aim for about 6 cuts per 10s and no shot over about 2s.
Remove all inter-phrase silence (target a median gap of 0s) but keep a pause of up to about 0.6s when the speaker is doing an action that proves the point, such as eating or a gesture.
Keep a stumble when it reinforces the message, and caption it verbatim (e.g. 'boop-- bloopers') so viewers catch the joke.
Pin one short title (under 5 words) at about 20% of frame height for the whole video, and keep phrase captions at about 70% height, so the face sits clear between them.
Use phrase-level captions that show one complete list item at a time and change on the cut, rather than word-by-word, when the items are short and repetitive.
Start speech at 0.0s and end the video within about 0.4s of the last word. Open and close on visually matching shots (same outfit and setting) to create a natural loop.

Color-code caption keywords by meaning: red for the problem or negative, green for benefits and actions, yellow for topics and nouns. Put adverbs in italics and use numerals for numbers.
Pop a relevant emoji next to the caption every 1–3s and pair each with a soft pop sound, so the screen changes roughly every second even on long shots.

When the speaker names a tool or URL, cut to a screen recording within ~0.5s of the name. Put it in a phone mockup over a blurred copy of the speaker shot and add a tap pointer and highlight box on the exact element being described.

Put the save CTA in the final ~2–3s, framed as 'if you just learned something new', and cut within ~0.3s of the last word.

An easy way to find that kind of content: go to google.com/alerts and create an alert for whatever terms and topics you want to be notified about.
I would recommend doing this for a few terms that relate to your niche.

study.format: explainer (framework / advice breakdown with whiteboard diagrams)
study.topic: Why 'being the niche' beats niching down, taught as a three-branch framework (what you say, who you say it to, why it matters to you) plus a bonus 'anchor' rule for selling.
study.hook: 'Alex Hormozi's top posts aren't about business, they're about dating.' The first word lands at 0.00s with no lead-in. The line is 10 words in 3.5s (~2.9 words/s), with a deliberate 0.44s pause after 'business,' (2.44s), the longest gap in the whole video, so the twist 'they're about dating' lands alone. Frames 0-2s show a wide, full-body seated shot in a dim, warm home office (dual monitors left, white curtains). The lowercase white title 'how to "be the niche"' sits in the upper third (~25-33% of frame height), and a single-word white caption ('Alex', 'Hormozi's', 'posts') sits at ~69%. At ~2.8s a 3-thumbnail collage of Hormozi clips pops in above his head, with view counts 8.3M / 7.3M / 28.8M. It stops the scroll for three reasons: a famous name in the first word, a counterintuitive contrast (business guru → dating), and proof on screen within 3 seconds. The pattern then repeats twice (Oprah 3.8s, his own posts 7.16s, each with a view-count collage) before the claim 'That is not an accident' at 10.82s.

beats.what: Hormozi's top posts are about dating, not business. A view-count collage pops in at ~2.8s.
Oprah's are about relationships, not self-improvement (Oprah collage, 10.7M).
'My whole business is teaching content, but my top posts are about my story.' His own collage: 25.1M / 32.8M / 24.8M.
'That is not an accident.' Names his concept, 'becoming the niche', and claims 5 years of saying it.
Everyone now says 'be your own niche / personal world / category'...
'But almost nobody's getting it right... this is why.' An open loop that promises the answer.
Core thesis: a niche was never a topic, it's the intersection of what / who / why. A 'you → what, who, why' diagram appears.
Branch 1, what you say: your message. It drives four content pillars: skill, perspective, lifestyle, passions. Red circles mark each pillar.
Branch 2, who you say it to: target avatar, split into demographic and psychographic (the one that matters more).
'Younger you principle': make content for yourself 2-3 years younger.
Branch 3, why it matters: message = what you believe, stories = why you believe it. Stories needn't be dramatic.
Two story-finding questions: 'How did I get here?' / 'What did I used to believe that I don't anymore?'
'They don't just learn from you, they trust you.'
'Here's where it all comes together.' The full framework diagram yields dozens of ideas under one personal-brand umbrella.
Bonus rule: have an anchor (what you sell). Talk about it a few times a week; everything else builds likability.
Contrast: niching down connects you by one thing, so people unfollow when you change; being the niche connects you many ways. X marks cross out parts of the diagram while the rest holds.
Closing line: 'And people buy into people.'
'If you want to become the niche but do it the right way, make sure to follow because I'll be breaking down all of this in a lot more detail.'

study.why_viral: 1) Authority-borrowing proof hook: famous names + counterintuitive claims + real view counts (up to 32.8M) in the first 10s make the premise feel proven before it's explained. 2) A named, ownable concept ('be the niche', 'younger you principle', 'anchor') delivered as a visual framework that builds piece by piece. Viewers stay to see it complete, and it's highly saveable/screenshot-able. 3) It solves a pain nearly every creator and business owner has ('still having a hard time figuring out yours, this is why') and gives permission to post about their whole life while still selling. 4) Dense, filler-free pacing (3.86 words/s, longest pause 0.44s) with a visual change every ~2-6s from red circles and reframes, so a 2:47 explainer never stalls.
lessons: Open on the first word at 0.00s with a named authority plus a contrast ('X's top posts aren't about A, they're about B'), and show proof (screenshots with view counts) on screen by ~3s.
Leave exactly one deliberate pause (~0.4s) in the hook, right before the twist; cut every other gap to under 0.3s so median word gaps are ~0.
Put cuts only at sentence boundaries, and use each cut as a framing reset: alternate wide (1.0x) and ~1.1-1.2x, and save the tightest push (~1.3x) for the emotional close.
If the footage is long clean takes (shots of 5-13s), keep attention by changing something visual every 2-6s: add a diagram step, an annotation, or a reframe.
When the speaker explains a framework, build the diagram cumulatively in sync with speech, and draw a red circle on the exact box at the moment its word is spoken.
Frame wide with ~30-35% headroom so titles, captions and graphics can live above the head without covering the face.
Switch caption position by layout: ~30% frame height when the frame is clean, ~70% when a graphic owns the top. Use one word at a time, white, bold rounded sans, soft shadow.
For long diagrams, switch to a split screen (graphic top ~45%, speaker bottom half), and periodically remove the graphic for 5-20s so the bare face shot reads as a reset.
Visualize the conclusion: cross out parts of the diagram with red X's while the speaker says 'even if one part changes, the rest holds'.
End within ~0.3s of the last word, with a CTA that promises a follow-up ('I'll be breaking all of this down in more detail') rather than a generic 'follow for more'.
creator_advice: Alex Hormozi's top posts aren't about business, they're about dating. Oprah's aren't about self-improvement, they're about relationships. 'My whole business is teaching content, but my top posts are about my story. That is not an accident.'
A niche was never a topic; it was the intersection between what you say, who you say it to, and why it matters to you.

What you say is your message, the belief you keep coming back to. It gives you coherence and decides what goes into your four content pillars: what you do (your skill), how you think (your perspective), how you live (your lifestyle), and what you love (your passions).

Who you say it to is your target avatar, with two parts: demographic (sex, age, location, occupation) and, more importantly, psychographic: what's going on in their heads, their struggles, their fears, what they actually desire.
Apply the 'younger you principle': make content for the version of you two to three years younger, because you know exactly what they're going through.

Why it matters to you: your message is what you believe, and your stories are why you believe it. Stories don't have to be dramatic, private, or super vulnerable, just moments that actually changed you.

To find your stories ask yourself: 'How did I get here?' and 'What did I used to believe that I don't believe anymore?' Where you started is exactly where someone watching your content is right now. When you show them how you got past it, they don't just learn from you, they trust you.

Fill out the entire framework and at the bottom you have dozens of ideas that fit under the umbrella of your personal brand. You're not a fitness, finance, travel, or tech creator; you can talk about your family, your skills, your faith, your relationships, and it all makes sense because they're based on you.

Bonus rule, have an anchor: what you sell or want to sell (a skill, a product, a service, or a business). Talk about it a few times a week so people know what you offer and see that you're good at it. Everything else you post helps people get to know you, so when you do sell, they're buying from someone they already like.

When you niche down, you're connected to your audience by one thing, so when you create about something different they will unfollow. When you are the niche, you're connected in many ways (your message, your story, how you live, what you love), so even if one part changes the rest will still hold firm. People buy into people.

study.format: business/day-in-the-life talk (credibility/proof reel: creator intro plus a portfolio list of client results)
study.topic: A social media agency owner (Sammy, Shout Hero Marketing) proves he has almost a billion views by walking through client accounts and their view counts, then asks small business owners and influencers to follow him to learn how.
study.hook: "I've had almost a billion views on social media, and I'm here to show you how to do the same." The first word lands at 0.05s, so there is no dead air. The line runs to 3.73s at roughly 5 words/s, faster than the 3.55 w/s average. On screen 0-2s: a casual side-angle medium shot of him seated, turned toward frame-left, fiddling with a fuzzy-windscreen mic as if he's just setting up. A big two-line title, 'How to Hit a Billion Views' (white, bold sans, sentence case, dark shadow), sits at about 17-30% of frame height. Captions start at 0.56s ('I'VE HAD ALMOST'). At 1.07s, on 'billion', a hard cut drops a full-width collage of about 18 viral video thumbnails with view counts over him, held to 3.37s. It stops the scroll because it opens with a huge specific number plus a promise ('how to do the same'). The proof wall of real view counts arrives within about 1 second, so the claim feels verified before a skeptic can swipe. The off-guard side angle also feels candid.

Back to the side angle for 'the same'; the title is still up.

Numbers roll call. Thumbnails pop in one by one and stack in a cascade as he says '24.3 million here, 22.4 million there, another 19.2 million right here'.
'Then we've got Brewsters of North Olmstead': TikTok and IG profile screenshots at 25.30.
'the very first account that I hit my first 1 million views on about 6 years ago', over two successive Bruster's video grids (27.13, 29.07).

study.audio: Close, clean voice from a lav or wireless mic with a fluffy windscreen, which he holds in frame. There is little room echo. Delivery is upbeat and quick (3.55 words/s) with no fillers. The data gives no clear evidence of a music bed; if there is one, it sits well under the voice. Audio peaks line up with overlay entrances, which points to light pop or whoosh accents on the proof graphics. No silence is used for effect; the longest pause is 0.72s.
study.length_and_ending: 54.8s total. It builds as an escalating proof list: a big claim (0-4s), who he is (4-10s), a ranked #1 client with multiple numbers (10.5-24.9s), an origin-story client (25-36s), then 'can't even rank the rest' speeding into three single-number examples (38-47.9s). The payoff 'the point is' lands at 48.95s (about 89%). The CTA 'follow me and I'll show you how' starts at 53.01s (about 97%) and ends at 54.37s. The video cuts 0.43s after the last word. The 'how' promised in the hook is never delivered, so the follow is the payoff. It's an open loop, not a cliffhanger story.
study.quality: 720x1280 at 30fps, HEVC at about 14.9 Mbps, sharp enough. The frontal shot is a chest-up mid-shot, centered, eyes at about 37% of frame height, with generous headroom filled by two symmetrical black, gray and gold abstract canvases. That empty upper area is deliberately left for overlays. He sits in a gray wingback chair against a light gray wall, under soft natural window light that is even and slightly warm, and wears a plain black tee. The opening side shot (door and chair visible, him adjusting the mic) feels candid on purpose. Overall: a tidy home-office set that looks professional but not studio, with high editing effort (synced screenshot stacking, karaoke captions) carrying the polish.
study.why_viral: 1) A huge, specific claim ('almost a billion views') is backed by visual proof within about 1 second and then kept up all video: every number spoken appears on screen as a real screenshot, which builds instant trust and a 'wait, how?' curiosity. 2) A relentless rhythm: about 4 cuts per 10s, 99% speech, and an overlay change every 1-2.5s through the list, so there is nothing to swipe away from. 3) A relatable niche: local small businesses (crepe, ice cream and coffee shops in Ohio) going viral makes it feel achievable for owners watching, and the CTA names them directly. 4) The hook promises 'how', which is withheld until the follow, so it ends on an unresolved promise that drives follows.
lessons: Put the boldest specific number in the first sentence, starting by 0.1s, and show proof of it on screen within about 1s (here, a grid of view counts cut in on the word 'billion' at 1.07s).
Add a 2-line hook title in the top 15-30% of the frame for the first 3-4s, then drop it on the first angle change so the frame clears.
When the speaker lists results, make every spoken number appear on screen exactly on that word: stack cards one by one (24.3M, then 22.4M, then 19.2M) instead of showing one static image.
Sync visual swaps to repetition in the speech: one new grid per 'banger' (13.7s and 14.93s).
Frame the talking head with lots of headroom (eyes at about 35-40% height) so overlays, screenshots and cards have a dedicated space, keeping some of the speaker visible around them.
Cut all fillers and keep gaps between words near 0s. Only leave pauses of about 0.3-0.7s where a cut or overlay swap covers them.
Aim for about 4 cuts per 10s, with a median shot of about 2s. Use short 0.4-0.6s bridge shots to get in and out of overlays cleanly.
Use karaoke captions of 2-3 words, ALL CAPS, heavy sans in white with the active word in yellow, at about 78-80% height. Make sure numbers get the highlight.
Open on a different, candid angle (side shot, adjusting the mic) for the first 4s, then switch to the main frontal angle as the visual reset for the 'who I am' line.
End by naming the target viewer ('small business owner or influencer') and a single follow CTA. Cut within about 0.4s of the last word.

study.topic: Three ways to use keyframes in the VN editor (smooth zooms, moving cursor/stickers, text that follows you) to make videos look premium and 'paid collaboration worthy'.
study.hook: "Your editing will never look premium if you do not know how to use keyframes." Speech starts at 0.00s, with no lead-in, at about 3.9 words/s (14 words in 3.64s). It stops the scroll because it is a direct 'you' threat ('never look premium'). It names an aspiration (premium, which later becomes 'paid collaboration worthy'). 'if you've missed any of the Edit Audit episodes, go binge.'

Viewers see the result before the tutorial. 2) Aspirational, money-linked stakes ('look more expensive... paid collaboration worthy') aimed at small creators who want brand deals, which makes it highly saveable. 3) Clear numbered structure with number cards and persistent section headers, plus a 'put these down' meme that explicitly prompts saving. 4) Relentless visual novelty: a new caption style, sticker or card every 1-2s over clean, pause-free speech at 3.9 words/s, plus a named series ('Edit Audit, EP 7') that drives binge viewing and follows.
lessons: Start talking at 0.0s and make the first line a 'you will never X unless Y' statement; put the payoff word ('premium') on screen as its own one-word text within the first 2s.
Cut a designed title card (topic name plus one visual of the tool) in at ~2.5-3s, before the hook sentence even finishes, to show quality early.
Remove every pause over ~0.3s except 1-2 deliberate beats before the biggest line (e.g. a 0.35-0.4s pause before the money/stakes phrase); aim for ~3.5-4 words/s and 0 fillers.
Keep median shot length around 2-2.5s (about 4 cuts per 10s), cutting between clauses on the talking head and mid-sentence only when switching into b-roll or a demo.
When the camera can't move, create motion with graphics: swap a keyword text or sticker every 1-2s in the intro, and give every stakes word (expensive, intentional, paid) its own font or sticker.
For list videos, insert a 0.5-0.7s full-frame 'Number X' card, then keep a section header pinned in the top headroom for the whole tip so viewers always know where they are.
Demonstrate the advice on the speaker's own footage (do the zoom while they say 'zoom', make text follow their hand); show, don't tell, and do it within ~2s of the claim.
Frame the speaker with ~30-35% empty space above the head so titles and stickers never cover the face; switch to bottom captions at ~75-78% height during instructional sections.
Add a 0.5-1s reaction meme on 'save/note this down' moments to prompt saves, and close with a series CTA ('go binge') plus a quick visual sign-off; end within ~0.7s of the last word.
Put a soft SFX pop on each graphic entrance and on the final sticker so the audio reinforces every visual change.
creator_advice: Your editing will never look premium if you do not know how to use keyframes. It is one of those tiny editing tricks that make your videos look more expensive, more intentional and honestly, paid collaboration worthy.
Smooth zooms: place one keyframe where you want the moment to start. Go a few frames ahead, zoom in or zoom out and VN automatically creates the smooth motion.

Moving cursor (like skincare videos with a mouse cursor moving along with the product, or arrows/stickers that move smoothly across the screen): just add your sticker or a cursor, place a keyframe, move it to the next position, add another keyframe and VN animates it for you.
Text that follows you: instead of keeping your text static, use keyframes to move it with you. It instantly makes your edit look so much more dynamic.
Tiny feature, massive difference.

study.why_viral: 1) A direct second-person insult ('You're not funny') plus a numbered promise (16 reasons, 'stuck below 10K views') targets every aspiring creator's insecurity, so people stay to self-score. 2) Very high information density: a new item, text line and meme roughly every second for 18s means there is never a static moment, and many viewers rewatch to catch the memes. 3) The accumulating on-screen list ends as a complete 16-item checklist on one frame, which is very save- and screenshot-able. 4) The joke turn 'last one, you don't follow me' converts the list into a follow ask without feeling salesy, then a concrete money claim ($20K/month, quit job) gives a reason to follow.
lessons: Start speaking at 0.0s with the first item itself, no intro. Put a title with a specific number and a pain point on screen from frame 1.
For list content, make every item a visual event: add the item's text line and swap a matching image on the first word of that item, every ~0.6-1.2s.
Cut so each new sentence starts within ~0.05s of the cut and keep word gaps near 0. Trim breaths between items so the next item begins 0.1-0.5s after the previous one ends.
Leave exactly one deliberate ~0.4s pause before the turn or punchline (here before 'And last one'), and no other pauses over 0.3s.
Paraphrase each spoken point into a 2-4 word label ('boring hooks', 'too slow') in a numbered list that stacks and stays, so the screen builds toward a complete checklist.
When the list column fills (~8 lines), flip the layout (move the image to the other side, start a second column) as a mid-video interrupt around 25-30% in.
Reveal the full list with images removed right on the payoff line, around 60% in, so the frame becomes screenshot-worthy.
After the payoff, strip all graphics and switch to small 2-3 word speech captions at ~78% frame height. The tone change signals 'now it's personal' for the intro/CTA.
Keep the intro + CTA under ~11s and anchor it with one concrete credential (a number and a timeframe). End within ~0.3s of the last word.
Frame the speaker with eyes at ~45-50% height so the top ~45% is free for title, list and images without covering the face.

Use memes.
Don't be scared to be controversial.
Don't make your hooks boring.

Experiment with formats.
Learn how to tell stories.
Use visual hooks.
Use pattern interrupts.
Don't have basic ideas.
Study viral videos.
Don't use difficult words.
Invoke emotion.
Post consistently.
Steal from other niches.

study.topic: A social media growth coach gives three quick ways to fix short-form video hooks: trim the dead first half second, stack hooks, and match your delivery to your audience's energy.

Speech fills 99% of the runtime at 4.41 words/s, an energetic but conversational pace. No prominent music bed is evident from the speech-dominated audio; if there is any, it sits very low. There may be light pop/whoosh hits near cuts and emoji pops (audio peaks at about 25.06 and 42.53, among others). Silence is used for effect once: the 0.36s pause after "super important." at 20.5s, before naming tip 2.
study.length_and_ending: 51.3s, 224 words. The structure is a 7s hook-plus-proof stack, then three tips. Tip 2 runs longest (about 19–38s) because it carries the twist. The payoff is the meta reveal at 29.78–35s (58–68%): the video's own opening was the hook stack he's teaching. It's immediately followed by "go back to the start of this video and listen carefully" (35.5–38.0, about 70%), a built-in rewatch loop. Tip 3 closes quickly. The ending CTA is "I'm just trying to help you get your first million views so follow me for more." The last word ends at about 50.8s and the video cuts 0.5s later.
study.quality: 720x1280 vertical at 30fps, HEVC at a high ~14.8 Mbps; sharp phone footage. Framing is a locked-off medium shot from mid-thigh/waist up, with eyes at about 30–35% of frame height and generous headroom showing the drop ceiling. That space is deliberately used for the title. The background is a plain grey wall with a black slatted acoustic panel at the right edge, in soft even daylight/office light. Clothing is a simple black tee and glasses. The look is casual-on-purpose (talking to his phone in an office) but polished in the edit, with tight cuts, styled karaoke captions, a proof collage, a screen recording and emoji pops. It reads as competent 'coach' content, not studio.
study.why_viral: 1) A specific, low-effort promise (3 ways, under 1 minute, 'even a 5-year-old'), with a proof stack of real view counts in the first 7s. 2) The meta twist: the opening he used is the technique he's teaching, plus a quote-overlay callback. It rewards attention and literally tells viewers to rewatch the start, boosting loops and watch time. 3) Show, don't tell: the editor screen recording demonstrates tip 1 while he says it, and the video itself starts with zero dead air. 4) Relentless pacing: 99% speech, a median word gap of 0.0s, a cut every ~3.4s, and per-word highlighted captions, so there's no moment to swipe.
lessons: Trim so the first spoken word starts at 0.00–0.10s, even clipping the first syllable is fine; never leave setup or phone-placing frames.

Stack a second hook within 3–4s of the first: a proof line ('helped clients hit millions of views') cut on a hard cut at the sentence break, with a 3–4s visual proof overlay (screenshots with view counts).
Remove every breath and pause between words (target median gap ~0s, nothing over 0.4s), except one deliberate 0.3–0.4s pause before naming the key tip.
Place cuts at sentence starts, right on the first word of the new thought. Only cut mid-sentence when an overlay is coming off, aiming for about one cut every 3–4s (2.5 cuts per 10s).
Use 1–3 word ALL-CAPS bold white captions with a dark stroke at about 75% frame height, highlighting each spoken word in yellow as it's said.
Put a two-line title restating the promise in the empty headroom (about 22–32% height) for the first ~3.5–4s, with a small 'it's easy' subtitle under it, and remove it on the first cut.
When the speaker describes an action (editing, a tool, a result), cover the frame with a 3–5s screen recording of exactly that action.
Pop a single emoji on concrete keywords ('hook' → 🪝, 'super hook' → 🪝x2, 'see' → 👀), holding about 1s, so no stretch goes longer than ~5–8s without a new visual.
If the speaker references something said earlier, overlay that earlier line as a quoted text card at mid-frame. If they say 'go back to the start', keep it near the 70% mark to drive rewatches.
End within 0.5s of the last word of the CTA; no outro.
creator_advice: Cut that first half second out of the start of your video, before you start talking or while you're setting your phone up.
Let your video start off right away with whatever you have to say, without any of that space in the beginning.

Start stacking your hooks: before you deliver the main value of your video, you hook and then you super hook, which is where you double down and increase the demand for the value you're about to give.
Example: start with a main hook, then follow it with a proof and dream concept hook (e.g. 'These have helped my clients hit millions of views regularly, and they can help you too').
Consider what you say and how you say it: your hook is the first thing people will see or hear, and your delivery is very important.
Make sure you're matching the energy of your target audience.

study.format: advice / tips (numbered series 'part one' with client case-study proof)
study.topic: A social media marketer says 'be controversial' is a video style that always gets views, and proves it with an ice cream shop client whose mint-chocolate-chip debate videos passed 15 million views.
study.hook: "Video styles that always get views, part one." starts at 0.00s with no lead-in: 8 words in 1.74s (~4.6 words/s, faster than the 3.92 average). The first 2 seconds hold a waist-up wide shot of the speaker seated in front of a marble wall, holding a small black wireless mic at his chest. A two-line white bold title with a black outline, 'Video Styles That Always Get Views', sits at the top (~17-27% of frame height) with a small 'Part 1' under it (~30%). Karaoke captions run at the bottom. He raises one finger on 'part one'. It stops the scroll because it promises a guaranteed outcome ('always get views') to a creator audience and signals a series. At 2.0s a cut stacks real view-count thumbnails (26.4M, 24.3M, 26M, 19.2M, 22.6M) over his face while he says 'hundreds of millions of views', so credibility lands inside the first 4 seconds.

beats.what: 'Video styles that always get views, part one.' Title card on screen, finger raised on 'part one'.
Credibility: 'I've had hundreds of millions of views with each of these styles.' At 2.0 a collage of view-count thumbnails pops over the shot.
'Number one is be controversial.' Cut back to the clean shot, title gone. A 0.44s pause after 'controversial' lets it land.
'If you have a hot take, then get it out there.'
Mechanism: controversy generates conversations in the comments, so 'your videos will grow exponentially.' At 10.8 a collage of like/comment-count screenshots covers him.
'For example, I found out mint chocolate chip ice cream is a very controversial topic.' At 15.2, on 'mint', two client TikTok screenshots of mint ice cream appear.
'This was a perfect fit for my ice cream shop client, Brewsters of North Homestead.' Client TikTok profile card (53.3K followers, 12.1M likes) pops in around 'client'.

'Comments like these…' shows a screenshot of toothpaste-debate comments. At 23.93, on '15', a scrolling screen recording of the 'Mint' playlist with per-post views (6.6M, 6.1M…) appears: 'over 15 million views on mint chocolate chip ice cream videos alone.'
'Each of these videos has thousands of comments.' Two stat columns (7,236 and 19.9K comments) are shown.
Back to the clean shot: 'I'm sharing all of the ways I hit almost 1 billion views, so follow me for part two.'

study.jump_cuts: Extremely tight. Speech fills 99% of the runtime, the median gap between words is 0.0s, there are zero fillers, and only 6 gaps reach 0.3s or more. The longest is 0.44s after 'controversial' (6.14s), a deliberate beat after the main point. Other kept pauses: 0.36s after 'styles' (4.36), 0.40s after 'exponentially' (13.44), 0.34s before 'Brewsters' (20.44), 0.36s after 'Homestead' (21.78) and 0.30s after 'alone' (26.92), all at sentence ends. There are 10 cuts in 33.3s (3.0 per 10s; median shot 3.0s, longest 6.13s from 4.67-10.8). Hand positions jump at 2.0, 4.67 and 13.87, so these are real jump cuts that removed breaths and retakes. About half the cuts fall at sentence starts (2.0, 4.67, 13.87, 18.2, 22.17, 27.2). The others land mid-sentence exactly on the word an overlay illustrates: 10.8 on 'happen', 15.2 right after 'mint', 23.93 on '15', 29.63 inside 'I'm sharing'. The result feels breathless but natural, because the delivery itself is fast (3.92 words/s).
study.zooms_punch_ins: None. Every clean shot keeps the same locked-off waist-up wide framing, with his head at ~35-50% of frame height and the same scale before and after every cut. The visual change comes from overlays instead of zooms. The picture changes every ~1.3-6s: overlay on at 2.0, off at 4.67, on at 10.8, off at 13.87, on at 15.2, off at 18.2, profile card at ~20.1, swap at 22.17, swap at 23.93, swap at 27.2, off at 29.63. The longest unchanged stretch is 4.67-10.8 (6.1s), during the verbal explanation.
study.captions: Word-by-word karaoke captions, 2-3 words on screen at once (e.g. 'VIDEO STYLES THAT', 'NUMBER ONE IS', 'FOUND OUT'). The currently spoken word turns yellow while the rest stay white, so the highlight moves through the phrase ('VIDEO' yellow at 0.15, 'STYLES' yellow at 0.55). Heavy bold sans-serif in ALL CAPS with a dark drop shadow/thin outline and no box. Medium-large size, about 60-75% of frame width per line. Centered at ~78-80% of frame height, rising to ~73% over the playlist screen recording. Phrases swap instantly with no bounce.
study.on_screen_text: Title 'Video Styles That Always Get Views' in white bold sans with a thick black outline, title case on two lines, centered at ~17-27% of frame height. A small white 'Part 1' sits below it at ~30%. It is on screen from 0.0s and disappears at the 4.67s cut, when point one starts. No numbered headers; 'Number one' is only spoken and captioned.
study.graphics_overlays: Real proof screenshots pop on with hard cuts, layered over the talking shot so his body stays visible around them. 2.0-4.67: five TikTok thumbnails with view counts (26.4M, 24.3M, 26M, 19.2M, 22.6M) staggered across the upper-middle frame, covering his face. 10.8-13.87: a six-tile collage of video stats (hearts 471K, 2.2M, 793.8K, 393K, 1.3M; comments 1,618 to 20.7K) filling ~10-70% of the height. 15.2-18.2: two client mint-ice-cream TikTok screenshots ('When someone hates on Mint ice cream', 'hot people picking out ice cream'). ~20.1-22.17: a white TikTok profile card for Bruster's North Olmsted (384 following, 53.3K followers, 12.1M likes) centered at ~35-60%. 22.17-23.93: a white comment-thread screenshot ('It's literally just toothpaste' 23K likes, 'brushing my teeth and eating Oreos' 41.9K). 23.93-27.2: a phone screen recording of the 'Mint 37 posts' playlist auto-scrolling (Post 1 6.6M views, Post 2 6.1M…), which drives the motion spikes up to 24.0 between 24.5-27s. 27.2-29.63: two tall stat columns (393K/7,236/17K/7,951 and 793.8K/19.9K/22.7K/11.4K). No emojis, arrows or progress bars.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. Each overlay enters and exits on a cut with no animation; the profile card pops in without a detected cut around 'client' (~20.1s).
study.broll_and_interrupts: The proof overlays are the b-roll: 7 overlay segments covering about 17.5s of the 33.3s (~53%). Each lasts 1.8-3.3s and they arrive every ~2-5s. The clean talking shot returns only for the claim sentences (4.67-10.8, 13.87-15.2, 18.2-~20.1, 29.63-end). The scrolling screen recording at 23.93-27.2 is the biggest motion moment and lands on the '15 million views' payoff. Strong audio transients at 1.97, 4.77 and 22.18 coincide with cuts/overlay entrances and may be pop/whoosh hits, but that can't be confirmed from the data. No angle changes, location changes or props other than the visible handheld mic.
study.audio: Clean, close voice from the handheld wireless mic, with little room echo. Delivery is fast and continuous with no fillers. The data can't confirm music; speech covers 99% of the runtime, so anything under it sits low. Possible light SFX on the overlay cuts (transients at 1.97, 4.77, 22.18). No silence used for effect beyond the 0.3-0.44s sentence-end beats.
study.length_and_ending: 33.3s, 129 words. The build: claim (0-1.7), credibility (1.9-4.4), point (4.7-8.1), mechanism (8.3-13.4), example setup (13.8-21.8), escalating proof (22.1-29.3). The payoff '15 million views' lands at 23.78-24.6s (~72%) and is reinforced by 'thousands of comments' at 28.9s (~87%). It ends on the CTA 'I'm sharing all of the ways I hit almost 1 billion views, so follow me for part two', which ups the credibility number from hundreds of millions to almost 1 billion and teases a series. It cuts 0.38s after the last word. No loop.
study.quality: 720x1280, 30fps, HEVC at a high ~14.4 Mbps, sharp. Locked-off tripod shot at medium-wide distance with generous headroom (top ~30% is wall, leaving room for the title), eyes at ~40% of height, looking straight at the lens. Soft even front light. Clean, premium-looking backdrop: white marble wall with dark wood slats on the left. A visible handheld mic signals 'pro podcast-ish'. The effort is in the edit (real analytics screenshots and screen recordings) rather than the camera work, which looks polished but simple.
study.why_viral: It promises a guaranteed outcome ('always get views') to creators and business owners, then backs every claim with real on-screen numbers within seconds (26.4M thumbnails at 2s, 15M playlist at 24s). The mint-chocolate-chip toothpaste debate is itself a mini controversy, so the video demonstrates its own advice and invites viewers to argue in the comments. Proof overlays change the picture every 2-5s, so a single static shot never feels static. The 'part one / follow for part two' framing plus the 'almost 1 billion views' flex turns watchers into followers.
lessons: Start speaking at 0.0s and say the full promise plus the series tag in under 2s ('X that always get Y, part one'), with a matching 2-line title at ~20-30% of frame height that stays only until the first point (~4.5s).
Put credibility proof on screen within the first 2-3s: cut to real screenshots of results exactly as the speaker states the number.
Cut each overlay in on the exact word it illustrates, even mid-sentence (e.g. on 'mint', on '15'). Return to the clean face shot for claims and the CTA.
Cover ~50% of a sub-35s tip video with proof overlays of 1.8-3.3s each, so the visual changes every 2-5s and never holds longer than ~6s.

Escalate proof in order: big totals, then the specific example, then the account/profile, then real comments, then a scrolling list of results. Use a moving screen recording on the key number for a motion spike.
Strip every breath and filler down to a 0.0s median gap. Keep only 0.3-0.45s pauses at sentence ends, and the longest one right after the main point.
Use 2-3-word ALL CAPS karaoke captions at ~78% height with the active word in yellow; nudge them up (~73%) when an overlay fills the lower frame.
End on a follow CTA that teases the next part with a bigger number than the opening claim, and cut within ~0.4s of the last word.
With no punch-ins available, a locked wide shot with ~30% headroom works if overlays carry the visual rhythm; frame wide enough that screenshots can sit over the torso and face.
creator_advice: Be controversial: video styles that always get views, number one is be controversial.
If you have a hot take, then get it out there.
These videos generate conversations, and when those conversations happen in your comments, your videos will grow exponentially.

Find the controversial topic in your niche: 'I found out mint chocolate chip ice cream is a very controversial topic for some people. This was a perfect fit for my ice cream shop client' — comments like these led to over 15 million views on mint chocolate chip videos alone, each with thousands of comments.

study.format: listicle
study.topic: A rapid-fire list of six specific sound effects to use for six parts of a short-form edit: hooks, transitions, captions, CTAs, reveals and on-screen text points.
study.hook:
"Use this sound effect for your hooks." starts at 0.00s with no lead-in. It is 7 words in 1.82s (~3.85 words/s), slightly faster than the video's 3.45 words/s average. The first 2 seconds show:
- **Framing:** a medium close-up of the creator in the driver's seat of a parked car, with lots of headroom above him.
- **Header:** a persistent two-column header, "WITH THIS:" (left) and "USE THIS:" (right), in white bold caps at ~24% of frame height, already on screen at frame 0.
- **Gesture:** his index finger goes up by 0.35s.
- **Sound card:** a sound-library card ("Record scratch 1 · 00:01 · DJ BAI") pops in under "USE THIS:" at ~1.0s, on "for".
- **Label:** "HOOKS" pops under "WITH THIS:" at ~1.6–1.7s, on the word "hooks".

Why it stops the scroll: the empty fill-in-the-blank header is a template the eye wants completed. The promise of a concrete, copyable resource (an exact named sound) arrives inside 1 second. Creators instantly recognise "hooks" as their own problem.

beats.what: "Use this sound effect for your hooks." Record scratch 1 card pops ~1.0s; HOOKS label pops on 'hooks' (~1.6s). Doubles as item 1.
Item 2: "...for your transitions." swish_whoosh card appears ~2.5–2.8s; TRANSITIONS label pops on 'transitions' (3.54s).
Item 3: "...for your captions." Apple Phone Typing card appears by ~5.2s; CAPTIONS label pops on 'captions' (5.80s).
Item 4: "...for your calls to action." Bell ding card appears by ~7.3s; CTAS label pops on 'calls to action' (~7.8–8.0s).
Item 5: "...for your reveals." Metallic Riser card appears by ~9.4s; REVEALS label pops on 'reveals' (10.22s).
Item 6: "...for your on-screen text points." 'pop! (tapping the...' card appears by ~11.4s; TEXT POINTS label pops on 'screen/text' (~12.8s).
Last word ends 13.64s and the video cuts 0.26s later. No CTA. The identical 'Use this sound effect for your...' opener makes the replay feel like the next item, so it loops seamlessly.

study.jump_cuts:
Six separate takes, one per sentence, each shot 2.17–2.83s (median 2.21s), at 3.6 cuts per 10s.
- **Word gaps:** the median gap is 0.0s and there are zero fillers. Only 3 gaps reach 0.3s or more: 0.38s after 4.0s, 0.34s after 6.18s and 0.42s after 10.6s.
- **Where those gaps sit:** all three are the tail between the end of one sentence and the next take. They are left in so the category label stays readable for ~0.3–0.6s before the cut.
- **Cut placement:** every cut lands between thoughts, right at the start of the next 'Use' (cuts at 2.2/4.37/6.6/8.87/11.07 vs words at 2.06/4.38/6.52/8.68/11.02). No cuts fall mid-sentence.
- **Feel:** extremely tight and metronomic. Speech fills 98% of the runtime. The rhythm comes from the identical sentence length rather than from trimming inside lines.
study.zooms_punch_ins:
None. The frames before and after every cut show the same framing and scale: same seat, same visor at the top, head at the same size. There are no digital punch-ins or zooms.

Visual change instead comes from three sources:
- **Hard cuts** every ~2.2s.
- **Two text/graphic pops per shot:** the sound card ~0.5–1s in, the label ~1.3–1.7s in.
- **His hand gestures:** finger raised by the head at each shot start, then pointing at the camera. These give the alternating motion values of ~10–14 vs ~4.

Net result: something new appears on screen roughly every 0.7–1.0s.
study.captions: none. There are no word-by-word speech captions; the spoken keyword is represented only by the category label.
study.on_screen_text:
1) **Persistent header.** "WITH THIS:" (left, ~x 12–47%) and "USE THIS:" (right, ~x 57–88%).
- Style: white, heavy geometric sans (Montserrat/Poppins ExtraBold style), all caps, soft dark drop shadow, no box.
- Position: ~24% of frame height.
- Timing: on screen from 0.0s to the end, never animated.

2) **Category labels** under "WITH THIS:" at ~31% height: "HOOKS", "TRANSITIONS", "CAPTIONS", "CTAS", "REVEALS", "TEXT POINTS".
- Style: same font and style as the header, slightly larger.
- Animation: each pops in (hard appear) exactly on or just after the spoken keyword (~1.5–1.7s into each shot).
- Duration: each stays only until the cut, ~0.4–0.9s.
- Wording: the label is a condensed version of speech ('calls to action' → CTAS, 'on-screen text points' → TEXT POINTS).
study.graphics_overlays:
One screenshot card per item, placed in the right column under "USE THIS:" at ~28–34% of frame height. Each is a dark rounded-rectangle row from an editing app's sound library, showing a thumbnail icon, sound name, duration and artist:
- Record scratch 1 · 00:01 · DJ BAI
- swish_whoosh (large · 00:01 · satak
- Apple Phone Typing and Te... · 00:04
- Bell ding · 00:03 · unknown
- Metallic Riser · 00:01
- pop! (tapping the... · 00:01 · LEOPARD

Each card appears ~0.4–0.9s into its shot, on 'sound effect'/'for', with a quick appear and no slide. It stays until the hard cut.

The resulting 2-column 'X → Y' chart sits fully above his head, so nothing covers the face.
study.transitions: hard cuts only. The 5 straight cuts at 2.2, 4.37, 6.6, 8.87 and 11.07s each reset the label and card for the next item.
study.broll_and_interrupts:
- **B-roll:** none. There are also no angle or location changes; it is one continuous car setup.
- **Interrupts:** the pattern interrupts are the two graphic pops per shot (card, then label), ~0.7–1.0s apart. Each shot change also clears the graphics.
- **Sound effects:** the strongest audio hits cluster at each shot's pop moments (3.61, 5.23/5.42/5.86, 7.84/8.02, 9.14, 11.39, 12.79/13.14). That is consistent with each named sound being demoed as its card/label appears, but which hit is which SFX can't be confirmed from the data.
- **Gestures:** his hand acts as a built-in interrupt (finger up near the temple → pointing at the camera) in every shot.
study.audio:
Clean, close voice from a clip-on wireless lav (a DJI-style mic transmitter is visible on his shirt). There is slight car-cabin room tone and no echo.
- **Music:** no music bed is evident.
- **Sound effects:** short SFX hits sit around the card and label pops in each shot (the audio hits listed above), so the content itself demonstrates the sounds.
- **Silence:** none is used for effect. The only pauses are the ≤0.42s gaps between takes.
study.length_and_ending:
13.9s total, 47 words.
- **Build:** there is no single build. The value is spread evenly across 6 equal ~2.2s items; the final, most specific item ('on-screen text points') starts at 11.07s (80%) and the last word ends at 13.64s (98%).
- **Ending:** no CTA, no sign-off. The cut comes 0.26s after the last word, straight back into the identical opening sentence, which creates a near-seamless loop.
- **Why it's this short:** the brevity plus the screenshot-worthy chart invites saves and rewatches to note the sound names.
study.quality:
Casual on purpose, with clear structure.
- **Camera and framing:** phone front camera in a parked car, medium close-up. The face sits in the middle of the frame (eyes ~47% height). There is generous headroom, with the top ~35% left for text.
- **Light and background:** soft natural daylight from the windshield and side windows, slightly cool and even. The background is the car interior (visor, seats, rear window), which is busy but neutral.
- **Sound:** a lav mic gives crisp sound.
- **Technical:** 720x1280, 30fps, HEVC at ~13 Mbps, sharp enough.
- **Effort split:** the high-effort part is entirely the graphic system: a consistent header, label and card chart. The filming itself is low-effort, everyday-creator style, which makes it relatable to the target audience of creators.
study.why_viral:
1) Extremely concrete, copyable value: six exact, named sound effects (with library screenshots) mapped to six edit moments. People save it to look the sounds up later.
2) A rigid, predictable structure with a new item every ~2.2s and a visual pop every ~1s. The viewer knows the next item is coming in 2s, so they don't leave.
3) A fill-in-the-blank 'WITH THIS: / USE THIS:' header from frame 0 creates a completion itch. The final chart works like a cheat-sheet screenshot.
4) A 14s runtime with an identical repeating sentence and an ending 0.26s after the last word, so it loops and racks up rewatches.
lessons: For list content, record one take per item and cut each to ~2.2s (range 2.1–2.9s), giving ~3–4 cuts per 10s. Put every cut between items, never mid-sentence.
Use one identical sentence frame for every item ('Use this X for your Y'). Repetition makes the rhythm predictable and fast to follow.
Put a persistent template header on screen from frame 0 (e.g., 'WITH THIS: / USE THIS:') at ~20–25% height. Leave its blanks empty so viewers wait for them to fill.
Pop the spoken keyword as a short all-caps label exactly on the word (within ~0.2s). Abbreviate long phrases to 1–2 words (calls to action → CTAS).
Show the actual resource (screenshot of the app item, product, tool) ~0.5–1s into each item. That makes the advice feel real and screenshot-worthy.
Add a new visual element roughly every 0.7–1.0s: card, then label, then cut. Static framing is fine when shots stay ≤2.3s and the speaker gestures.
Trim inter-sentence gaps to ≤0.4s and leave just enough tail (~0.3–0.6s) after the keyword for the label to be read before cutting.
Frame the speaker with extra headroom (eyes ~45–50% height) so all text and graphics sit in the top third without covering the face.
Pair each text pop with a short SFX hit, and when the topic is a sound or tool, let the content demo itself.
End within ~0.3s of the last word with no sign-off, and make the last line structurally identical to the first, so the loop is seamless.
creator_advice: Use this sound effect for your hooks — Record scratch.
Use this sound effect for your transitions — swish/whoosh.
Use this sound effect for your captions — Apple phone typing sound.
Use this sound effect for your calls to action — bell ding.
Use this sound effect for your reveals — metallic riser.
Use this sound effect for your on-screen text points — pop (tapping) sound.

study.format: listicle
study.topic: A creator-founder walks through the three things his $200/month Claude AI subscription does for his business (builds websites and funnels, edits every reel, powers his own AI product), each tied to a dollar figure, then sells a free guide.
study.hook: Speech starts at 0.00s with no lead-in: "This is everything I spend my $200 a month AI subscription on, but each thing makes me increasingly more money" (0.00–5.10s, about 3.6 words/s, quick and smiling). Frame for the first 2s is a close handheld selfie. His face fills the middle of the frame, and the room behind him is lit neon blue/purple with a night window. A two-line white lowercase hook title sits at about 22–25% of frame height: "i pay Claude $200/month ... it pays me $400k/month". It stops the scroll by setting a tiny cost against a huge return ($200 vs $400k) using a brand name people know (Claude). The spoken line adds a curiosity gap: what are the 'things'? The '$200' is said at 1.00s, inside the first second and a half.

beats.what: "This is everything I spend my $200 a month AI subscription on, but each thing makes me increasingly more money" over the cost-vs-return title card.
"Number one": every website, landing page and funnel is built by Claude Code. An 'agent 1 / Websites' label appears and website screenshot cards pop in one by one.
He no longer pays for '$100 a month website building' tools. Five app icons with monthly prices pop up ($30, $97, $39, $25, $39).
The webinar funnel made about $300,000 in 30 days. Funnel-page screenshots build left to right with arrows. A 0.38s pause is left in after '$300,000'.
He would have paid a designer $4,000, 'but Claude does it for me'.
"Number two": AI edited every Instagram reel. An 'agent 2 / Video editing' label appears and the edit cuts to handheld screen b-roll of Claude Code.
80 videos edited in 30 days: $9,600 or 322 hours saved. He shows it with finger-pointing b-roll of his dashboard ($9,675, 80 videos, 322.5 hrs).
"Here are some examples": before/after view of raw talking-head clips turned into captioned videos with a text hook.

lessons: Open on the first frame with speech at 0.0s and a two-line text title stating a cost-vs-result contrast with specific numbers; keep the title up until the first cut (about 6s).

Structure listicles with a chapter label on each 'Number X' (small 'agent 1' over a large bold title, top-left at about 15–20% height), and pull the label off once the point moves into b-roll or a new setup.
Every time the speaker says a number or names a tool, show proof within 1s: a screenshot, a dashboard being pointed at, or a built-up graphic like an invoice that totals the figure as it's said.
Build lists of things visually one item at a time, in step with repeated phrases ('every single landing page, every single funnel'): add a card each 0.5–1.5s, all in the top third above the face.
Keep shots around 3–4s (median 3.9s, max about 7s) and let half the cuts fall mid-sentence when switching to b-roll, so the VO carries over the cut.
When there's no zoom footage, get variety from setups: rotate close selfie, seated wide, low angle and handheld screen b-roll every 10–25s instead of digital punch-ins.
Put speech captions as 1–3 word phrases in a fixed center position (about 55% height), small white with a shadow, and keep graphics above them so nothing overlaps.
End with a single-keyword comment CTA in the last 5% and show it happening (a comment box typing the word), then cut within 0.3s of the last word.

study.format: business/day-in-the-life talk (daily challenge-series vlog entry, 'Day 3' of a 30-day $1M challenge) with storytime and mindset reflection
study.topic: Day 3 of a 30-day 'make $1M or go bald' challenge: sales fell from $20K a day to $4K, and the creator admits his 'it's not about the money' story only shows up on slow days.
study.hook: "I'm giving myself 30 days to make a million dollars where I have to go bald" starts at 0.00s with no lead-in. It is fast: 10 words in 2.3s (~4.3 w/s), and the whole hook ends at 3.34s. In the first 2 seconds the framing is a handheld selfie from a desk chair: medium shot with his outstretched arm visible on the right, a night city window behind him and blue/purple ambient light. A two-line white title, 'POV: your sales drop from $20,000 a day to $4,000', sits at ~20-25% of frame height, and a small white phrase caption ('I'm giving myself', '30 days', 'a million dollars') sits at ~65%. The last frame before the 3.87s cut flashes a bald version of him as a visual gag on the stakes. It stops the scroll because it stacks three hooks in about 3 seconds: a huge money goal, an absurd personal penalty (going bald), and a POV title promising a crash ($20K to $4K).

beats.what: Challenge premise with stakes: 30 days to make $1M or go bald. POV title shows the sales crash, and a bald-head flash closes the shot.
'And I realized today, it's really not about the money.' Wry, sarcastic delivery that sets up the irony.
Proof: 'We went from doing 20K a day to 4K today' over two quick laptop-dashboard b-roll shots (yesterday ~$25.5K, today ~$4.4K).
Grimacing, self-mocking 'it's about the impact... not about the money, guys.'
'DAY 3' label and a $/1M progress bar appear. 'Now we have done officially 51K', with a dashboard b-roll and the counter ticking up to $51,588.
Pre-empts the viewer's objection. A reply-to-comment bubble appears: 'ah Mino, that's really f*cking good. What are you complaining about?' He acts out the commenter.
'Well, you math that out': a wooden progress bar shows $51,588 in 3 days against the pace needed for $1,000,000. 'We're not moving as fast as we need to be... anywho, anywho, right?'
Cutaway to a different location (typing on laptop, AirPods, watch) while the voiceover explains the mindset trap: when business is good, 'momentum is everything, we got to double down.'
Contrast: when days are slow, the story flips to 'not about the money, not about the numbers, just showing up and the impact.'
Self-awareness: 'I noticed these narratives forming in my head', then he acts out the urge to over-intellectualize ('what went wrong, dude?... we need to change things').
'Honestly, some days are just slower. That's okay.'
'So we'll see how this goes, yeah. Thank you guys for watching. I'll see you tomorrow for day four.' Back to the handheld selfie framing from the open, as a series cliffhanger.
