'Reaction': '7 - Reaction' with a reaction-video example
'Screen Share': '8 - Screen Share' with a diagram/screen example
'Yapp': '9 - Yap' with a walking-and-talking example, one finger left
'Talking Head': '10 - Talking Head', hands now fists (count complete), example clip pops a big 'CONTENT' title
Ends 0.16s after the last word with fists closed, which loops cleanly back to ten open fingers and 'Clone'

study.jump_cuts: No cuts at all: one 8.8s take, 0 cuts per 10s. It feels tight because the delivery itself is tight, not because of editing. Speech fills 98% of the runtime. Median gap between words is 0.24s and the longest is 0.4s (after 'Screen' at 1.46s). Only five gaps reach 0.3s or more: 0.4s, 0.36s, 0.34s, 0.36s and 0.32s. These are the natural breaths between list items and all fall between items, never mid-item. No fillers, false starts or repeats. The 'tightness' comes from a pre-scripted, one-word-per-item list delivered in one breath.
study.zooms_punch_ins: None. The frame stays a locked-off waist-up wide for the full 8.8s, with median motion 1.9/100 and no spikes until 24.2 at 8.5s. That final spike is the overlay clip changing ('CONTENT' title appearing), not a zoom. The visual change comes from the overlay instead: the label and example clip swap about every 0.7–1.2s (10 swaps in ~8.2s, ~0.85s average). The speaker's finger count changes on the same rhythm.
study.captions:
No word-by-word speech captions. The numbered item labels act as the caption: one label on screen at a time, showing the exact term being said.
- Text: '1 - Clone', '2 - Split Screen', ... '10 - Talking Head'.
- Style: bold sans-serif, sentence/title case, yellow with a soft dark shadow, no box.
- Size: small–medium, about 5% of frame width per character.
- Position: centered at ~52–55% of frame height, just above the example clip.
- Animation: hard swap on each spoken item, roughly synced to the word onset (e.g. '6 - Ranking' already showing at 5.06s for the word at 5.02s).
study.on_screen_text:
The persistent title '10/10 Viral Content Formats' sits on two lines: '10/10 Viral' and 'Content Formats'.
- Style: heavy rounded bold sans-serif, bright yellow, slight shadow, no background. '10/10' and 'Content Formats' are larger than 'Viral'.
- Position: centered at ~14–21% of frame height, above the speaker's head.
- Timing: on screen from 0.0s to the end, static with no animation.
- The numbered labels are described under captions.
study.graphics_overlays: A small vertical picture-in-picture example clip sits over the speaker's chest. It is a rounded-corner 9:16 card, about 25% of frame width, centered horizontally, spanning ~55–81% of frame height. It plays a real example video of each format: clone desk shot, split-screen, green-screen collage, b-roll, text listicle, tier-list ranking, reaction, screen-share diagram, walking yap, and talking head with a 'CONTENT' title. It hard-swaps on every item (~0.85s each). No emojis, arrows, progress bars or stickers. The speaker's own fingers work as a physical progress bar, counting down from 10 to 0.
study.transitions: hard cuts only (no camera cuts; only the overlay clip and label hard-swap on each item)
study.broll_and_interrupts: The only pattern interrupt is the overlay example clip, which changes 10 times in ~8.2s (roughly every 0.7–1.2s). Each swap shows a different real video, with its own on-video text, as instant proof of the format. Hand gestures change on every item: one finger folds per format, which is a constant visual tick. No angle or location changes, no props beyond the desk and laptop corner, no added sound effects that can be confirmed.
study.audio: Clean, close voice in a quiet room, with energetic, punchy, list-style delivery. The strongest audio hits (0.05, 0.63, 1.12, 1.35, 1.83 ... 8.34s) mostly line up with word onsets every ~0.3–0.5s, which is consistent with voice-driven peaks. Any music bed would be low and can't be confirmed from the data. No silence used for effect.
study.length_and_ending: 8.8s total. The build is pure accumulation, with the count visibly progressing from 10 fingers to fists. The payoff of hitting 10/10, 'Talking Head', starts at 8.16s (~93%). There is no CTA. The last word ends at ~8.64s and the video cuts 0.16s later. Closed fists at the end match the ten-open-fingers opening, so the loop is near-seamless and many viewers rewatch to catch the example clips they missed.
study.quality:
Resolution is 576x1024 at 30fps, h264, ~398 kbps, which is low bitrate but sharp enough.
- Framing: waist-up medium shot, centered. The head sits at ~22–45% of frame height, with the title filling the headroom. Eye line is straight to the lens.
- Lighting: soft, even, natural-looking, against a plain off-white wall. A wooden desk sits in the foreground with a laptop corner at bottom right.
- Wardrobe: a busy patterned shirt gives visual texture.
- The camera and shot are casual; the effort is in the edit, with ten matched example clips and synced labels. It reads as a high-value cheat sheet made simply.
study.why_viral: 1) Extreme value density: ten named, shown-with-example formats in under 9 seconds, so it's saveable and shareable as a cheat sheet for creators. 2) A built-in progress bar in the finger countdown plus the '10/10' title, so viewers know exactly how much is left and stay to the end. 3) The example clip swaps every ~0.85s, so visuals change constantly even though the camera never moves. 4) The seamless loop (fists back to ten fingers) and too-fast-to-catch examples drive rewatches and saves.
lessons: Start on the first content word at 0.00s: no greeting, no 'here are'. Let the on-screen title carry the setup.
For list videos, keep each item to ~0.7–1.2s and swap a visual on every item so something changes at least every 1s.
Pin a 2-line hook title in the top ~15–20% of the frame for the whole video so the promise is always visible.
Label each item with its number and name ('3 - Green Screen') centered around 50–55% height, swapped exactly on the word onset (within ~0.05s).
If the take has no dead air (median gap ~0.24s, longest ≤0.4s), don't add cuts or zooms just to be busy. A locked shot plus overlay swaps is enough.
Use a picture-in-picture example card (~25% of frame width, rounded corners, mid-lower frame) to prove each point instead of describing it.
Give the viewer a visible countdown or progress cue (fingers, 'x/10', progress bar) so they know how close the end is.
End within ~0.2s of the last word with no CTA, and match the final pose or frame to the opening so the loop is seamless.
Keep the whole list under ~10s when items are single words. Density drives saves and rewatches.
creator_advice: The 10 viral content formats to use: 1 Clone, 2 Split Screen, 3 Green Screen, 4 Voiceover B-roll, 5 Listicle, 6 Ranking, 7 Reaction, 8 Screen Share, 9 Yap, 10 Talking Head.

study.format: advice / tips (numbered listicle of 3 editing rules, filmed as a casual selfie talk)
study.topic: A video editor explains the three things every talking-head video needs to stop people skipping: a text hook, auto captions, and clean audio with a trending song underneath.
study.hook: First word lands at 0.00s with no lead-in: "When you're editing a talking head videos like this, you don't want too much editing", about 4.2 words/s, spoken while he gestures toward the lens. In the first 2s the frame is a handheld night selfie inside a car. His face sits mid-frame (roughly 35-55% of height). A two-line title box sits at the top (~13-20% height): "WHY PEOPLE SKIP / YOUR TALKING HEADS" in bold white caps on black boxes, with "TALKING HEADS" in yellow. Speech captions build word by word below his face, and "talking head" pops large in yellow at ~1.0s. It stops the scroll for three reasons: the title names a pain the target viewer (creators and business owners) has. "like this" makes the video itself the demo, so the viewer starts checking whether this edit follows the rules. At 2.8s a red tilted "TOO MUCH" stamp adds a visual jolt.

beats.what: "When you're editing a talking head videos like this, you don't want too much editing" with the title WHY PEOPLE SKIP YOUR TALKING HEADS; red TOO MUCH stamp pops at ~2.8s on "too much".
Cut to "but you just want to have enough"; the stamp swaps to a yellow JUST ENOUGH label at 4.92s.
"For me, a good editing needs to have three things." A cut at 6.47 lands right before "three" with a big yellow "3" caption, and he holds up three fingers on "things."
"Number one, text hook." At the 8.2s cut the title returns as an outlined version plus a yellow pill "1 · TEXT HOOK". The video points at its own hook.
Reason: most of the shot is just you talking, so you need text that makes people curious. A thinking emoji pops beside the title on "curious" (~14s).
"Number two, auto caption." Yellow pill "2 · AUTO CAPTIONS" plus a yellow-outlined box around the captions themselves.
"A lot of people actually watch your reels or your TikTok with no sound." A mute speaker icon appears at the top on "no sound" (~19.4s).
"having auto caption will keep them gauged and they can keep watching your content". "engaged," and "keep watching" pop large in yellow.
"And number three, audio." Yellow pill "3 · AUDIO" plus an animated VOICE / SONG level-meter graphic at the top.
Make your voice stand out and clear. The VOICE meter row gets a yellow highlight box on "voice" (~26.4s).
"And also have a really good trending song in the background." The SONG row highlights on "song" (~30.3s); the video ends 0.35s after the last word.

study.jump_cuts: Extremely tight. Speech covers 99% of the runtime, the median gap between words is 0.00s, the longest gap is 0.22s (after "enough." at 4.68 and after "things." at 7.24), there are 0 gaps over 0.3s and 0 fillers. Gaps between sentences were trimmed to 0.12-0.22s, and at 28.72 "understand." runs straight into "And" with zero gap. There are 14 cuts in 31.6s, 4.43 cuts per 10s, with a median shot of 1.55s, shortest 0.63s (20.27-20.9) and longest 4.82s (24.1-28.92). Roughly half the cuts sit between thoughts, right at a sentence start: 3.38 "but", 4.92 "For", 7.47 "Number", 15.33 before "Number", 16.75 "A", 24.1 "number". The rest land mid-sentence: 6.47 just before "three", 8.2 between "text" and "hook", 10.42 "talking | in", 14.46 inside "what", 20.27 on "having", 20.9 "caption | will", 23.33 "your | content", 28.92 "And | also". The mid-sentence cuts remove stumbles and also re-trigger attention on keywords. It feels breathless but natural, because the handheld framing barely shifts between takes.
study.zooms_punch_ins: No clear digital punch-ins or animated zooms. Comparing frames before and after each cut, the scale stays close to 1.0x. Framing shifts come from the handheld phone moving between takes: a slightly tighter, closer face at the end of the 7.47 shot on "things." (~1.1x versus the shot after), and the camera moving closer and lower at 20.27 and 28.92. Motion is low throughout (median 5.4/100). The one spike is 16.2 at ~20.5s, from a hand swipe right after the 20.27 cut. Visual change instead comes from cuts every ~1.5s on median plus caption keyword pops and graphic swaps, so something new happens on screen roughly every 1-2s.
study.captions: Word-by-word build-up, timed to speech. About 3-6 small words per line, and lines clear at sentence or phrase breaks. Body words are a clean white sans (Helvetica/SF-like), regular-to-medium weight, sentence case, small (~4% of frame height). They have a light shadow and no box, and upcoming words fade in from grey. Key nouns and phrases jump onto their own line about 2x larger, in bold yellow: "talking head", "too much", "things.", "3", "text hook.", "talking", "curious", "auto caption.", "no sound.", "engaged,", "keep watching", "voice", "clear", "song". Captions sit in the lower-middle (~62-80% of frame height), under the chin over the chest. During point 2 (16.04-~20.9s) they are wrapped in a rounded yellow-outlined dark box to show off the caption itself. Captions are lightly cleaned up rather than verbatim: "gauged" is written as "engaged", "For me" shows as "And for", and "having auto caption" as "Having an auto caption".
study.on_screen_text: 1) Hook title, 0-~2.8s: "WHY PEOPLE SKIP / YOUR TALKING HEADS" in bold white sans caps on solid black rounded boxes, "TALKING HEADS" in yellow, top center ~13-20% height. 2) "TOO MUCH", ~2.8-4.9s: red caps in a red-bordered, slightly tilted rubber-stamp box at ~17% height, stamped in on the words "too much". 3) "JUST ENOUGH", 4.92-~7.4s: black bold caps on a solid yellow box at the same spot, swapping in on the cut. 4) From the 8.2s cut to 15.33s: the hook title returns, restyled with yellow outline boxes, plus a small yellow pill below it, "👆 1 · TEXT HOOK" (~24% height). 5) 16.04-~20.9s: yellow pill "👆 2 · AUTO CAPTIONS" at ~63% height, attached to the caption box. 6) 24.1s to the end: yellow pill "👆 3 · AUDIO" at ~13% height above a VOICE/SONG meter. Each numbered label appears on the word naming the point and stays for that whole section. There are no headers between points; the text resets with each new section.
study.graphics_overlays: A thinking-face emoji pops at the top-right corner of the title box around 14s on "curious". A white muted-speaker icon pops at ~23% height when "no sound" is said (~19.4s) and stays until ~20.9s. A rounded yellow-outline frame surrounds the captions during point 2. From 24.1s to the end, an audio level-meter panel sits at ~18-23% height: a mic icon labeled "VOICE" and a note icon labeled "SONG", each with segmented green-to-yellow/orange bars that bounce like a live meter. The VOICE bar is louder than the SONG bar. A yellow highlight box moves to the VOICE row on "voice" (~26.4s) and to the SONG row on "song" (~30.3s). Every graphic illustrates the exact word being spoken. There is no B-roll, split screen, or progress bar.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only (jump cuts within one continuous selfie setup). Overlays appear and swap with quick pop/stamp entrances on the cuts or keywords; there are no whips, flashes, or glitches.
study.broll_and_interrupts: No B-roll, no angle or location changes. Attention is reset by text and graphic pop-ups, timed to keywords at intervals of roughly 1-5s: TOO MUCH stamp ~2.8s, JUST ENOUGH 4.92s, big yellow "3" 6.47s, three-finger gesture ~7.3s, title plus "1 · TEXT HOOK" 8.2s, emoji ~14s, "2 · AUTO CAPTIONS" plus caption box ~16s, mute icon ~19.4s, "3 · AUDIO" plus meter 24.1s, VOICE highlight ~26.4s, SONG highlight ~30.3s. Hand gestures act as natural interrupts: a finger point on "text hook", three fingers on "three things", a hand swipe at 20.3s. The strong audio hits at 2.42, 8.03, 15.7/16.3, 19.01 and 24.38 sit close to the graphic entrances. These are likely pop/whoosh sound effects on overlays, though this can't be confirmed from the data.
study.audio: Close phone-mic voice recorded in a quiet parked car. It is dry, with slight cabin boxiness but intelligible, and it sits at the front of the mix. Speech runs continuously at 4.23 words/s with no silence, so nothing is used for dramatic pause. The many evenly spread strong audio hits (about one per second) suggest a low background track and/or pop sound effects under the voice, which fits his own advice about a trending song kept below the voice. The on-screen meter, where VOICE sits higher than SONG, visualizes that mix. There is no audible music change or drop.
study.length_and_ending: 31.6s total, 132 words. The structure is a promise (too much versus just enough, 0-4.7s), the count ("three things", 4.9-7.2s), then three points at 7.46s, 15.46s and 24.04s. Each section runs about 8s and uses the same pattern: named point, one reason, then the benefit. Point 2's payoff, "keep watching your content", lands at ~23s (73%), and the final rule, the trending song, lands at 28.7-31.2s (91-99%). There is no CTA and no sign-off. It ends on the last tip, "background.", cutting 0.35s after the last word. That abrupt end, plus the self-demonstrating edit, makes it easy to rewatch to check the edit against the rules.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 24fps, h264 at only 523 kbps: soft, noisy and visibly compressed, filmed at night in a car. The phone is handheld at arm's length slightly below eye level. He looks just above the lens with plenty of headroom; the head sits around 35-55% of height, leaving the top band free for title graphics and the lower band for captions. Lighting is dim, from the interior dome light and parking-lot lights, with dark shadows and some grain; the background is the car headliner, a seatbelt and blurred lights through the window. The footage is deliberately low-effort, a quick 'yap in the car' vibe. The editing layer, by contrast, is polished and branded: consistent yellow/black/white system, animated meters, styled pills. The contrast of casual footage with a professional edit is the selling point for an editor showing what editing adds.
study.why_viral: 1) The video is its own proof: he says "videos like this" and then visibly applies each rule (text hook, styled auto captions, voice-forward audio with a meter), so viewers learn by watching and rewatch to spot the techniques. 2) The hook title "WHY PEOPLE SKIP YOUR TALKING HEADS" targets a large, anxious audience of creators and business owners, and the "3 things" promise gives a clear finish line in a 31s runtime. 3) Zero dead air (longest gap 0.22s) and a visual change every ~1.5s keep low-quality car footage watchable. 4) Simple, saveable, actionable advice that's easy to send to a friend or client who edits.
lessons: Start speaking at 0.00s and put a 2-line bold caps title in the top ~15-20% of the frame that names the viewer's problem (e.g., 'WHY PEOPLE SKIP YOUR ___'), with the key noun in an accent color.
Cut every gap between sentences down to ~0.1-0.2s and remove all gaps over 0.3s; aim for ~99% speech coverage and around 4 words/s.
Target ~4-5 cuts per 10s with a median shot of ~1.5s, and never let a shot run past ~5s on low-motion handheld footage.
Put about half your cuts mid-sentence right before a keyword (e.g., cut just before 'three' and drop a big '3'), so the cut and the keyword pop hit together.
Build captions word by word in white, ~3-6 words per line, in the lower-middle (~62-80% of height). Promote 1-2 key words per sentence to a separate line ~2x larger in bold yellow.
For listicles, give each point a persistent small label ('1 · TEXT HOOK') that appears on the word naming it and stays for that whole section (~6-8s), then replaces itself at the next point.
Match every graphic to the exact spoken word: a stamp on 'too much', a mute icon on 'no sound', a highlight on 'voice' or 'song'. Pop each in on the word, with an optional light pop sound effect.
Keep the top band and bottom band of the frame for text, with the face centered around 35-55% of height so overlays never cover the mouth or eyes.
If the speaker refers to 'videos like this', make the edit visibly demonstrate each claim; self-proving edits earn rewatches.
End on the final point with no outro and cut ~0.3-0.4s after the last word.
creator_advice: When you're editing talking head videos, you don't want too much editing, but you just want to have enough.
A good edit needs to have three things.
Number one, text hook: because most of the shot is just you talking in front of the camera, you want some kind of text that makes people curious to know what you're talking about.
Number two, auto captions: a lot of people watch your Reels or your TikTok with no sound, so having auto captions keeps them engaged and they can keep watching your content.
Number three, audio: edit to make sure your voice stands out and is clear enough to understand.
Also have a really good trending song in the background.

study.format: listicle (no-speech text-and-music listicle over blurred b-roll; a 'save this' resource post)
study.topic: Seven viral background songs matched to the mood of your video: cinematic, motivational, dramatic, powerful, nostalgic, mysterious and chaotic.
study.hook: There are no spoken words; the first word on screen is text, visible from frame 1 (0.0s). A bold white all-caps title, 'VIRAL BACKGROUND MUSIC', sits at about 20–28% of frame height over a medium-wide shot of the creator at his desk (monitor, energy drink, lamp). Album covers pop in one at a time into a grid under the title. The butterfly cover and 'Now or Never' are there at 0.15s, five covers by 0.55s, and all seven by 1.2s (butterfly, Now or Never, My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy, Timeless, a blue forest cover, The Weeknd, Eminem). The background darkens as the grid fills. It stops the scroll because creators instantly recognise the covers as the songs they keep hearing, and the stacking grid promises a list of ready-to-use tools. The headline names the payoff in three words.

beats.what: Title 'VIRAL BACKGROUND MUSIC' with a 7-cover grid building up over 1.2s, held to 2.67s
#1 CINEMATIC: butterfly cover labelled 'Good Man With a Now or Never Broken Heart', song plays, blurred stage b-roll with green curtain
#2 MOTIVATIONAL: 'Now or Never', blurred b-roll of a phone on a tripod filming the creator at night
#3 DRAMATIC: 'Runaway' (red MBDTF cover), blurred green-lit studio b-roll of the creator in a chair
#4 POWERFUL: 'Timeless', blurred living-room b-roll with a softbox and phone in the foreground
#5 NOSTALGIC: 'Snowfall', blue-lit blurred b-roll of the creator talking on a stool
#6 MYSTERIOUS: 'Lost In The Fire' by The Weeknd, side-angle blurred b-roll of the creator gesturing
#7 CHAOTIC: 'Without Me' by Eminem, the highest-energy track (densest audio hits), saved for last; the video ends inside this item

study.jump_cuts: No speech, so there are no word gaps, fillers or breaths to cut (words: 0). There are 8 shots in 38.8s, 1.8 cuts per 10s. The median shot is 4.93s and the longest is 6.0s (DRAMATIC, 11.73–17.73). Every cut lands exactly on an item change, together with the song swap and the text change, never mid-item. The rhythm is steady and predictable, about 4.5–6s per item after a short 2.67s hook. It feels tight because nothing in a segment overstays the song snippet.
study.zooms_punch_ins: No zooms or punch-ins; the before/after frames at each cut show completely different b-roll locations, not tighter crops. The visual changes every 4.5–6s at the cuts. Inside each shot, the motion comes from the animated waveform, the mood word typing in and out, and slight camera drift in the b-roll. Motion is about 0.5–1.3 in the first half and rises to about 1.5–3 between 17.7s and 32.9s, where the handheld or moving b-roll has more motion. Spikes at the cuts reach 4.8–12.2.
study.captions: none
study.on_screen_text: Hook title (0–2.67s): 'VIRAL BACKGROUND MUSIC' on two lines, heavy condensed sans, all caps, white with a soft dark drop shadow, centred at about 20–28% of frame height, static. Item template (2.67s–end): a two-line sentence 'Use this background music / if your video is [MOOD]', centred at about 34–39% of frame height. It is set in a clean regular-weight white sans (SF/Helvetica-like), sentence case, with no box. The mood word (CINEMATIC, MOTIVATIONAL, DRAMATIC, POWERFUL, NOSTALGIC, MYSTERIOUS, CHAOTIC) is bold all caps in an orange-to-red gradient, the only coloured text. It types or reveals in letter by letter from the cut ('POW', 'NO', 'MY', 'CH' just after cuts) and is fully written about 1s in. It dissolves or wipes out in the last ~0.5s before the next cut, so the old word fades as the new one starts ('CINEMATIC MO' at 7.20s, 'MOTIVATI_D' at 11.73s). Song title label: white serif (Times-like), under the album cover at about 58–60% of frame height, appearing with each cover: 'Good Man With a Now or Never Broken Heart', 'Now or Never', 'Runaway', 'Timeless', 'Snowfall', 'Lost In The Fire', 'Without Me'.
study.graphics_overlays: Album art: in the hook, a grid of seven square covers (3-3-1) pops in one by one between 0.0s and 1.2s under the title at about 31–68% of frame height. In each item, a single square cover sits left of centre at about 42–57% of frame height, swapped hard on each cut. Audio waveform: white vertical bars to the right of the cover at the same height (about 45–55%), animating subtly as if reacting to the song. Background treatment: every b-roll shot is heavily blurred and darkened (strong gaussian blur plus a vignette or dim layer) so the white and orange text and the covers read cleanly. No emojis, arrows or progress bars.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only, 7 of them, each landing with the song change. The only 'transition' feel comes from the mood word's type-out and type-in straddling each cut.
study.broll_and_interrupts: The whole video is b-roll: seven different blurred clips of the creator's filming setups and spaces. These are a stage with a green curtain, a phone on a tripod at night, a green-lit studio chair, a living room with a softbox, a blue-lit stool, a dark-teal side angle, and a dark green room. Each location and lighting colour changes every 4.5–6s and acts as the pattern interrupt. The real interrupt is the music: each cut swaps to a new, instantly recognisable song. Strong audio hits cluster in the cinematic song (3.14–6.7s), the dramatic one (13.79s), the powerful one (18.1–21.6s), and densely in 'Without Me' (33.23–38.57s, about every 0.25–0.5s). No added sound effects.
study.audio: No voice. The audio track is a run of song snippets, one per item, hard-switched at each cut and played at full level as the 'content'. Energy builds toward the end: 'Without Me' at 32.93s has the densest beat hits in the video. There is no silence; music runs to the last frame.
study.length_and_ending: 38.8s. A 2.67s title hook, then seven items of 4.5–6s each in a flat list structure, with the most energetic track (CHAOTIC/Eminem) last at 32.93s (85%). There is no CTA and no outro: it cuts at 38.8s, about 5.9s into the last item, mid-song. Ending in the music invites a rewatch, and the instant restart on the cover-grid title loops cleanly. The format is built to be saved.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 24fps, h264 at only 241 kbps; the low bitrate is hidden because every background is deliberately blurred and darkened. The hook shot is a clean medium-wide desk scene with a warm practical lamp. The item shots use moody coloured lighting (green, blue, warm red) that matches each mood word. The overlays are crisp, consistent templated graphics. It feels high-effort through the design system (repeated layout, gradient accent word, serif labels) while needing no on-camera performance.
study.why_viral: It is a save-worthy creator resource: seven named songs mapped to seven moods you can use today, and people save and share it to their editors. The recognisable album covers and songs give instant pattern recognition in the first second, and the 7-cover grid shows exactly how much value is coming. One rigid repeating template ('if your video is [MOOD]') makes each new item easy to anticipate, so viewers stay to see the next mood and hear the next track. The energy also escalates to Eminem's 'Without Me' at the end. The blurred shots of the creator's own filming setups quietly prove he makes the kind of content this music is for.
lessons: Put the full promise on screen at frame 0 in 2–4 big words ('VIRAL BACKGROUND MUSIC') and preview every item visually (here 7 covers popping in by 1.2s) so the viewer knows the size of the list.
Keep the hook under 3s (here 2.67s) before item #1 starts.
Use one repeating sentence template for every list item and change only one keyword, colour-highlighted (orange-red gradient vs white) so the eye goes straight to the new info.
Give each item an equal 4.5–6s slot and cut exactly on the item change (with the music or topic switch), never mid-item; about 1.8 cuts per 10s is enough when each cut brings new content.
Animate only the changing keyword: type it in over ~1s after the cut and wipe it out in the last ~0.5s, so the text carries momentum across the hard cut.
When the footage is low quality or filler, blur and darken it heavily and let a clean overlay layout carry the video. Here 241 kbps footage still looks polished.
Change location or lighting colour on every item (green, blue, warm, teal) as a free pattern interrupt, and match the colour to the item's mood.
Save the highest-energy item for last (here the densest audio hits at 32.9–38.6s) and end inside it with no outro, so the restart on the hook loops cleanly.
Keep the layout fixed: title text at about 35% of frame height, the graphic at 42–57%, nothing in the bottom 30% where platform UI sits.
creator_advice: Use this background music if your video is CINEMATIC: 'Good Man With a Now or Never Broken Heart' (butterfly cover).
Use this background music if your video is MOTIVATIONAL: 'Now or Never'.
Use this background music if your video is DRAMATIC: 'Runaway'.
Use this background music if your video is POWERFUL: 'Timeless'.
Use this background music if your video is NOSTALGIC: 'Snowfall'.
Use this background music if your video is MYSTERIOUS: 'Lost In The Fire' (The Weeknd).
Use this background music if your video is CHAOTIC: 'Without Me' (Eminem).

study.format: advice / tips (step-by-step app tutorial with screen-recording overlays)
study.topic: How to get your 'first million-view video' by letting TikTok's AutoCut feature turn random photos and clips into an edited video, plus a plug for an AI analysis app called Blow Up.
study.hook: First word "You're" lands at 0.14s. The line "You're going to make your first video with a million views and I'm going to help you do it right now" runs 20 words in 4.9s (0.14-5.02, about 4.1 words/s, slightly faster than the 3.78 w/s average). Frame 0.15s is a motion blur (motion 26.2, the highest in the video until the final frame) as the speaker settles into a medium close-up. He holds a small round wireless mic at his mouth, white cap, dartboards and RGB-lit sloped ceiling behind. From the first frame a title sits in the empty headroom: a red siren emoji 🚨 above a white rounded box with bold black uppercase sans text 'YOUR FIRST VIDEO TO HIT 1 MILLION VIEWS ✅' at about 25-28% of frame height. It stays until about 5s. It stops the scroll because it promises a huge, specific outcome (1 million views) to beginners, framed as 'your first' and 'right now'. The siren reads as urgent, and the spoken and written hooks say the same thing, so the viewer gets it with or without sound.

beats.what: Promise: your first million-view video, and I'll help you do it right now. Siren title card stays on screen.
Step 1: 'Okay, tap the plus button at the bottom.' A screenshot of the TikTok nav bar pops in with a red hand-drawn circle, the word 'here' and an arrow on the + button.

Step 2: 'find create and tap it, then look at the top and find autocut.' A floating screen recording of the CREATE screen covers his torso. A red circle sits on CREATE, an animated hand points to the top row (9.47s) and a red circle lands on AutoCut (10.58s).
Step 3: 'Tap on that, now go to your gallery and choose as many photos or short videos as you want.' Back to the talking head.
Lowers the bar with relatable examples: 'holiday photos, walking your dog, working out at the gym... It literally doesn't matter.'
Step 4: 'tap next and TikTok will turn all of that into a video.' Screen recording of the gallery selection with Next (4) at 22.9s, then a 'Processing… 20%' screen at 23.6s.

What it does for you: 'It'll add transitions, cuts and even music.' Rule: 'keep the trending music TikTok suggests.' A template screen shows from 27.2s, with a red arrow and circle on the music label at 28.57s and the template visibly changing at 29.6s.

Step 5: 'scroll through the templates... choose the one you like best and post the video.' The arrow and circle move to 'Select template' (about 30.6s), the template changes again at 31.8s, and the Drafts/Post bar appears at about 35.0s with an animated hand tapping Post.
Escalation: 'And if you want to take things even further, there is an app called Blow Up.' An App Store screenshot pops in top-left at about 39.1s.

Blow Up 'analyzes your videos and shows you your strengths but also what you need to improve.' Screen recording of the app analysing his own account, which scrolls at about 44s to 'Topics that drive his views', 'His strategy' and 'His virality elements'.
'If you want more TikTok tips to actually help you grow, make sure you follow me because I share them every single day.'

study.jump_cuts: Dead air is fully removed. Median gap between words is 0.0s, the longest is 0.18s, there are no gaps of 0.3s or more and no fillers, and speech fills 99% of the runtime. No pauses were left in on purpose; even the step transitions ('Okay,' at 5.02 into 'tap' at 5.56) run straight on. There are 17 cuts in 52.4s (3.25 per 10s), median shot 2.42s, longest 6.77s (16.13-22.9), shortest 0.7s (22.9-23.6). About half the cuts land mid-sentence or even mid-word: 7.2 between 'find' and 'create', 16.13 inside 'doesn't', 22.9 inside 'tap', 25.13 inside 'into', 27.2 between 'transitions' and 'cuts', 37.43 inside 'even'. These are driven by the overlays: the cut happens when the screen recording swaps in or out or changes state, not at a thought boundary. The audio stays continuous across them, so the edit feels relentless and breathless rather than choppy.
study.zooms_punch_ins: No deliberate punch-ins or zooms. The before and after frames at every cut show the same medium close-up at roughly the same scale (head and shoulders, cap top around 34-38% of frame height); differences are just his own head movement between takes (e.g. 5.47, 12.13, 37.43 are same-size jump cuts). The visual changes instead come from overlay state changes and the lighting. Counting cuts plus in-shot overlay changes (nav bar about 5.9s, hand 9.47s, circle 10.58s, arrow 28.57s, arrow move about 30.6s, Post bar about 35.0s, tap animation about 35.8s, App Store about 39.1s, app scroll about 44s), something changes roughly every 1.5-2.5s. The longest stretch with no change is the 16.13-22.9 talking-head shot, about 6.8s.
study.captions: One word on screen at a time, swapped word by word in sync with speech. White serif font (Times-style), regular weight, sentence case as spoken (e.g. 'You're', 'Holiday', 'TikTok'), small (about 4% of frame height), with only a faint shadow and no box or stroke. Centered horizontally at about 81% of frame height, just below his hands and the mic. No highlighted or colored words and no animation beyond the hard swap. There is a visible typo, 'liteitally' at 21.7s, which adds to the casual feel.
study.on_screen_text: Hook title from 0s to about 5s: 'YOUR FIRST VIDEO TO HIT 1 MILLION VIEWS ✅' in bold black uppercase condensed sans on a white rounded rectangle, with a large red siren emoji 🚨 above it, centered at about 18-28% of frame height in the headroom. It is static, already present at 0.15s and gone by the 5.01s frame. There are no other headers or numbered steps; the only other text is red handwritten 'here' on the nav-bar graphic (about 5.9-7.2s) and text inside the screenshots and recordings.
study.graphics_overlays: 1) About 5.9-7.2s: cropped TikTok bottom nav bar (Home, Shop, +, Inbox, Profile) on a white strip at about 27-31% height, with a red hand-drawn circle around +, red script 'here' and a white curved arrow. 2) 7.2-12.13s: a portrait screen recording of the TikTok CREATE page floats in the center over his torso (about 13-70% height), leaving his cap and face edges visible. A red circle marks the CREATE tab with a white cartoon pointing-hand emoji 👆 beneath, an animated white glove hand slides to the top icon row at about 9.5s, and a red circle lands on AutoCut at about 10.6s. 3) 22.9-25.13s: same floating style showing the gallery grid with Next (4), then at 23.6s a 'Processing… 20%' modal. 4) 27.2-32.73s: template picker recording, blurred at first then playing meme templates. A red arrow and red ellipse point at the music label (28.57s) and later at 'Select template' (about 30.6s). 5) About 35.0-36.0s: Drafts/Post button bar at about 20-28% height, with an animated pointer hand and burst lines tapping Post just before 36.0s. 6) About 39.1-40.07s: App Store listing screenshot 'Blow Up: Go Viral With AI' top-left at about 9-37% height. 7) 40.07-46.8s: floating screen recording of the Blow Up app analysing @viralityadam1 ('Spotting what keeps coming back'), scrolling at about 44s through 'Topics that drive his views', 'His strategy' and 'His virality elements'. All overlays appear and disappear on hard cuts with no slide or fade.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only: same-framing jump cuts between talking-head takes, and hard cuts in and out of the floating screen-recording overlays. No whips, flashes, zoom transitions or swipes.
study.broll_and_interrupts: The 'b-roll' is the screen recordings and screenshots layered over the speaker (he stays partly visible behind them), not full-screen cutaways. These overlays run about 5.9-12.13s (about 6.2s), 22.9-25.13s (2.2s), 27.2-32.73s (5.5s), about 35.0-36.0s (about 1s), about 39.1-40.07s (about 1s) and 40.07-46.8s (6.7s), so roughly 22s of the 52s carries a demo overlay. They are spaced so the bare talking head never runs longer than about 10.7s (12.13-22.9). The background RGB LED slowly cycles color through the whole video (neutral/pink → green about 4-12s → blue about 12-16s → purple about 16-22s → pink/red about 22-27s → green about 30-35s → teal/blue about 36-41s → purple about 44-48s → pink about 49-52s), so every jump cut also shows a slightly different color, a free low-key interrupt. Hand gestures with the round mic act as a constant visual prop. No angle or location changes. Strong audio hits (e.g. 5.59, 6.0, 22.36, 23.0, 39.62) sit on stressed words or overlay entrances; whether any are added SFX can't be confirmed from the data.
study.audio: Clean, close voice recorded on the small handheld wireless mic he holds at his mouth, with slight room tone from a small bedroom. Delivery is fast and energetic (3.78 words/s overall, about 4.1 in the hook) with no pauses. The data doesn't show clear background music, and speech covers 99% of the runtime. The strongest audio hits line up with spoken emphasis and overlay pops rather than a beat. No silence is used for effect.
study.length_and_ending: 52.4s. It builds as a linear 5-step follow-along (plus → create → AutoCut → pick media → next → template → post) from 5.0 to 35.5s. The core payoff, 'post the video', lands at 35.48s (about 68%). An 'even further' escalation plugs the Blow Up app from 35.76 to 46.72s (68-89%), shown analysing his own account. The CTA runs 46.72-52.22s: 'If you want more TikTok tips to actually help you grow make sure you follow me because I share them every single day.' The video cuts 0.15s after the last word, with no outro or loop.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps, h264, only 692 kbps, so a soft, compressed re-upload. Medium close-up, centered, from a phone at roughly chest-to-eye height; eyes sit at about 40% of frame height with generous headroom (about 35% above the cap), and that headroom is deliberately left for the title and overlays. Even, soft front light on the face; the background is a sloped-ceiling bedroom with two dartboards and a color-cycling RGB LED strip. The mic sound is clean. It's casual on purpose (cap, T-shirt, bedroom, plain serif captions, even a caption typo), while the effort goes into the annotated screen recordings with circles, arrows and hand pointers, which make it feel like a genuine helpful tutorial rather than a polished ad.
study.why_viral: 1) A massive, specific promise to beginners ('your first video to hit 1 million views… right now'), backed by a siren title, so the exact target audience self-selects in the first 2 seconds. 2) It's an actionable follow-along with real screen recordings and red circles on every button: viewers can do it while watching, and they save and share it as a how-to. 3) It removes all effort and skill ('doesn't matter what they are… holiday photos, walking your dog… it literally doesn't matter'), which makes the promise feel achievable. 4) The non-stop pacing (no gap over 0.18s, a visual change about every 2s, rotating light colors) leaves no exit point before the 'even further' tease, which carries viewers past the main payoff into the app plug and the follow CTA.
lessons: State the outcome in the first sentence and start talking within 0.2s; put the same promise as a bold boxed title with one urgency emoji in the empty headroom for the first ~5s.
Frame the speaker with ~30-35% headroom so titles and UI screenshots can sit above the head without covering the face.
Remove every pause: target a median word gap of ~0s and nothing over 0.2-0.3s, with zero fillers; for tutorials, keep the voice continuous even across cuts.

For step-by-step content, show each step as a floating screen recording over the speaker the moment the step is named (within ~0.3s of the word), and switch the overlay state on the next instruction even if that's mid-sentence.
Mark every tap target with a red circle, arrow or animated hand; move the marker each time the instruction changes (here roughly every 1-3s).
Never let the bare talking head run longer than ~7-10s without an overlay, cut or visual change; aim for some visual change every ~2s.
Add relatable, low-stakes examples ('holiday photos, walking your dog, the gym') right after a step to lower the barrier before the next instruction.
After the main payoff (~65-70% in), add an 'if you want to take things even further' tease to carry viewers into the plug or CTA instead of letting them leave.
End on a reason-based follow CTA ('because I share them every single day') and cut within ~0.15-0.3s of the last word.
When all takes share one framing and there are no punch-ins, a slowly changing background light makes each jump cut feel like a fresh shot.
creator_advice: Tap the plus button at the bottom, find Create and tap it, then look at the top and find AutoCut.
Go to your gallery and choose as many photos or short videos as you want; it doesn't matter what they are, they can be anything: holiday photos, walking your dog, working out at the gym.
Tap next and TikTok will turn all of that into a video; it'll add transitions, cuts and even music.
Keep the trending music TikTok suggests.
Scroll through the templates it gives you, choose the one you like the best, and post the video.
To take things further, use an app called Blow Up: it analyzes your videos and shows you your strengths but also what you need to improve, so your content is easier to understand and performs better.

study.format: Not a talking head: a silent behind-the-scenes POV (business / day-in-the-life style) showing a dessert shop owner photographing a menu item with a phone and an LED light stick. There is no speech, and the last ~95s is unedited dead footage.
study.topic: A gloved worker dusts powdered sugar on a waffle/crepe dessert, shoots it with a phone mounted on a Neewer LED light arm, then pulls the light off the stand and lights the plate by hand while shooting it on the phone.
study.hook: No spoken words: the transcript is empty, so first_word_s is null. At 0.0s the frame is a high, angled POV over the counter. A dark Neewer light bar cuts diagonally across the top half, and a phone clamped to its arm shows a live preview of the dessert. Below it, a white square plate on a cooling rack with a gloved hand shaking a metal sugar duster over the dessert. There is no opening text. The scroll-stopper is purely visual: a 'how I shoot my menu photos' rig plus the satisfying sugar-dusting action. Motion is 25.9 at 0s and peaks at 38.5 around 2.5s as the shaker moves.

beats.what: Sugar duster shakes over the dessert while the phone on the light arm shows the live shot.
Jump cut, same angle slightly closer; the dusting continues for 11.5s in one shot (2.87–14.4) as the sugar builds up.
Wider reveal of the rig: light bar on a stand, phone mount, organizer of toppings behind.
Gloved hand adjusts the light/phone; at 18.2 both hands grab the bar to detach it.
Rapid cuts of 1.0s, 0.83s, 1.77s and 1.23s (23.33–28.17) while the light bar is removed from the stand and turned vertical.
The method: holding the light stick vertically in one hand and the phone in the other, lighting the plate from the side. A 19.1s shot (28.17–47.3) with the phone screen showing the lit dessert.
More angles of the handheld light plus phone shooting from 47.3 to 65.0 (cuts at 48.57, 55.77, 56.53, 57.8); the camera moves around the plate.
Light lowered, wide counter views; the light is set down on the counter around 72s and the phone is checked around 75s.
Short cuts (1.97s, 0.97s, 0.87s) of the counter and plate as the session wraps; the last motion-heavy shot ends at 84.87.
Black screen 84.87–94.47 (motion 0.2–0.8); the camera was covered.
85.8s static upside-down shot from a camera left on a surface: shop ceiling, a branded cup, and the staff walking past. Motion ~1.4–3 with brief spikes. No payoff, no CTA.

study.jump_cuts: No speech, so there are no word gaps, fillers or breaths to measure. The edit is cutting dead handling time out of POV footage. The first 94.47s has 24 cuts, about 2.5 per 10s. Over the full 180.3s that drops to 1.33 per 10s because the final 85.82s shot is uncut. Median shot is 2.33s. Shots range from 0.77s to 19.13s. The tightest run is 23.33–28.17, four cuts in under 5s, during the clumsy job of taking the light off the stand. Cuts fall between actions, not mid-action. The first ~85s feels moderately tight; the black and static tail feels completely untrimmed.
study.zooms_punch_ins: No digital punch-ins or zooms. Before/after frames at each cut show the same handheld POV with natural camera drift, not a scaled crop. At 2.87 the frame sits slightly closer only because the camera moved. Visual change comes from body/camera movement and cuts. Motion runs 20–60 through 0–84s, peaking at 63.7 around 58s. It then drops to near zero.
study.captions: none
study.on_screen_text: none
study.graphics_overlays: none (the only 'screen' is the real phone display showing the live camera preview of the dessert, which is in-camera, not an overlay)
study.transitions: Hard jump cuts only from 0 to 84.87. At 84.87 there is a hard cut to black, and at 94.47 a hard cut to the static upside-down shot. No whips, flashes or zoom transitions.
study.broll_and_interrupts:
The whole video is effectively b-roll; there is no talking A-roll. Interrupts come from action changes:
- sugar dusting (0–14.4)
- rig reveal (14.4)
- hands detaching the light (18.2)
- quick-cut handling burst (23.33–28.17)
- handheld lighting shots (28.17–65)
- wrap-up cuts (78.47–84.87)

Audio peaks at 15.85, 19.41, 22.53, 26.47, 34.78, 41.97, 48.29, 57.64, 66.98, 71.97–73.59 and 80.11–92.72 line up with handling moments. These are likely handling or ambient sounds, not designed SFX. Later peaks (122.66, 123.91, 128.15, 144.58–166.31) fall during the static shot, consistent with shop noise or people moving.
study.audio: No detected speech. The audio data gives only peak times, not music or genre. Peaks clustered around physical actions suggest in-camera ambient and handling sound rather than an added track, though music can't be confirmed or ruled out from what's given. Silence isn't used deliberately.
study.length_and_ending: 180.3s total, but the usable content ends at 84.87s (47%). The clearest payoff, the handheld light-stick technique, arrives at 28.17s (16%) and runs to ~65s (36%). After that comes 9.6s of black (84.87–94.47), then 85.8s of static upside-down footage until the end. No CTA, no loop and no cliffhanger. With no spoken words, there is no last word to measure from.
study.quality: 1552x2064 (3:4, not 9:16), 30.01fps, HEVC at 14,649 kbps: sharp, high-bitrate source. Handheld first-person POV, likely a head or chest mount given the high angle and visible feet and shirt. The LED bar and the bright white kitchen keep it clean and evenly lit. The organized topping drawers make a tidy background. It feels casual and raw on purpose for the first 85s. The black section and the upside-down static tail read as an unedited or accidental recording rather than a stylistic choice.
study.why_viral: 1) A useful, copyable trick for small food businesses: shoot menu photos on a phone, then detach an LED stick and side-light the dish by hand. 2) Satisfying ASMR-style visuals, especially the sugar dusting over 11.5s and the live phone-screen preview proving the result. 3) Authentic behind-the-counter small-business POV. 4) The long dead tail may itself drive comments, rewatches and 'did they forget to stop recording?' engagement, though it hurts completion rate.
lessons: Cut every dead section ruthlessly. This video's last 95s (black plus static) should be removed; end within 1s of the last meaningful action.
Lead with the most satisfying motion in frame at 0.0s (here the sugar dusting). For talking footage, start on the first word, with no setup frames.
Show the proof on screen early: the phone preview of the result is visible from frame one. Put the outcome or 'after' in the first 2s.
Compress clumsy logistics into 0.8–1.3s fragments, as the 23.33–28.17 burst does, instead of letting setup play in real time.
Let the core payoff breathe once it arrives: one 19s shot (28.17–47.3) holds because the technique is the point. Keep longer shots only when the key information is happening.
Silent process footage needs on-screen text. Add a hook title in the first 1s (e.g. 'How we shoot menu photos with a phone') and 3–5 step labels, since there are no words to carry it.
Aim for a visual change every 2–3s (median shot here is 2.33s in the edited part), and never let a frame go static for more than ~5s without motion, text or a cut.
Reframe 3:4 sources to 9:16 so nothing important sits in the cropped area.
Fix orientation. Never ship upside-down or black footage; auto-detect motion under ~3 for over 3s and flag it for removal.
